News.title: US wife of Afghan migrant ‘suitcase killer’ is ‘completely convinced’ he killed Brit – as cops sit on bombshell CCTV
News.content:
THE distraught wife of the Afghan migrant accused of killing a Brit in Athens is “completely convinced” her partner is behind the aid worker’s death.

Alaina Hall, who shares a 16-month-old baby with murder suspect Sharif Ahmadzai, helped Greek cops arrest her husband after her brave testimony revealed crucial new details.



Alaina first met Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, in February 2026 after a volunteering mission for a refugee charity in Athens alongside Ahmadzai.

In her testimony Alaina described Elisabeth as “a very pleasant and sweet person, kind-hearted, with a good soul”.



The American also told cops she was “revolted” by her “very stubborn” husband and firmly believes he is Elisabeth’s killer, police sources told The Sun.

George Kalliakmanis, honorary head of the union of police officers in Greece, said Alaina has decided to stay in Athens with her baby but will have “nothing to do with” Ahmadzai ahead of his murder trial.

Kalliakmanis told The Sun: “She is completely convinced he did it. She has no desire to be mixed up with him.

“She wants nothing to do with him. She is appalled.”



A fellow volunteer added that the American was “never going to give Sharif the time of day again. Her thoughts, now, are with her [Elisabeth].”

During two rounds of questioning by Greek police, Alaina reportedly said: “Sharif is very persistent, very stubborn.

“Even if you put all the evidence, all the hard facts, right in front of him, he never admits anything.”

Police have footage allegedly showing the Afghan boxer transporting the Brit’s body in a suitcase via a cart-trolley, Kalliakmanis said.

He claims the video is unlikely to be released publicly, before adding: “It all boils down to one thing: motive. Why did he murder her, because that is what all the evidence points to.”



The married couple founded the NGO Love Every Nation a few years back but due to the chilling allegations, friends in the volunteer movement believe Alania is considering shutting it down.

Ahmadzai remains holed up in a hellish Greek jail – the notorious Korydallos prison – which is packed to the rafters with terrorists, rapists and murderers.

He is due to stay locked up until his trial which could still take months to begin as investigations continue.



Ahmadzai denies killing Elisabeth, but has confessed to stuffing her body in a suitcase and dumping it in a derelict building five minutes away from the flat where she was staying.

He has insisted he found the Scottish woman dead inside the apartment’s bathroom.

The Christian convert had keys to the flat because it was used as a regular meeting spot for the NGO with his wife.

The Afghan also confessed to withdrawing more than 10,000 euros with her credit cards.

Ahmadzai converted to Christianity within a year of arriving in Greece, but Alaina reportedly started questioning whether it was genuine or whether he had been trying to strengthen his refugee case.



Alaina’s friends believe that Lisa, who was a devout Christian herself, got caught up in the middle of the couple’s difficulties.

One theory is that Alaina may have confided in Lisa about her doubts, before the Brit confronted Ahmadzai and came under attack.

Authorities are still waiting for final toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissue that will determine Elisabeth’s exact cause of death.



Alaina reportedly told cops about her husband after she became suspicious he was involved in Elisabeth’s death.

Shortly after news broke that a woman’s body had been discovered inside a suitcase close to the couple’s home, Alaina recalled waking up with a “terrible” feeling.

In the morning she then texted Elisabeth and got two replies which made her suspicious.

Alaina said: “These messages were not in Lisa’s style, both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used.”

When she tried calling Elisabeth she didn’t get a reply.



Alaina also told police she had grown suspicious of her husband after she woke to find him missing on the evening of July 15.

When she checked his shared location, she saw he was in Elisabeth’s flat.

Having later confronted him, he told her he had been watching a football match but had gone to Elisabeth’s apartment to use the toilet.

She told police: “I don’t know what to tell you, but all of the above made me feel strange.

“Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband’s behaviour, I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable.”

News.title: Luxury £6.8million superyacht SINKS in the Med – just four days after being delivered to new owner
News.content:
A LUXURY £6.8million superyacht has sunk in the Mediterranean just four days after being delivered to its new owner.

Dramatic footage shows the lavish 98ft vessel slowly disappearing beneath the waves before rolling onto its side, leaving just a sliver of the yacht poking above the surface.



The 30m Angiola II remained lying on the seabed, around 23ft below the surface, after a tense rescue operation lasting nearly three hours.

Sinking off Porto Cervo, Sardinia, the multi-million-pound vessel plunged beneath the waves between Cappuccini Island and Capo Ferro.



It had reportedly been handed to its Italian owner just four days earlier following an extensive refit.

Initial reports suggest a terrifying engine failure sparked a fire in the seals before water began pouring into the yacht.



The blaze was quickly extinguished, but the suspected failure may have caused the vessel to lose buoyancy as water flooded in.

However, the exact chain of events behind the dramatic sinking has yet to be officially established.

Fourteen guests and crew were aboard when disaster struck.

Twelve were rescued by a nearby vessel, while the owner and a friend remained aboard the stricken yacht awaiting help.



A La Maddalena Coast Guard patrol boat eventually arrived and took the pair to safety in Poltu Quatu.

Remarkably, no injuries were reported.

The luxury Amer F100 is nearly 30m long and boasted room for up to ten guests across five lavish cabins.



After the rescue, the stricken yacht was secured on the seabed to stop it sinking any further.

Containment booms have also been deployed around the wreck as authorities race to prevent an environmental disaster.

Initial checks found no fuel leaking into the sea.

A huge recovery operation is now being planned, with a pontoon weighing around 200 tonnes reportedly set to haul the wreck from the seabed.

The La Maddalena Port Authority is also preparing measures to force the area to be restored and prevent further environmental damage.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The shock sinking is now under investigation by the Coast Guard, which will attempt to piece together exactly what happened aboard the newly delivered superyacht.

Investigators are yet to establish whether the engine failure triggered the fire, whether the blaze caused the water ingress, or precisely how the yacht ultimately lost buoyancy.

News.title: Huge explosion rocks port in Rotterdam killing at least one and injuring several others during ‘work on pipelines’
News.content:
ONE person has been killed and several others wounded in an explosion in The Netherlands.

The blast took place on a road called Moezelweg in Europoort, a massive, heavily industrialised petrochemical section of the Port of Rotterdam, at around 11.30am.



Six ambulances, a trauma helicopter and fire crews have been deployed to the scene and a number of victims have been taken to hospital.

The cause of the blast is still unclear and is currently being investigated, a spokesperson for the Rotterdam Police said.



A hired maintenance crew had been working on a number of pipelines at the Gunvor Energy refinery and storage site shortly before the incident.

A spokesperson told Dutch broadcaster Rijnmond that something may have gone wrong during the disconnection of those pipelines.

“We are cooperating with local authorities,” they added.

Pictures circulated on social media showed visible traces of the explosion on a storage tank.



“An explosion took place on the Moezelweg around 11.30am, a statement from the police said. “We are investigating how this happened.

“A crime scene has been established and the labor inspectorate is also arriving on site. Several people were injured in the explosion and one person has died.“

The incident happened about two hours after emergency crews were also deployed to another major incident in the port.



A Grip 2 emergency, the second level of a crisis management protocol used in the Netherlands, was declared at a refinery on Botlekweg due to a power outage.

The facility has since halted production as a precaution.

The Port of Rotterdam is home to a number of oil and gas companies, so fire crews were standing by.

It is the largest seaport in Europe and the 11th busiest in the world by cargo tonnage.

News.title: How fake pregnancy spiralled into horror newborn kidnap plot after desperate mum-to-be suffers 3 traumatic miscarriages
News.content:
ON THEIR wedding day, they danced joyously to “their special song”, Unchained Melody, as family and friends cheered them on.

Nine years later, Eleonor Alejandra Mendoza and her husband Arturo, unexpectedly heard it played again, but his time while they were in the back of a police car after having been arrested for the kidnapping of a baby.



The extraordinary story of how a young Mexican woman felt such pressure to give birth in a country where family is everything, that she concocted an elaborate plan to fake her pregnancy, is told in the Netflix documentary A Child of My Own.

What starts as an elaborate lie turned into a complex charade that threatened to upend her life and relationship, and ultimately unleashed a media scandal that shook the country.



“I was drawn into problems that got bigger and bigger,” says Ale.

“And I started making decisions and taking actions which got more complicated, until there was no way out. No turning back.”



The documentary is told in an imaginative way by Oscar-nominated director, Maite Alberdi, in which the first half plays out like a drama with actors in the roles of the principal characters in an extended flashback, while the second half features interviews with Alejandra and Arturo, explaining their actions first-hand.

The pair married in July 2000 when Eleonor, known as Ale, was just 17.



“I was pregnant and that’s part of the reason we got married then but I also loved Arturo,” she says.

“I always dreamed of being a mum and I was full of hope.

“I have a large family. All my cousins are mums. I felt like it was fulfilling my dream by having a family of my own.

“When I got married, I felt pressured to please Arturo’s family. I didn’t feel accepted by his mum and that made me want to do everything I could to win her over.”

Ale was devasted when she miscarried while living with her in-laws and felt the “blame” lying heavily on her shoulders.



“I was crying in my bedroom, not wanting to see anyone but they came up to my room.

“One of Arturo’s aunts said, ‘Why are you crying? We all go through this.’ Then his mum said, ‘You should have been more careful. You can’t behave like that.’”

While family continued to talk about them having kids soon, Ale felt the pressure increasing.



“Soon after that first miscarriage, I was pregnant again.

“Arturo would tell me, ‘You have to be careful. Don’t do this, don’t do that.’

“Then I had a second miscarriage. After a few years we started to worry when I didn’t get pregnant.”

Following fertility treatment, she fell pregnant again in 2009, but while working at The General Hospital in Mexico City as an administrative assistant, she had another miscarriage.

It was then, she says, that she met a young woman called Mayra Navarro Vega who was there because she wanted to have an abortion.



“Mayra told me she already had a baby girl from a different father and that her mum would kick her out of the home if she had another.

“She also said the father wasn’t accepting any responsibility, because he didn’t believe the baby wasn’t his.

“Then she said, ‘I’d rather give it away than throw it away.’ I asked her if she was serious, and she said, ‘Yes.’”

The pair then agreed an audacious deal to secretly give the baby to Ale.

“When I got home, I decided I wouldn’t tell anyone that I had lost the baby, especially not Arturo. I didn’t want anyone saying it was my fault, again.”



Instead, she began eating lots of calorific food to put on “pregnancy weight” month by month, going from 119 pounds to 143, 176, all the way to 216.

“My tummy really looked like I was pregnant and I felt so special because people close to you start treating you so lovingly and come up and touch your belly so sweetly.”

Mayra told her that the due date was the week of 16 June, and that the doctors thought it was a girl.

While working in the hospital, Ale looked at the ultrasound Mayra had of her baby and brought a picture of it home to show the family.

Arturo was happy, even though he wanted a baby boy.



When his mum told Ale that she didn’t look like she was carrying a girl, Ale replied that doctors should know better than old wives’ tales of being able to tell the sex from the shape of a woman’s belly.

On a shopping trip with Arturo to buy maternity clothes, she mentioned a baby that her friend was adopting and became upset when Arturo said that he could never adopt because it’s not the same as flesh and blood.

Ale tried to put on a happy face at a baby shower for family and friends but she was feeling the strain of her lie.

“It was awful, seeing everybody happy, my parents, my family, my grandma. I wanted someone to burst that balloon of lies. To spill everything out.”

It was when she was unable to stop Arturo from accompanying her to a doctor for a medical in order to get her maternity leave, that she thought the truth would be revealed.



As Arturo sat in the room, she told the doctor that she was 38 weeks gone.

Then came the moment she was dreading, as he listened to the baby’s heartbeat but couldn’t hear one.

Thinking it was the fault of the device he was using, the doctor went and got an old-fashioned type, and this time, to her disbelief, he said he could hear the baby.

“The doctor gave me my 90 days of maternity leave. I was thinking, ‘Am I pregnant? I lost it, didn’t I? Did I get pregnant again?’ Too much was messed up in my head.”

When Mayra gave birth, Ale pretended to the hospital that she was her neighbour and wanted to see her.



In the ward, Mayra had a fever but pointed to the baby and said the deal was still in place.

“I was holding the baby, when around two or three in the afternoon, a man arrived. He turned out to the be the baby’s father and he took the baby from me and held her.”

Ale walked out and returned later, after visiting hours ended, and says that Mayra was getting dressed to leave.

“I said, ‘You can’t leave me here with her. We have to do this right,’ but Mayra replied, “I did my part. Take the baby.”

Ale put the tiny four and a half pounds tot in a shopping bag and walked out of the hospital. This was later found to have been captured on CCTV camera, which is shown in the documentary.



Outside, she was startled by her husband arriving, who asked her what she was doing. Ale got in the car, with the baby still in the bag, and confessed to what she had done.

Stunned, he angrily ordered her out of the car, telling her to give the baby back.

But he eventually relented and she got back in and they booked into a hotel for the night to talk things over.

Here, Arturo asked her what the plan was going to be. She explained, “Mayra was going to be discharged tomorrow morning. I was going to pretend to be her relative to expediate things.

“By the time you got to the hospital, I’d have the baby, and the paperwork.”



Still angry and shouting, he eventually calmed down enough to hold the baby, telling her, “You’ll be happy with us.”

The three of them fell asleep on the bed, until they were awoken by the police pounding on the door.

They took the baby away and arrested the pair for kidnap, while Ale screamed that the baby had been given to her.

“We were in the police car when on the radio they started playing Unchained Melody, the song we danced to at our wedding,” she recalls.

“It was our special song and, at that moment, I thought, it was a sign. We love each other. We’ll be okay.”



That was Ale’s story and she has stuck by it ever since.

However, Mayra and the baby’s father firmly dispute this and say that their baby, Katya, was simply kidnapped.

A court found Ale guilty of kidnapping and she was given a 13-year prison sentence.

Arturo was locked up for two and a half years until the end of the trial when he was acquitted.

“At the time I felt that Ale had done something unforgivable and that she was evil and I didn’t want to see her again,” says Arturo.



“But being in jail gives you a lot of time to think things over. I reflected on where I might have failed as a partner.

“When I said, ‘I don’t want to adopt, I want a child of my flesh and blood,’ maybe I contributed to closing myself off in that way.

“I admit I did push her a bit, because I wanted to be a dad and I wanted to have a son.”

Once released, he started writing to his wife in prison saying that he forgave her and that he loved her with all his heart.

In the documentary, Mayra gives her side of the story.



“There was never a deal,” she says.

“I didn’t meet her until Katya was born. I only went to the hospital to give birth.

“I had my pregnancy check-ups in another health facility, so I never got to see Ale any earlier.”

Documents confirmed this.

Mayra had not been at the hospital until a few weeks before she gave birth.



“When I was in the hospital, Ale wandered over and showed me her hospital ID badge and said she was doing a survey and she asked me questions like, Was this my first baby? Was she from the same marriage? How was my relationship with her dad?

“That’s where she got all the information.”

Ale denies this but a folder with surveys inside was found beside her jumper and ID badge at the hospital.

There is also footage taken by Katya’s father on his phone, of him tenderly holding his new-born daughter in hospital and talking sweetly to her.

“I had a fever of almost 104F,” says Mayra.



“I couldn’t be discharged because I had an infection. I was asked for urine samples so I left the room and when I returned, my baby was gone.

“My first thought was that maybe a nurse had taken her for a bath or to feed her.

“I never thought she had been stolen.”

The documentary shows Ale being released from prison, having served her sentence, and being reunited with Arturo, who tells her, “It’s over, my love.”

But in a further twist, his yearning to have a son, caused them to part – temporarily.



“Soon after leaving prison, Arturo told me he still wanted to be a dad,” explains Ale.

“I replied that he had the right to pursue his happiness but that I wasn’t willing to undergo any treatment, and with me, he wasn’t going to be a dad.

“We were separated for a while, we gave each other space, and he had a short relationship with another woman and a son was born.

“After that, Arturo came back looking for me.

“We talked and he told me what had happened.



“He said that he missed me, that he loved me, and that he wanted me in his life.

“He asked me to try again and I decided to do so.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It makes me happy to see him fulfilled as a father.

“But even more, it makes me happy that he sees me in his life as the other parent figure of his child.”

News.title: Dangerous criminals including sex offenders are released daily, top cop warns – after blunders left killer free to roam
News.content:
DANGEROUS criminals including vile sex offenders are being released on bail every day, Britain’s top cop has warned.

Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley admitted his force “could have done better” after serial killer Simon Levy was allowed to roam the streets.



Levy, 40, unleashed a sadistic rampage across London last year during which he murdered two women and raped a third while on bail.

He was jailed for life yesterday after killing Carmenza Valencia Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, amid a string of missed chances to stop him.



Two officers, a police constable and a detective sergeant at the Met are now being probed by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

While accepting his force’s failings in the case, Rowley slammed the justice system for putting dangerous lags “back on the streets”.



He vowed the Met would do “everything we can do”, but accused the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) of ignoring police warnings over Levy.

Rowley told BBC’s Today programme: “He was repeatedly, by the police, put before the courts seeking remanding in custody.



“The police were saying this guy is too dangerous to be on the streets, and between [the CPS] and the courts, they kept bailing him.

“We’re seeing far too many cases day in and day out – knife carriers, sex offenders – who are being bailed.

“A few years ago, they would have been remanded in custody, and we can’t carry all of that load in communities.

“We will do everything we can do to do better – but the justice system needs to carry more of the load than it is at the moment rather than passing it back onto the streets.”

Rowley described the situation as a “whole system failing”, after Levy was previously jailed for groping two women at music festivals in 2018.



He was caged for three years in September 2021 over the attacks, but was released from prison in February 2023.

Levy was subject to a sexual offenders’ order and should have been carefully monitored – but was instead left free to kill and assault.

The killer remained free to strike repeatedly, despite continually coming to the attention of the law.



Following his release from jail, Levy was arrested on suspicion of murder and twice charged with groping women on the Tube, but freed each time.

He also failed to appear at three crown court hearings over the sexual assaults on trains – but no warrant was ever sought for his arrest.

Levy killed Carmenza, before dumping her body in the stairwell of a derelict building in Peckham, South East London, on March 17 last year.

Five months later, he murdered Sheryl near a B&M store in Tottenham, North London.

The Met had previously closed the investigation from the January rape, despite the victim knowing where Levy lived.



And officers did not formally interview her until after he had carried out the double murder.

By the time of the second murder, Levy had been arrested three times by the British Transport Police for a string of sex attacks on the Tube.

But the serial sex attacker was granted bail each time.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He was also arrested over Carmenza’s murder but was released under investigation – leaving him free to kill again.

The Metropolitan Police, British Transport Police and Crown Prosecution Service admitted failings in how they dealt with Levy.

News.title: When will the A31 open? What National Highways has said after New Forest fire closed major road
News.content:
THE A31 has been closed all week after a van fire spread into the nearby New Forest.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) received more than 160 emergency calls reporting a vehicle fire on the eastbound A31 at around 5:24pm on Sunday August 9.



The flames spread to the central reservation before reaching heathland that forms part of the New Forest.

The road has remained since Sunday, causing lengthy diversions and delays for drivers – here’s what we know about when it will reopen.



When will the A31 open?

According to National Highways, the A31 is unlikely to re-open until at least Thursday, August 20, due to ongoing repair works.

A statement from HIWFRS read: “Alongside colleagues from other fire services, we have been using various different techniques to support firefighting efforts, including mulching and tree felling.

“Specialists in a technique known has backburning have been brought in to purposefully burn away strips of heathland, in a controlled way, in order to remove available fuels, creating a fire break which helps to prevent the blaze from spreading further.”

Repair works will only get underway once National Highways have been given clearance from the HIWFRS to access the area.

The statement continued: “Wind is blowing smoke from the fire into the direction of Roger Penny Way, so we ask that you drive with caution in that particular area.

“Our teams continue to make good progress, but we still expect to be on the scene for the next few days, with the A31 remaining closed.”



Due to the road closure, drivers are being advised to allow extra time for their journeys while ensuring they have enough fuel and water.

An area spanning roughly 1.6 kilometres has been affected by the fire, meaning repairs are required on 1,000 metres of boundary fencing.

What is the A31 diversion route?

National Highways has urged drivers not to follow their satnavs and to use the official local diversion instead.

It has also asked motorists to stick to speed limits on local roads and watch out for the New Forest’s livestock, which roams freely.

Westbound motorists should leave the M27 at junction 2 (Ower Interchange) and use the A326 and A35 through Ashurst, Lyndhurst, Allum Green, Hinton Admiral and Christchurch.



At the Iford roundabout they should take the third exit onto the A3060, then the third exit at the Cooper Dean roundabout onto the A338, travelling north to rejoin the A31 at Ashley Heath.

Eastbound drivers should leave the A31 at the Ashley Heath roundabout onto the A338 and continue south towards Bournemouth.

At the Cooper Dean roundabout they should take the first exit onto the A3060, then the first exit at the Iford roundabout onto the A35 through Christchurch, Hinton Admiral, Allum Green, Lyndhurst and Ashurst, before heading north on the A326 to rejoin the M27 at junction 2.

News.title: Tragic details revealed after boy, 7, drowned alongside hero cousin, 15, and her mum on family holiday to seaside
News.content:
BEACH TRAGEDY Tragic details revealed after boy, 7, drowned alongside hero cousin, 15, and her mum on family holiday to seaside

A YOUNG boy who drowned alongside his 15-year-old cousin and her mum on a family holiday suffered a fatal brain injury, an inquest heard.

Musa Ahmed, seven, died in hospital six days after getting into difficulty in the water in West Mersea, Essex, on July 22.



His cousin Sameeha Rahman, 15, and her mother Shelina Rahman, 41, also died in the horror.

An inquest heard today the trio had been on a family holiday at the time of the triple tragedy.



Musa was brought to the shore, stabilised and then flown to the Royal London Hospital, Chelmsford County Hall was told.

Post-mortem examinations gave a provisional cause of death as drowning for all three.



For Musa, hypoxic ischaemic brain injury was also recorded as a provisional cause of death.

Senior coroner for Essex Lincoln Brookes said: “Clearly it is so tragic to come across any death of any individual but when three occur at the same time and of the same family, one cannot underestimate the tragic nature of such an incident.”



Mr Brookes offered his “deepest condolences” to the family, friends and loved ones of the victims.

The coroner adjourned the inquest to January 19, 2027.

Musa, Sameeha and Shelina were among a group of five relatives who were caught up in the horror close to the Sea View Holiday Park.

It is understood the mum and daughter sprang into action in a desperate bid to save Musa from the tide when they got into difficulty themselves.

The dad of the daughter and wife, Dr Mansur Rahman, 49, previously told The Sun he was still suffering from shock and is “fighting to overcome” the tragedy.



He added: “I lost my daughter I lost my wife. Please pray for them.”

In a statement, the boy’s family said: “We would also like to thank the Royal London Hospital intensive care unit team of doctors and nurses who demonstrated outstanding care and dignity for whilst we have been at the hospital.

“We would also like to thank the whole community for their support and prayers.

“We would appreciate privacy during this very difficult time.”

Essex Police have asked anyone who was in the area at the time and has information or footage which could assist their investigation to contact them on 101 and quote incident 1090 of 22 July.

News.title: Terrifying blaze guts FIVE homes as 20 residents evacuated in dead of night and 12 crews battle huge inferno
News.content:
BUNGALOW INFERNO Terrifying blaze guts FIVE homes as 20 residents evacuated in dead of night and 12 crews battle huge inferno

A TERRIFYING blaze has gutted five homes with 20 residents evacuated in the dead of night as fire crews battle the flames.

There were scenes of carnage in Newbridge, South Wales, on Wednesday with the homes left completely devastated.



The inferno ripped through six neighbouring bungalows, completely destroying at least five homes on Hazelwood Road in Pantside.

Shocking images show their charred wreckage as the properties were reduced to burnt-out shells with families’ belongings turned to ash.



Their gardens were also scorched with overhead photos showing a scorched landscape from above.

Fire crews descended on the scene yesterday afternoon with locals urged to stay away and keep their windows and doors shut due to smoke.

Around 20 people were supported at temporary accommodation or Newbridge Leisure Centre overnight.

By about 2.30am, all those affected had been checked into a Premier Inn.



The council said it will work with affected families today to arrange longer-term temporary accommodation, while structural engineers assess the damaged properties.

No casualties have been reported and the cause of the fire has yet to be determined.

Fire crews remain at the scene with plumes of smoke still pouring from the wreckage.

Local councillor, Adrian Hussey, told the BBC the houses were absolutely “gutted” with residents’ cars also damaged in the blaze.

He added that residents had attempted to put the fire out themselves but were beaten back by flames.



Julie Nichols, 74, told the broadcaster how she could hear the flames from inside her home and was left in “absolute fear”.

“We were sat in the leisure centre and there were a few people that had actually lost their homes,” she said.

“They were being so brave, I mean to lose everything.”

Newbridge RFC said they were “absolutely heartbroken” in a message on social media and said their clubhouse was open to those affected.

A fundraising page has also been set up by a local resident which said: “There’s a number family’s in Pantside that’s lost everything due to a massive fire that’s spread throughout their homes & gardens.



“As a community I’m praying we can get some sort of fund together to go towards anything they may need. Money isn’t everything but right now any little helps.”

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service said in a statement on Wednesday: “Shortly before 16:00 today, crews were deployed to the scene and a number of resources have been mobilised, including 12 fire appliances, two water bowsers, and an aerial ladder platform.

“Members of the public are urged to stay away from the area to allow emergency services to operate safely and to avoid flying drones, as they can disrupt incident operations.

“Due to smoke in the area, residents are advised to keep windows and doors closed and follow public health advice.”

News.title: Water bills set to rise for many after firms permitted extra funding
News.content:
Water companies have been given the green light to increase bills for customers by an extra Â£3.4bn in coming years to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Nearly a third of the extra funding provisionally approved for 13 water companies in England and Wales is earmarked for making sure water services are maintained.

Some of the rest will be used to meet rising demand from housebuilding and data centres and to address pollutants known as "forever chemicals".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the proposal was "real money out of family budgets at a time when they are struggling with the cost of living", and an environmental group described the decision as "an insult".

The regulator, Ofwat, said the extra spending would enable the firms to support growth and better environmental outcomes, and ensure important upgrades were not delayed.

"We will track performance to ensure companies are delivering the expected improvements for customers and the environment," said Helen Campbell, executive director for delivery at Ofwat.

"If they don't, expenditure can be clawed back."

Water companies need approval from the regulator, Ofwat, to raise customers' bills, a process that takes place every five years to set spending budgets for the years ahead.

This decision to allow increased charges comes on top of already-agreed bill rises that were negotiated with the water companies in 2024.

The process allows firms to apply for additional funds for projects that were not known about at the time of the last review.

As part of the outlined increase, Ofwat has approved funding for schemes including provision for new data centres in Manchester, additional wastewater capacity in Newquay and to bring forward work by Wessex Water to tackle PFAS pollutants, originally planned for 2030-35.

However, the decision is provisional. There is a period of public consultation, with a final decision due in December.

Some of the additional spending would be recovered through customer bills before the end of this decade, some would come after 2030.

Bills will rise for customers of five of the 13 water companies before 2030: customers of Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Thames Water, Wessex Water, and South East Water will experience price rises of Â£1 to Â£43 in the 2027/28 and 2029/30 financial years.

Ofwat said water companies had submitted a total of Â£4.3bn worth of requests, but some of their proposed extra spending had been rejected.

Burnham said he understood why people were angry as they had been asked to pay more for years while pollution incidents and leaks continued.

"Where water companies seek to pass unnecessary costs onto households, they will be challenged," he said.

Amy Fairman, from campaign group River Action, said: "Ofwat waving through yet more water bill hikes is an insult."

Water companies had failed to make sufficient investment over the last 30 years, she said, leaving customers with "leaks, pollution and soaring bills".

There should be greater public control of water companies, she added. "No more blank cheques for failure."

News.title: Man, 102, dies after alleged pub assault
News.content:
A 102-year-old man has died after allegedly being assaulted at a south Wales pub.

Phillip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following the incident at the Crow's Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

Gwent Police confirmed on Thursday that he had since died.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains under investigation.

Emergency services were called to the pub at about 22:25 BST following a report of an assault.

Det Ch Insp Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said: "We understand the public interest in this incident but want to remind people that, not only is this an active criminal investigation, but there is a family at the heart of it processing the loss of a loved one."

She urged people to "consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments" including "online commentary" could have.

The force is urging anyone who was at the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 on the night of the incident to contact them.

News.title: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes by looking at the eclipse
News.content:
Eye experts are warning people to be on the alert for any signs their vision has been damaged by looking at the sun during Wednesday's eclipse.

The symptoms can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot and increased sensitivity to light.

After the previous total eclipse of the sun that was visible in the UK in 1999, around 70 people were left with damaged sight.

Many of them had spent less than a minute looking at the spectacle, without realising they were harming their eyes.

The danger comes because staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

The sun is incredibly bright, even when partially obscured by the moon.

Normally if we stare at it, we wince and quickly look away.

But when it is darker, during an eclipse, that instinct may not kick in, even while our eyes are being damaged.

The bright light and ultraviolet radiation given off by the sun can lead to a condition known as "solar retinopathy".

And because the retina has no pain receptors, it's hard for people to notice the damage as it happens, so symptoms may only appear several hours later.

Leading up to the eclipse itself, experts were warning only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

News.title: Watch: Key moments from Karoline Leavitt's White House tenure as Trump says she will leave post
News.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her role at the end of August to spend time with her young children and family, after welcoming her second child in May.

"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," President Donald Trump wrote in a social media post announcing her departure.

Leavitt became the youngest press secretary in the country's history when she took the job in January 2025 at age 27.

News.title: Harvey Nichols bought by Sports Direct owner
News.content:
Luxury department store Harvey Nichols has been bought by the owners of Sports Direct.

Mike Ashley's Frasers Group will take control of the six Harvey Nichols stores, including its flagship in Knightsbridge, as well as the international franchise.

It will also acquire the online business, and stores will continue to operate under their existing licensing.

Harvey Nichols, immortalised in BBC sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has over 1,000 employees. Its other stores are located in Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

Earlier this week, it warned in its latest accounts that it would need to "cease trading" within a year if it failed to secure new investment.

The luxury store, founded in 1831, had appointed an administrator in June.

Frasers Group's chief executive Michael Murray said: "Harvey Nichols is an iconic British institution with significant potential, but it is clear meaningful change is needed.

"The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term."

Its restaurant in the Oxo Tower, London is being sold off separately and is not included in the deal.

Julia Goddard, Harvey Nichols chief executive said today marked "an important milestone" for the company and "provides a strong platform for the next phase of the business's evolution".

"Over the past year, we have made significant progress in repositioning this iconic business, investing in our flagship store, broadening our customer proposition, and strengthening the brand DNA," she added.

News.title: Heatwaves drive A&E attendances up to record high
News.content:
England's A&Es are experiencing their busiest period ever, with the record-breaking heat cited as a key factor.

More than 2.4 million patients attended emergency departments each month for May, June and July â the three highest monthly totals recorded in history.

NHS bosses say the pressure has been as bad as it is in winter months. The extreme heat has caused people to fall ill with dehydration and heatstroke, and has increased the risk of complications for those with heart, kidney and respiratory problems.

It comes as unions warn staff are being forced to work in inhumane conditions because of the heat, with reports of some collapsing and others having seizures.

The problems have been further complicated by equipment, including scanners and IT systems, breaking down.

NHS medical director Prof Frankie Swords praised the "outstanding professionalism" of staff and said the situation was making delivering care challenging.

She advised: "With temperatures peaking today, please take sensible precautions to stay safe - keep hydrated, avoid the sun during the hottest part of the day, especially if you are clinically vulnerable, and check in on older or vulnerable friends, relatives and neighbours."

News.title: Met chief accepts mistakes made over Simon Levy but defends investigation into murders
News.content:
The head of the Metropolitan Police Sir Mark Rowley has defended the force's investigation into double murderer Simon Levy.

Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later, as well as violently raping a third woman.

Sir Mark acknowledged mistakes over the force's handling of Levy, but said suggestions it had not tried to build a case over his first murder were "just not true", following criticism including from Labour MP Jess Phillips.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that detectives had done "serious" work but "didn't have enough evidence" for a charge.

The Met did not seek a charging decision from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) over Valencia-Trujillo's murder until after Wilkins had been killed.

The police and CPS has apologised over a series of decisions that left the convicted sex offender free to attack the women.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is currently examining how Levy, 40, was managed over the four-year period from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, he was given a whole life prison sentence, meaning he will never be released.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark - who on Wednesday called the case a "whole system failing" - said he had already apologised for what the Met had got wrong.

It emerged after Levy's conviction that the Met did not class Valencia-Trujillo's death in March 2025 as a murder, or pass the case to specialist homicide detectives, until after he had killed again.

Sir Mark said "the public debate needs to be better informed" because "the facts on that are much more complex than people want to acknowledge".

He said that while Valencia-Trujillo's death was "clearly very suspicious and concerning", a pathologist was unable to determine a cause of death and the force "didn't have enough evidence to get to a charge".

Sir Mark added it was only after the murder of Wilkins that the Met had the "combined evidence" to move forward.

"So the inference that the Met didn't try on that case is just not true, the Met tried," he said.

However, the Met did not ask the CPS for advice about Valencia-Trujillo's death, let alone a charging decision, until after the murder of Wilkins, the BBC has previously reported.

The fact there was no formal cause of death would not have prevented the case being taken on by specialist homicide detectives, who are skilled at building murder cases even when there is not a formal cause of death.

Levy's semen was on Valencia-Trujillo and his blood was at the murder scene. CCTV that showed Levy in the area, walking in the same direction as Valencia-Trujillo shortly after she passed a camera, was not viewed by the local team despite being gathered.

Other possible relevant CCTV was never gathered, and had been deleted by the time the specialist murder team took over months later.

In that case, the local team investigating the death did not engage with the Met's specialist murder teams apart from the day her body was discovered in March 2025.

A specialist homicide team attended the crime scene that day and recommended the case stay with local officers pending further enquiries, but there was no further contact until after Wilkins was murdered in August.

News.title: Voting under way in Clacton by-election
News.content:
Voting is under way in the Clacton by-election as a record number of candidates vie to become its next MP.

Fifty-one polling stations in the Essex resort, which includes the towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze, opened at 07:00 BST and will shut at 22:00.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
News.content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.

The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.

Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.

The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.

Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant failings
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: Farm show bans cattle and sheep amid outbreak
News.content:
Some 353 cases of bluetongue serotype 3 (BTV3) have been recorded in the UK in the 2026/27 season - most of them in the south-west of England.

The virus is spread by insects and is generally found in cattle, sheep and goats. It does not affect people or food safety but it causes a high rate of death in infected sheep and fertility problems in infected cattle.

Barrow said the team had been working closely with vets ahead of the show.

"We've worked through lots of different scenarios as to ways that we could keep the cattle and sheep and goat sections going, such as only bringing vaccinated sheep or putting on a really reduced, very local show.

"But, we thought because the situation is ever-changing and the volume of cases was just increasing exponentially, that the best thing for us to do for this year was to withdraw our cattle sheep in eight sections."

"We felt because we have a big cattle and sheep section, that bringing people in from quite far out of area, just wouldn't have been the best thing for us to do while it's still a new and emerging situation, and we're still learning all about it," she added.

Organisers of the Launceston Agricultural Show took the same decision in July regarding cattle and sheep.

News.title: Residents' 'absolute fear' as massive fire destroyed their homes
News.content:
People preparing to watch the eclipse were instead witness to a massive fire that destroyed homes and left 20 people evacuated to a leisure centre, a councillor in south Wales has said.

There are no reports of casualties, but six bungalows were evacuated near Hazelwood Road, Newbridge, in Caerphilly county, on Wednesday.

"Everyone was getting ready yesterday to witness the eclipse, and for this to happen last night was a total shock," said councillor Gary Johnston.

Julia Nichols, 74, was one of the people evacuated from her home and said the fire left her in "absolute fear".

News.title: Three teenagers guilty of man's murder and robbery
News.content:
Three teenagers on a violent mission "to obtain money or drugs" have been found guilty of murdering a man.

The body of David Cuthbert, 49, was discovered with stab wounds at a house in Egglescliffe Close, in Stockton, on 10 January.

Layton Lightfoot and Jesse Reaney, both 18, and Charlie Wilcock, 19, were convicted of murder and robbery following a trial at Teesside Crown Court on Wednesday.

Lightfoot, of Stockwith Close in Middlesbrough, Reaney, of Lowthian Road in Hartlepool, and Wilcock, of no fixed address, are due to be sentenced on 27 November.

Det Supt Daryll Tomlinson, of Cleveland Police, said the three defendants were "heavily involved in criminality" and had sought to "assert their authority" and "brazenly brag about their violence to those online".

He said: "[They] were on a mission that day to use violence through the use of weapons to obtain money or drugs from those living within the community."

News.title: Man jailed over one-punch death after pub row
News.content:
A man who fatally punched a fellow regular at a pub in a row over a phone charger has been jailed for five years after being convicted of manslaughter.

Harry Mannion, 28, punched 62-year-old Tony Powles to the ground during a row at the Red Lion on Batley Road in Wakefield on 9 October.

Powles, a father-of-four who was due to marry his partner the following week, suffered a "catastrophic brain injury" when he hit his head on the floor and died 13 days later, Leeds Crown Court heard.

In a victim impact statement, his daughter Rebecca Powles described him as the "absolute pillar of our family", adding: "He had so many friends and was loved by absolutely everyone who knew him."

Rebecca Powles said the family had been "forced to suffer beyond the boundaries of normal grief", telling the court: "We will never, ever forget having to make the excruciating decision to turn off his life support."

Mannion, himself a father of a five-year-old daughter, had denied manslaughter - claiming to have acted in self-defence - but was found guilty following a trial in June.

The court heard how the pair were both regulars at the Red Lion and had been "pub friends".

At the time Mannion, from Barnsley, was in a relationship with the pub's manager, while Powles had gone there that evening with his family.

Tensions arose when the defendant "took a dim view" of one of Powles's daughters serving behind the bar as part of her training to work there, prosecutor Matthew Harding said.

Later, Mannion was said to have taken exception to Powles's sister, Linda Wilson, using a phone charger belonging to him which had been behind the bar.

An argument ensued and Wilson left the bar.

When Powles found out about the disagreement, CCTV footage showed him approach Mannion at the bar, "when words were exchanged", said Judge Simon Phillips KC.

Powles then threw the charger, catching Mannion on the side of his head, before headbutting him.

About a minute later, when Powles was being restrained with his hands by his side, Mannion "threw a forceful punch at [the victim's] head", Judge Phillips said.

"This was retaliation from you, done in drink, from what had gone on moments before," Judge Phillips told the defendant, who appeared in court via video link from HMP Leeds.

News.title: Man dies days after explosion at bungalow
News.content:
A man has died in hospital days after a suspected gas explosion at a bungalow.

The blast, which happened at 09:45 BST on Sunday, destroyed the home on Cobb Hall Road in Newton Longville, a village near Milton Keynes.

Thames Valley Police said a man in his 60s was taken to hospital where he was receiving treatment for his injuries. His death was announced on Thursday.

He has been named as Steve Woodward in a tribute post by Newton Longville Parish Council and in a fundraising page set up in the aftermath of the explosion.

More from Beds, Herts and Bucks

Det Insp Philip Turner-Robson said: "This is a tragic development and our thoughts are with the man's family and friends at this extremely difficult time.

"Thames Valley Police is managing a coronial investigation into the circumstances surrounding the explosion and collapse of the property, working jointly with the Health and Safety Executive.

"Our inquiries remain ongoing as we seek to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

News.title: Arrest in Thetford migrant address sharing investigation
News.content:
Police have arrested a man as part of an inquiry into how the addresses of asylum seekers were shared during disorder linked to anti-immigration protests in a town, the BBC can reveal.

Properties in St John's Way, Bracken Road, Clover Way, Elm Road and Chester Way in Thetford, Norfolk, were recently targeted by crowds over three nights.

The man, in his 60s, was arrested on Friday on suspicion of assisting an offender and inciting racial hatred and has been released on bail until 14 October.

The houses are believed to have been used by Serco, a firm contracted to accommodate migrants, which said it was investigating allegations "relating to how address information has been made public".

The firm added it was working with the Home Office and Norfolk Police "to ensure that appropriate safeguarding measures are in place".

After his arrest, the man in his 60s was taken to Wymondham Police Investigation Centre for questioning.

News.title: Transfer news LIVE: Chelsea set Enzo Fernandez deadline, Barcola to Liverpool latest, Konsa to Arsenal
News.content:
Chelsea have told Manchester City that they have until Friday to submit a bid for midfielder Enzo Fernandez. The Blues have informed their Premier League rivals that they will need to sepnd £120m to sign the World Cup runner-up. City, meanwhile, remain in talks with Barcelona over Rodri, who is available for £60m, and are also interested in the signing of World Cup breakout star Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille. Winger Savinho is moving closer to leaving the Etihad for Tottenham in a £65m deal though.

Mikel Arteta has said that Arsenal’s business is not done yet, with the Gunners receiving interest in Gabriel Martinelli from Galatasaray as well as Chelsea and Manchester United reportedly turning down the chance to sign Myles Lewis-Skelly. Arsenal have set their sights high and are interested in adding a marquee signing: they will have to play the long game in moves for Atletico Madrid’s Julian Alvarez and Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola.

Barcola also leads Liverpool’s list of transfer targets and the Reds are in talks with PSG over a fee, though the European champions are demanding £145m to sell the winger. PSG chairman Nasser Al-Khelaifi did not rule out a move for Barcola, however, saying: “We’re working calmly, we don’t talk too much. I can’t say whether he will leave or not. Today, he is a PSG player. We’ll see.”

News.content:

Andy Burnham has accused water companies of treating customers like a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures” and said he is “angry” at the proposal to raise household bills.

Troubled Thames Water is among five water companies that have received provisional approval from the industry regulator to raise household bills further for millions of households under plans allowing suppliers an additional £3.4bn in spending.

In its draft determination, Ofwat stated that five out of 13 providers across England and Wales will be permitted to increase tariffs.

The prime minister said: “I understand why people are angry – I am too.

“The truth is customers have been asked to pay more for years, yet serious pollution incidents are at record levels and the pipes are still leaking.

“None of which is the billpayer’s fault, who should not be treated as a bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures.”

open image in gallery Thames Water personnel handing out bottled water to residents at Roding Sports Centre in Chigwell, Essex, following a water main burst on Chigwell Road in South Woodford ( PA )

He added: “Customers cannot be treated as a blank cheque. Where water companies seek to pass unnecessary costs onto households, they will be challenged.

“Our water industry has clearly not been working for people for far too long. That’s why this Government will be looking at how we can give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible.”

The extra funding, to be deployed by 2030, is intended to modernise infrastructure to cope with new housing developments and data centres, as well as target forever chemicals to safeguard drinking water supplies.

Financially burdened Thames Water is among the firms provisionally cleared to raise prices between 2027 and 2030, alongside Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Wessex Water and South East Water.

It will likely stoke further anger, with the water sector repeatedly under fire over rising bills at a time of poor performance for sewage spills, water quality and supply failures.

Ofwat has already allowed water firms to put up bills by 36 per cent between 2025 and 2030, with eye-watering increases seen in 2025 and another 5.4 per cent on average from April this year.

open image in gallery Prime minister Andy Burnham took aim at Ofwat’s draft decision and said customers ‘cannot be treated as a blank cheque’ ( Reuters )

It sees additional bill increases allowed for Thames Water – Britain’s biggest water supplier with around 16 million customers – which is on the brink of collapse as it sinks under a more than £20 billion debt mountain with creditors looking to secure a rescue deal to stave off temporary nationalisation by the Government.

South East Water, which is also set to increase bills for the investment programme, is another in the line of fire after a series of supply interruptions that has left thousands of households, businesses and schools without water.

Helen Campbell, executive director for delivery at Ofwat, said: “The newly agreed funding will help unlock much-needed new housing development and boost business growth across a range of sectors, as well as improving drinking water quality and the removal of PFAS and forever chemicals.

“We will track performance to ensure companies are delivering the expected improvements for customers and the environment. If they don’t, expenditure can be clawed back.”

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said: “I know that households across the country are watching every pound and I share their frustration that years of underinvestment and toothless regulation has led to this.

“We have already ringfenced money earmarked for new infrastructure so it can only be spent on fixing the problems, and will go further by fundamentally reforming the water sector so that it works for the public; keeping bills as low as they can be, and delivering higher standards, better performance and cleaner waterways.”

The news comes as Thames Water faces fresh scrutiny after revelations that it paid £1m to a chief financial officer appointed a year ago.

open image in gallery Five water firms across England and Wales, including Thames Water, have been given the provisional go-ahead by the industry watchdog to hike bills ( PA Archive )

The beleaguered firm is struggling under almost £20bn in debt, with cash running out to see the firm through beyond the end of this year and widespread concern about which direction is best for the future of the business.

The company hired Steve Buck in April of 2025 as CFO, who previously worked at water utility companies Pennon Group and Anglian Water. The £1m fee paid to Mr Buck was a delayed signing-on fee, as first reported by Sky News.

Among the other 14 executives to have seen retention payments agreed, two are with workers no longer at the firm and others are for smaller amounts than originally agreed or on more favourable terms.

The Independent understands the water firm took legal council prior to payments being agreed and made, in line with fulfilling its current financial obligations, while the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee (Efra) were informed last week about the payment to Mr Buck.

Mr Buck’s joining fee was agreed to be deferred when he joined, but his contractual rights ultimately dictated he was to be paid the full sum.

Thames Water also paid chief executive Chris Weston over £1m last year, as shown in their own financial records released last month.

Podcaster Vogue Williams has called out Red Hot Chili Peppers frontman Anthony Kiedis for previously dating a 19-year-old while he was 50.

The musician started dating Australian model Helena Vestergaard in 2013, and they split after being together for approximately two years.

Before that, Kiedis, now 63, had a relationship with Heather Christie, who was 22 years his junior. When the pair welcomed their son, Everly Bear, in 2007, Kiedis was 44 and his partner was 21.

In the latest episode of My Therapist Ghosted Me, Williams and her co-host Joanne McNally discussed age-gap relationships, with the former I’m a Celebrity campmate saying: “Do you know who else I find really disappointing, because I really like the Red Hot Chili Peppers? Anthony Kiedis.”

Seemingly referring to his romance with Vestergaard, Williams continued: “He is like 54 or something, and he is going out with a 19-year-old. And it is like, ‘Dude, what are you talking about?’”

open image in gallery Kiedis with Vestergaard in 2013 ( Getty )

McNally replied: “I've seen this. I just accept now that most men, all men, are drawn to – I'm going to be very careful how I say this – significantly younger women. That's all I'm going to say. It is what it is and I don't think there's any getting away from it. We judge it but it's not going to change.”

“I would have to say that it is not all men,” Williams continued. “Because I do think it is a very specific thing.”

Addressing why younger women might decide to date older men, McNally added: “And of course, people like him [Anthony Kiedis] and rockstars like him can get away with it because no 19-year-old girl wants to be going out with some old lad who is driving a Toyota Corolla around town.

open image in gallery Red Hot Chili Peppers frontman Anthony Kiedis ( Getty )

“They want to be going out with a millionaire rockstar who is going to treat them like a princess and they're going to have a gorgeous life. And he's cool because he's in the Red Hot Chili Peppers, do you know what I mean?”

The Independent has contacted Kiedis’s representative for comment.

The rocker is currently dating podcaster Eileen Kelly, who is 33 years his junior. ​​Kelly defended their romance in April via a Vogue essay titled My Boyfriend is Double My Age.

open image in gallery The musician's current girlfriend, pictured in 2023 ( Getty )

“There is something to be said for a man who’s simply had more time to get his s*** together, and my much older boyfriend seems genuinely excited to be with me – not like he’s biding his time before he can swipe for someone better,” she wrote.

“Is it really so difficult to imagine that connection can exist across generations, and that two people of different ages can find something real in each other?” Kelly added.

Each year, a small selection of automobiles quietly reaches the end of production. For the average car buyer, these product line cancellations usually fly under the radar. However, discerning consumers who know where to look can find a valuable opportunity to secure a strong deal on an expiring vehicle.

Dealerships frequently seek to clear out leftover inventory when a model is retired, creating favorable conditions for buyers to negotiate on price. Over time, some of these discounted cars may even mature into highly valued classic vehicles. Automotive experts at Edmunds have singled out five prominent models that will no longer be available after 2026. All listed pricing figures include destination delivery fees.

Ford Escape

After 25 years and four generations, the Escape is departing dealership showrooms. Ford’s small SUV doesn’t fully measure up to top rivals like the Hyundai Tucson and Toyota RAV4, but there are enough positive attributes to make it worth considering, especially if you can get one at a discounted price.

The Escape has comfortable seating, a smooth ride quality and easy-to-use controls. It’s also available with two powertrains to help you save on gas: a hybrid that delivers an EPA-estimated 39 mpg combined or a plug-in hybrid that can go up to 37 miles on all-electric power before switching over to its gas engine.

2026 Escape starting price: $31,845

open image in gallery The Escape has comfortable seating, a smooth ride quality and easy-to-use controls ( Ford Motor Co. via AP )

Volkswagen ID.4

The ID.4 was one of the first electric SUVs to challenge the Tesla Model Y when it was released in 2021. Its ample driving range and long list of standard features made it a viable choice for an EV, but over time, the ID.4 has been outclassed by competitors such as the Hyundai Ioniq 5 or undercut on price by less expensive options such as the Chevrolet Equinox EV.

However, picking up a 2026 ID.4 makes a lot of sense. Based on Edmunds’ analysis of transaction data, you’ll likely be able to get about $10,000 off the sticker price. For the best value of a 2026 ID.4, check out the Pro trim with standard rear-wheel drive. It comes generously equipped with heated front seats, wireless charging, a 12.9-inch touchscreen and several driver assist features.

2026 ID.4 starting price: $46,570

open image in gallery The ID.4 was one of the first electric SUVs to challenge the Tesla Model Y when it was released in 2021 ( Volkswagen of America via AP )

Jaguar F-Pace

If you’ve ever dreamed of owning a new Jaguar, then the 2026 F-Pace is your last chance at a gas-powered version because the company is transitioning to an all-electric ultra-luxury brand. The F-Pace is the last surviving model from Jaguar’s internal-combustion-engine past, and it won’t be replaced.

Although the F-Pace has soldiered on for 10 years without a redesign, it still boasts an attractive design, potent optional engines and sharp handling. The Jag can’t fully compete with newer small luxury SUVs, but scoring a good deal might be enough to tempt you. As a potential future classic, check out the performance-oriented SVR 575 Edition that comes with a muscular 567-horsepower V8 engine.

2026 F-Pace starting price: $58,375

open image in gallery The F-Pace is the last surviving model from Jaguar’s internal-combustion-engine past, and it won’t be replaced ( Jaguar Land Rover North America )

Toyota GR Supra

The GR Supra is Toyota’s flagship sports car and the modern successor to the iconic Supra from the 1990s. After a seven-year run, 2026 will be its final year. Like its predecessor, the GR Supra boasts a powerful 382-horsepower engine, an engaging driving experience and an available manual transmission. The car’s swoopy styling remains one of the more distinctive shapes on the road too.

The GR Supra’s end isn’t necessarily because of slow sales. Toyota built it as part of a manufacturing partnership with BMW, which sold the related Z4 roadster. With Z4 production ending, there wasn’t a way to keep the Supra going. While it’s possible that a Supra successor is in the works, this GR Supra could easily qualify as a future classic.

Starting price: $59,595

open image in gallery The GR Supra is Toyota’s flagship sports car and the modern successor to the iconic Supra from the 1990s ( Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A. via AP )

Tesla Model S

The Model S will forever hold a place in automotive history as one of the earliest mass-produced electric vehicles. The 2026 model year is its last, however. The Model S’ longevity has rendered it a bit of an afterthought for a luxury EV, but it is a roomy electric sedan that’s ideal for daily driving and long road trips.

A base Model S has all-wheel drive, an EPA-estimated range of 410 miles, and enough power to get you from zero to 60 mph in a Tesla-cited 3.1 seconds. Another reason to buy the Model S over the competition is Tesla’s Full Self-Driving feature, which enables automated driving on most roads as long as the driver is ready to take control if needed. Tesla is no longer selling new Model S sedans from its website, but used versions are available.

Used 2026 Model S pricing: starting around $110,000

open image in gallery The Model S will forever hold a place in automotive history as one of the earliest mass-produced electric vehicles ( Edmunds via AP )

Edmunds says

If you’re in the market for one of these vehicles, act fast because the remaining inventory will likely be limited.

Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group has acquired Harvey Nichols following the troubled department store chain’s collapse into administration.

Executives at Sports Direct owner Frasers stated they will oversee a turnaround at the historic chain, which could become a "smaller business" in the short-term.

The transaction follows an auction process for Harvey Nichols that saw Frasers battle retail rival Next to take control of the brand.

Earlier this week, Harvey Nichols warned in its latest accounts that it would need to "cease trading" within a year if it failed to secure fresh funding.

The deal encompasses the retailer's estate of six stores in Knightsbridge London, Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

Harvey Nichols has been bought by Frasers Group after hiring administrators ( PA Archive )

Frasers Group’s chief executive Michael Murray said: “Harvey Nichols is an iconic British institution with significant potential, but it is clear meaningful change is needed.

“The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term.”

Frasers Group has recently sought to take over Hugo Boss, which already holds approximately 26 per cent of the German fashion house. The offer proposed paying around €1.98 billion (£1.73 billion) for the remaining shares, equating to €38 per share.

The Frasers Group, which also owns House of Fraser and Flannels, reported that group revenues jumped by 8.7 per cent to £5.33 billion in the year to 26 April, compared with a year earlier.

This was supported by rapid growth in its international retail arm, on the back of acquisitions last year.

International revenues surged by 59.2 per cent to £1.6 billion, amid boosts from takeover deals for brands including Holdsport in South Africa and XXL in Norway.

Frasers is continuing to seek growth through takeovers, having offered to pay around €1.98 billion (£1.73 billion) for the 74 per cent of the business it does not already own.

Meanwhile, its UK sports retail division saw revenues fall by 4.7% year-on-year to £2.57 billion.

Bosses said the group’s growth strategy, which has seen it grow its luxury brands and snap up competitors, has been positive but highlighted weaker consumer confidence.

News.title: The Titan disaster was an anomaly — submersibles are ‘safer than flying’ and can save our dying oceans, expert says
