Tottenham summer special podcast You can listen to the podcast or watch the show on YouTube to hear the full thoughts of ex-Spurs midfielder Jamie O'Hara and Sky Sports News' Michael Bridge and Lyall Thomas on Tottenham's summer so far.

O'Hara said: "I like Savinho. What I've seen of him, there have been bright sparks. It hasn't massively worked for him at Manchester City, but he's obviously a talented player.

"I like Gakpo, but the problem with him is he maybe needs four or five chances to score one, but he has got something about him. I wouldn't be disappointed in the signing - he's a player who I wouldn't mind.

"I just don't know why we don't go for Marcus Rashford. I really think that Spurs should just go, how much do you want? How much can we get him for?

"I know he's on £350,000 a week, and obviously Spurs potentially can't afford that, but he's such a brilliant player.

"If you get him at it with a point to prove, I just think he's still one of the best players around.

"If he stays at Man Utd, I think he'll play, so I just don't know why we've not been interested in him."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the Sky Sports Premier League podcast, Michael Bridge and Lyall Thomas look at why now is a good time for Cristian Romero to make a move from Tottenham Hotspur to Atletico Madrid.

'De Zerbi can get best out of Rashford'

Rashford has returned to the Man Utd squad, having spent last season on loan at Barcelona, who opted against signing him despite scoring 14 goals and providing 14 assists in 47 appearances as they won LaLiga.

O'Hara feels the 28-year-old would fit the "bomba" signing De Zerbi teased last month, with it understood the Italian wants to sign at least one wide attacker in the final weeks of the summer window.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rashford has returned to the Man Utd squad. Credit: @rachaelandimogenmufc

"I think De Zerbi is the perfect man-manager for someone like Rashford," O'Hara said. "He's a manager who will get the best out of him.

"I think he'd be a good signing for us. Maybe he doesn't want to sign for Tottenham, or maybe he may be looking elsewhere.

"But the left side is something we still need to address. Mathys Tel is a decent young player, but he isn't the answer.

"We have got to sign someone who's a top-drawer player, who gets us to another level and really pushes us on.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rashford's Man Utd future was discussed on Sky Sports' Man Utd summer special podcast

"If we've got the money, and it looks like we have, and De Zerbi's come out and said we're signing another big player, well, let's go and make something happen."

Spurs have spent £237m on six new players this summer, but their most recent signing - the club-record £100m arrival of Sandro Tonali - came over a month ago.

It has led to concerns that the club's recruitment drive has stalled, with the forward line still in need of reinforcement ahead of the window closing in just under three weeks.

Sky Sports News reporter Michael Bridge told the Tottenham summer special podcast: "Tottenham know what they need, and from the conversations I continue to have, and what I've seen so far this summer, I'm confident they'll get that done.

"I've been impressed with the midfield signings, and I've got that feeling from De Zerbi in his interviews this summer that he knows, and he's got a good feeling about what's to come.

"He has been so hands-on, and Spurs have said, 'Keep us up, you get the keys', and he has got the keys, so let's see if he opens the door on those forwards."

'I'd be disappointed if Spence is sold'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player James Savundra and Mark McAdam explain the reasons why Spurs have decided to sell Djed Spence to Inter Milan

Meanwhile, Rashford's England team-mate Djed Spence looks set to leave Tottenham this summer.

The 26-year-old is closing in on a move to Inter Milan in a deal that could be worth up to £30m.

But O'Hara has questioned the defender's potential exit, which would leave Pedro Porro as the club's only recognised right-back.

He said of Spence's possible departure: "I'd actually be disappointed to let him leave. I just don't think that we should let him go.

"He can play in different areas, multiple areas - left-back, right-back and on the wing. He's athletic, he's strong, he's decent on the ball.

"Maybe he lacks a little bit going forward in terms of his attributes. But if you look at him not being a starter, he's definitely one that you're going to use. Porro or (Andy) Robertson could get injured, and you can't rely on (Destiny) Udogie's fitness.

"If Porro picks up an injury, who is the guy who's going to step in there? It can't be Archie Gray. We've got to allow Gray to develop into a midfield player; that's what we've signed him for.

"So, if you're going to get rid of him [Spence], you're going to have to bring someone else in.

"I wouldn't be gutted if we sold him, but I'd be disappointed if we let him go."

Should Spence seal a move to Serie A, Sky Sports News understands Tottenham will look to add another right-back before the window shuts on September 1.

Sky Sports News senior football news editor Lyall Thomas told the Tottenham summer special podcast: "If Spence leaves, then I think Spurs should be looking at a right-back who's a little bit younger and more of a development project.

"Porro's one of the few players at Spurs who you can bank on playing every game - he hasn't got that injury record that others have got.

"He's a World Cup winner and if you've got him as your leading right-back then having him as a mentor to develop would be a good shout."

For the full thoughts of Jamie O'Hara, Michael Bridge and Lyall Thomas, including analysis of the Spurs captaincy and expectations for the upcoming season, listen to the Tottenham summer special podcast as a podcast, or watch on YouTube.

Sports.title: LIV season finale tickets no longer on sale amid cancellation reports
Sports.content:
Tickets for LIV Golf's season-ending Team Championship event in Michigan are no longer on sale on its official website amid reports it has been cancelled.

The Telegraph reported on Wednesday that LIV's players had been told that the lucrative Team Championship event, scheduled to take place in Michigan in two weeks' time, had been cancelled.

At that point, tickets were still being advertised for sale on LIV's website but that was no longer the case as of Thursday morning. A message on the pages where tickets had been available, for both grounds and hospitality passes, read: "The tickets you were looking for are no longer available."

LIV Golf is yet to make an official announcement on whether the Michigan event will take place.

Sky Sports has contacted both LIV Golf and The Cardinal at Saint John's Resort, the event's host, for comment.

Tickets for next week's Indianapolis event, which concludes the league's individual season, remain on sale as normal.

Image: Jon Rahm at Trump National Golf Club for LIV Golf New York

Speaking last week at LIV Golf New York, an event which saw Jon Rahm clinch his third successive individual title with one event to spare, Cameron Smith said he expected the Team Championship to go ahead.

"We have been told to prepare as though it's going ahead. So we are expecting it to happen," he said.

"I'm really unsure, but we had a great year there last year in Detroit, and we're hoping we get back there.

"It is a great golf course, a great venue, and the crowds really turned up as well. I would be disappointed if it wasn't."

Bryson DeChambeau, who along with Rahm is LIV's highest-profile name, led a player meeting to discuss the future of the league ahead of the New York event.

LIV's future into 2027 remains in doubt.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced in April it would be ending its financing of the league at the conclusion of the 2026 season, leaving LIV Golf searching for new investors.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Bryson DeChambeau claims that LIV Golf players were left 'surprised' by the Saudi Public Investment Fund's decision to withdraw funding from the organisation

LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil announced last week that the league had reached an agreement with a new unnamed 'lead investor' to provide funding for the 2027 season.

O'Neil said the deal was set to be finalised later this month but added the new investor had "signed a term sheet".

Sports.title: Gold medallist Thomas chases 'own legacy' after AJ comparisons
Sports.content:
Commonwealth Games gold medallist Damar Thomas wants to create his "own legacy" after being compared to former Team GB super-heavyweight stars following his triumph in Glasgow.

The boxer followed in the footsteps of Joe Joyce, Frazer Clarke and Delicious Orie when he beat India's Narender Berwal via unanimous decision to win gold in the super-heavyweight category.

Standing at 6ft 6in, Thomas has earned inevitable comparisons with Anthony Joshua and represents one of the great hopes for the future of British heavyweight boxing.

The 21-year-old, who is targeting success at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles, is unfazed by such comparisons and insists he is focused on his own development.

"Yeah, it's a great feeling [to win gold]. I managed to add my name to the British heavyweights that won the Commonwealth [gold]," he said.

Image: Thomas is aiming for gold at the LA Olympics in 2028

"Hopefully in LA I'll be able to add my name to those great heavyweights that managed to get Olympic gold.

Image: Thomas brushed off comparisons with Anthony Joshua

"I'm just in my own race at the minute and taking it in my own strides. I'm not comparing myself to anyone. I'm doing everything at my own pace, which is great. What I want to do is create my own legacy, which is a good feeling."

Thomas demonstrated significant boxing IQ in his 5-0 victory over Berwal, marking his 11th consecutive win in a run that extends back to November.

"My main asset is my feet and my speed," Thomas said.

"That's what works for me with these heavyweights, because a lot of these heavyweights rely on one shot. I don't rely on that, so it's great."

Image: Thomas has not lost a fight since November 2025

While Thomas' main ambition for now is to remain amateur and win gold in LA, he has his sights set on becoming a professional after the games in 2028.

"First, I want to tick off that box with LA. I'm taking one tournament at a time," he added.

"It's a marathon, not a sprint. And I'm just taking everything at my own pace.

"The main goal is the Olympics. Until then, I'm thinking about Olympics and nothing else. But after the Olympics, I'll definitely turn professional."

Sports.title: Jodar's bid for history halted in Nakashima defeat as Rybakina beats Gauff
Sports.content:
Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar's bid for ATP Tour rankings history was put on hold after he was beaten by Brandon Nakashima in the semi-finals of the Canadian Open.

Jodar, 19, had been hoping to make history in the Montreal for the fastest rise into the top 10 of men's tennis but his attempt to make a first Masters 1000 final was ended in straight sets by American Nakashima.

Nakashima, the 28th seed, had never previously made it past the third round at the tournament but was too strong for Jodar in a 7-6 (7-3), 6-4 triumph.

Jodar saved four match points before Nakashima finally converted his fifth to overcome the world No 15 in two hours and two minutes of play on IGA Stadium.

"Going into the tournament, I knew I was playing at a really high level, so I knew that I could get a go on a deep run here," said Nakashima.

"Obviously, wasn't thinking about the final or anything."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Ben Shelton against Learner Tien from the Canadian Open.

Nakashima will face defending champion Ben Shelton in an all-American final on Friday, live on Sky Sports Tennis.

Shelton beat compatriot Learner Tien in the night's second semi-final and said afterwards: "Super happy with the performance.

"Learner is a guy who presents me with a lot of problems in my game. A tough challenge to overcome.

"To get a win over him in the fashion that I did, I'm super pleased with that."

Rybakina fights back to beat Gauff to set up Swiatek final

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Elena Rybakina against Coco Gauff at the Canadian Open.

At the women's semi-finals in Toronto, second-seeded Elena Rybakina beat fourth-seeded Coco Gauff 5-7, 6-2, 6-2 to book her place in the final.

Rybakina will play seventh-seeded Iga Swiatek on Thursday night after the Pole saw off ninth-seeded Elina Svitolina 6-3, 1-6, 6-3.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Canadian Open match between Iga Swiatek and Elina Svitolina.

The 6ft Rybakina finished off Gauff just before 1am local time to bring the rain-delayed night session to a close. The Kazakh has won the Australian Open and Stuttgart titles this year, taking her career tally to 13 titles.

Sports.title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 8: Crystal Palace
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 16th (NB: this is not necessarily Ed Aarons’ prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 15th

Prospects

After winning a third trophy in the space of 12 months under Oliver Glasner with the Conference League triumph at the end of May, Crystal Palace fans were brought down to earth with a bump at the start of July when the Austrian was unveiled as Nottingham Forest’s new manager. Seeing the man who led the south London club to the first major honours in their history jump ship to the team who many believe played a part in Palace’s demotion from the Europa League was a bitter pill to swallow, even if the highly rated Pierre Sage had been confirmed as Glasner’s replacement three weeks earlier.

While the fans must wait until October for him and Forest to visit Selhurst Park, the Frenchman’s task is now to try to build on Glasner’s unprecedented success while juggling the demands of a Europa League campaign. The departure of Maxence Lacroix has left Palace’s defence without a natural leader and replacing the France defender with a similar character could go a long way to determining how they fare.

Daichi Kamada’s decision to sign a new one-year contract rather than follow Glasner out of the door means that – at the time of writing – eight of the players who started in the FA Cup final victory over Manchester City last year remain at the club. The tricky bit will be holding on to the likes of Daniel Muñoz, Adam Wharton and Ismaïla Sarr until the window closes, with Muñoz attracting interest from Saudi Arabia.

Spending around £80m on Jørgen Strand Larsen and Brennan Johnson in January looks even more mistaken after agreeing a deal with Everton to swap the latter for Dwight McNeil seven months later. That has restricted Palace’s budget this summer and could come back to haunt Sage if he cannot strengthen the squad sufficiently with another marathon season ahead.

Off-field picture

To everyone’s great relief, work finally started on the new main stand at Selhurst Park this summer almost a decade after the plans were first announced. Expected to cost at least £150m and be completed by late 2028 or early 2029, it will increase the capacity of Selhurst Park to 34,000. Yet the financial strain of a much-needed project has complicated matters off the pitch, with Josh Harris, David Blitzer, and Woody Johnson reportedly keen to sell their combined 79% stakes despite Palace’s recent success. It will be up to Steve Parish, the chair who has guided Palace through their best-ever era, to convince them to stay on or find some new partners.

Owner-fan relationship

Having stepped in to help rescue Palace from administration in 2010, lifelong supporter Parish has been instrumental in establishing the club in the Premier League and will always be remembered for leading them to a first major piece of silverware. But that doesn’t mean he is exempt from criticism and there are many fans who blame the 61-year-old for failing to keep hold of Glasner after not strengthening the squad sufficiently last summer after their FA Cup success. Palace are still missing the calming influence and talent-spotting skills of Dougie Freedman, the former sporting director who surprisingly left for Saudi Arabia last March.

The manager

Sage worked wonders at Lens last season in only his second senior post as a manager, guiding them to second place in Ligue 1 before winning the Coupe de France. Having cut his teeth as a youth team coach at Lyon, the 47-year-old from eastern France who stopped playing at the age of 24 to concentrate on his coaching career seized his opportunity when he was promoted to become interim manager in November 2023. But he lasted only a year having been given the job permanently before moving to Lens six months later. Sage has still yet to manage 100 matches at professional level and his appointment looks risky. Palace are banking on him bringing stability.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Óscar Mingueza: from Barcelona to south east London via Celta Vigo. Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty Images

Óscar Mingueza missed out on being part of the Spain squad that won the World Cup but the former Barcelona defender who was signed on a free transfer after his contract with Celta Vigo expired looks an excellent addition. He is capable of playing on the right of a back three but prefers wing-back and was outstanding for Celta last season. Aston Villa and Newcastle were rumoured to have been interested in the 27-year-old, who’s won four caps for Spain’s senior team and came through Barça’s La Masia academy, making 66 appearances. His sister, Ariadna, also plays for Spain.

Stat attack

The biggest challenge facing the new Crystal Palace manager is making the side’s attack more productive. While just seven teams in the 2025-26 Premier League generated more expected goals in open play, only Wolves scored fewer. The gap between the figures was 0.31 per game for Palace, the second-worst mark in the big five leagues behind Pisa (0.36), who finished bottom of Serie A.

Set for a breakthrough

Joél Drakes-Thomas made his senior debut in the Conference League at the age of just 16 years and 192 days in December before becoming Palace’s youngest-ever Premier League player by more than a year two days later. The winger has been a regular for England’s Under-16s and starred for Palace’s Under-18s as they won the Premier League Cup in April, as well as playing 45 minutes for the first team in their FA Cup defeat to non-league Macclesfield. There are high hopes that Drakes-Thomas could be the next big star to emerge from Palace’s academy that was upgraded to category one status in 2020.

World Cup impact

Yéremy Pino only managed 69 minutes in two substitute appearances for Spain during the group stages before suffering a collarbone injury that ruled him out of the rest of the tournament. But the forward still picked up a winners’ medal – the first-ever Palace player to do so. Elsewhere, Sarr continued his brilliant club form with four goals for Senegal, with Kamada and Muñoz making it eight in total for the Palace contingent. Meanwhile, goalkeeper Dean Henderson became the first Palace player to feature for England in a World Cup finals match in the third place playoff against France.

Sports.title: Kieran Trippier: ‘The Championship is relentless … it’s totally different to the Premier League’
Sports.content:
When the question inevitably comes, Kieran Trippier is happy to set the record straight. Fresh from training, head to toe in Wolves kit – vest, shorts and club-branded sliders – he walks into a suite at their Compton Park base, conversation soon shifting to an episode that rocked supporters and stopped outsiders in their tracks: three days after signing, the manager Trippier cited as a significant driver behind his decision to drop into the second tier, Rob Edwards, had been sacked. All the while, a deal for his replacement, César Peixoto, was being accelerated.

“I’m not going to sit here and lie, I wasn’t expecting it,” Trippier says. “But it’s the club’s decision. I had good chats with Rob, of course, but I’m here to play for Wolves. There are many surprises in football and that certainly was a surprise, I’m not going to deny that. But I just cracked on, I was with my kids on holiday, training in Mallorca and just looking forward to day one in pre-season.”

Other reports followed the bombshell news. “I’ve read it all: that I was looking to rip my contract up, and all this nonsense. I was just looking forward to reporting back to Wolves. I don’t know where it even came from to be honest, that I was looking to rip my contract up – it certainly didn’t come from me, otherwise you would have heard it from me, that’s just the player that I am.”

It is a line in keeping with Trippier’s endearing straight-talking character that has made him a big hit everywhere he has been. He left Newcastle at the end of last season after playing an instrumental part in their rise under Eddie Howe, the crowning glory the Carabao Cup win last year. He spent three seasons at Atlético Madrid under Diego Simeone, where he won La Liga, after four at Tottenham under Mauricio Pochettino, culminating in a Champions League final appearance. He represented England at four major tournaments, playing every game en route to the Euro 2024 final.

Now he is back in the second tier for the first time since promotion with Burnley 12 years ago, poised to start Wolves’ Championship opener against Blackburn on Friday. He accepts it is not a natural segue. For entertaining Barcelona at St James’ Park last September, read Bolton at Molineux in October.

View image in fullscreen Kieran Trippier in a huddle with his new teammates during Wolves’ 3-0 friendly win against Racing Santander. Photograph: WWFC

“I’m not ashamed to go to the Championship because I played in it for many years,” Trippier says, recalling his first taste of the division: defending alongside Darren Moore while a teenager at Barnsley. “I had a good chat with Eddie Howe and Ross Wilson [Newcastle’s sporting director] and made my decision at the end of the season that I wanted to try something new. There were a few [interested] clubs but it was important for me that I was close to my children.”

Trippier, who calls Manchester home, knows what to expect from an unforgiving league. He recalls being part of a Burnley side that triumphed 2-1 at Wolves in the penultimate game of 2012-13, to extinguish lingering fears of relegation and all but condemn Wolves to League One. “I’ve been speaking to my teammates because the majority of them have never played in the Championship, so it’s important for myself and the lads who have to help them and try and make them understand that it’s going to be difficult.

“I’ve just said: it’s relentless, because it is … and it’s totally different to the Premier League. Going to Lincoln away is going to be a difficult game, but they’re good lads who have listened to me, Tommy [Doyle], Adam [Armstrong]. The lads will be ready.”

This is Trippier’s first external interview since joining Wolves on a two-year contract with the option of a further 12 months. He canvassed the opinions of Doyle, Conor Coady, John Ruddy and Sam Johnstone, with whom he was on holiday in Turkey before signing, to tap into “the insides of the club”. Edwards’s sudden departure – a month after André committed his future to the club and 48 hours after Raúl Jiménez returned to enhance the feelgood factor generated by Trippier’s arrival – warrants discussion, but the full-back is well placed to talk on numerous fronts, including Howe’s exit after four-and-a-half years.

“He helped the club stay in the Premier League, twice qualified for the Champions League, won a trophy, but the most important thing he did was reconnecting the supporters with the team. I was told before the [Saudi Arabia-led] takeover that it was not a good place to be – the fans were against the owners, the board etc – but when the new owners came in, and the manager, he [Howe] connected everyone, just like Gareth Southgate did with England.”

Is Howe’s legacy deserving of a statue? “He’s won a trophy, hasn’t he?” Trippier replies with a smile, “but that’s not for me to decide … the parade was incredible, the big banner of the manager showed the love the supporters had for him and still have now. When I first went there, it was a tough place [to play], especially after getting beat by Cambridge [in the FA Cup third round], but maybe that was a blessing, really, so we could just focus on [staying in] the Premier League … he will go down in history there, for sure. I’m gutted to see him go.”

View image in fullscreen Kieran Trippier holds the Carabao Cup trophy aloft with Alexander Isak on board the open-top bus with their teammates and manager Eddie Howe (front row, left) as they pass St James’ Park. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

Then there is England’s World Cup semi-final collapse against Argentina, when their low block crumbled late on. “I’ve been in that position many, many times with Simeone – I could name 30 games when he’s done it and we’ve managed to see it out, typical Simeone for you. He’s the master of the dark arts and seeing out games. Thomas Tuchel has been in that position many, many times, won a Champions League trophy with Chelsea, did unbelievable with Bayern Munich … it just didn’t happen. We were against one of the greatest players ever who can flick a switch,” Trippier says of Lionel Messi, clicking his fingers. “I’ve played against him many times where he just walks for 60 minutes, but then he can score a hat-trick. That’s just the magic of him.”

Peixoto is unknown to most but Trippier says he was aware of the Portuguese’s pedigree before the 46-year-old, who spent last season in charge of Gil Vicente, succeeded Edwards. Peixoto’s command of English has meant Trippier has not needed to dip into his Spanish to converse. “When the postman used to come in Madrid, I used to get my son to answer because he was fluent,” Trippier says, smiling.

So, what’s Peixoto like? “Really demanding. Honest. On the training field he is 100mph, nuts – in a good way – but he’s really, really demanding and I think that’s what we need as players if we want to be successful. He’s very demanding, like Pochettino and Simeone. He has his own rules: don’t break his trust, don’t be late. I wouldn’t like to be on his bad side, let’s put it that way.”

View image in fullscreen The Wolves manager, César Peixoto (second right), slows down from his 100mph on the training pitch to speak with Kieran Trippier (left), Andre (centre) and Toti Gomes at a pre-season training in Faro, Portugal. Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Getty Images

Trippier turns 36 in September, twice the age of Mateus Mané, an exciting talent who Trippier witnessed first-hand when marking him with Newcastle last season and one of those Wolves hope will illuminate a positive season. “I feel good, I feel probably in the best shape I’ve been in for many, many years. I’m not as fast as I used to be but I always believe I am clever and fast up here,” Trippier says, tapping his temples. “I feel like I’ve still got many years left in the tank.”

For Wolves, his signing was a coup. “It’s similar to when I went to Newcastle, when I left Atlético Madrid … There were a lot of eyebrows raised, but throughout my whole career I’ve had no regrets.”

Trippier, who is part of Peixoto’s leadership group, acknowledges he and his teammates will begin the campaign with a target on their backs. “Going into the Blackburn game, the first game of the Championship season, all eyes will be on us,” he says.

“When teams get relegated from the Premier League, everybody wants to beat them. It was a tough year for Wolves last year, but this season is a new season, like a reset. The reality is now we’re in the Championship, so you have to forget what happened last season and look forward, be positive. Our goal has to be to go straight back up to the Premier League.”

Sports.title: ‘He has a very high ceiling’: Madjo makes instant mark on delayed Aston Villa bow
Sports.content:
At first glance there was the usual stuff: the wide smile, the guttural release, the punch of the air, teammates quickly on the scene to offer congratulations. But then the real celebration followed for the 17-year-old Brian Madjo. After scoring his first Aston Villa goal 45 minutes into an unforgettable debut, the teenager clasped his hands behind his back and then unlocked them with the kind of force he exhibited on the pitch. “No distractions, I’m free,” he posted on Instagram after finally being cleared to pull on a Villa shirt in a competitive game.

After confirmation that the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) had upheld Villa’s appeal to register the 6ft 4in striker, the Madjo movement gathered pace. John McGinn and Amadou Onana responded to the club sharing the news on social media by posting “#freemadjo”. After Madjo shone in defeat in Salzburg, McGinn alluded to the painful and protracted waiting game. “Brian has had a terrible year,” the Villa captain said. “A player born in England should be able to play in England. He has the potential to be an unbelievable striker and he showed that.”

For Madjo, it was a moment eight months in the making. Unai Emery, who pushed for his £10m signing from Metz, had been keen to unleash him towards the end of last season. It became apparent to staff across recent months that, such is Emery’s admiration of Madjo, it was unlikely the striker would be made available for loan like many of Villa’s other teenagers. After all, Madjo was signed as a first-team player, joining on his 17th birthday after Emery requested his chief scout, Alberto Benito, to personally review Madjo’s talent at Metz, for whom, last August, he made his Ligue 1 debut aged 16 and 217 days.

At the Red Bull Arena in Salzburg on Wednesday night, it was easy to see why Emery was so enthused by the imposing striker, who made his England Under-17s debut this time last year. He was never going to be flawless against Paris Saint-Germain but it was an evening when he picked holes in one of the best centre-back partnerships in the game. Madjo’s raw power and attacking instincts ensured he gave Marquinhos and Willian Pacho a rough ride.

Tyrone Mings has been there himself against Madjo in training. “He is a tough person to defend against,” Mings said. “I think he is about 100kg – he is a big old boy. He has got a very high ceiling. He is very, very difficult to play against and I just hope that his goal fills him with confidence, and he can go on and contribute to the team.

“He has obviously had to be very patient until he could play, so I think that says a lot about his character. Clearly, mentally he is able to deal with setbacks. He missed a few chances and scored probably the hardest of them all. He is a fantastic guy. I think you could see the reaction of everybody when he scored.”

View image in fullscreen Brian Madjo impressed with his holdup and general play as well as his finishing against PSG. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

Some of Madjo’s holdup play was excellent, his strength formidable to hold off Pacho before emphatically volleying in at the back post to break Patrick Kluivert’s 30-year record as the Super Cup’s youngest goalscorer. About 60 seconds earlier, he had bulldozed Pacho to release Emi Buendía on PSG’s goal.

If Villa supporters thought they had seen that movie before, that is because last week, against the Thai Premier League side BG Pathum United, an opposition defender suffered a similar fate. When the ball squirted to the edge of the six-yard box after McGinn smacked the crossbar, the defender’s attempt to barge Madjo out of the way to reach the loose ball ended with Madjo in possession and the defender on all fours.

Until last week, Madjo had been unable to represent Villa owing to Fifa regulations that deemed the £10m January arrival from Metz as the transfer of an “international minor”. He was raised in Luxembourg, for whom he has played in friendly matches, but born in Enfield, north London, to Cameroonian parents. His father, Guy, played for Plymouth and Shrewsbury. Mings believes watching footage of Ollie Watkins, who has hit double figures in each of the past six top-flight seasons and will return to training this week after an extended break, has helped him settle.

View image in fullscreen Brian Madjo takes on Kritsada Kaman of Pathum United during another impressive pre-season display. Photograph: Pakawich Damrongkiattisak/Getty Images

“I think the manager is big on what we do off the ball, probably more than what we do on the ball,” Mings said. “Ollie’s a great person to watch, because of his work-rate and what he brings to the team. He’s got Tammy [Abraham], too – that’s two very experienced strikers he has got in and around him. I’m sure he’ll learn a lot.

“I had a few chats with him in the last 24 hours [before the game] in terms of what he’s about to go into and the experience. He said he was nervous, of course. He’s 17 and it’s a huge game. But I did say: ‘You get an amazing opportunity as a striker to just have one good moment and it can change everything for you.’ I’m so glad that after missing a couple of chances, he got that goal. He’s a very humble lad.”

Madjo departed to a standing ovation from Villa’s travelling supporters after 72 minutes against PSG; 27 touches, six shots, one memorable strike. It has been quite the few weeks for Madjo – until Wednesday, Chelsea’s João Pedro was the only Premier League player to outscore him in pre-season – and now he will attempt to build on his tally of five goals.

Villa flew to Düsseldorf at midday on Thursday in preparation for their final friendly against Borussia Mönchengladbach on Saturday, before beginning their league campaign at Brighton a week on Sunday. For Madjo, it feels as if this is just the start. “He’s a beast,” said the Villa defender Matty Cash. “He’s so good – all pre-season he has put his body around and scored goals.”

Sports.title: Chelsea set Friday deadline for Fernández suitors as City reject new £51m Barça bid for Rodri
Sports.content:
Manchester City have rejected Barcelona’s second bid of around €60m (£51m) for Rodri, while Chelsea have set a 5pm (BST) Friday deadline for the club to bid £120m for the midfielder’s potential replacement, Enzo Fernández.

On Tuesday Barça improved on their initial offer of €45m but this has been turned down. City, it is thought, want between £60m and £65m for Rodri, who captained Spain to victory at the World Cup and is a former Ballon d’Or winner.

As the 30-year has expressed a preference for Barça, City accept it is all but inevitable he will head to the Camp Nou so Fernández has been identified to take his place in Enzo Maresca’s squad.

As Chelsea’s captain and a World Cup winner at Qatar 2022, Fernández would add seniority and leadership. However Chelsea’s stance is that as City and other suitors have already had two months of the transfer window to firm up interest in Fernández, if the £120m valuation is not met by an official bid for this sum by 5pm on Friday, the 25-year-old will remain their player.

To generate some of the finance required Tijjani Reijnders may be sold to Al-Qadsiah. Discussions are advanced between City and the Saudi Arabian club for a package worth around €60m for the 28-year-old Dutchman who joined last summer.

Jérémy Doku has signed a contract extension that will keep him at City until 2031. The 24-year-old winger said: “With Enzo [Maresca] here now I am really excited about the new season. His style of football is the kind we love, so that’s exciting for the players.

“The City fans are also a huge reason I have signed this new contract. I feel their love and support, and it means the world to me. I want to focus of bringing them the success they deserve.”

Sports.title: Championship 2026-27 preview: the contenders, hopefuls and strugglers
Sports.content:
Contenders

The relegated teams, naturally, will be the favourites to go back up but two have endured confusing summers. Jarrod Bowen committing to West Ham was a bonus and the quality available to Nuno Espírito Santo should make bouncing back straightforward for the calmest of the clubs to have dropped down. They brought in huge fees for Crysencio Summerville and Mateus Fernandes but incoming activity has been pedestrian, which is the only minor cause of concern.

Wolves sacked Rob Edwards out of nowhere and appointed César Peixoto for reasons few could comprehend, because why would you want a head coach with experience of success in a league when you can bring in one who has never been involved with English football? This overshadowed the positive work done on transfers, acquiring Kieran Trippier and Raúl Jiménez, two who will lead the charge upwards.

View image in fullscreen Raúl Jiménez is back at Wolves after a three year break at Fulham. Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Getty Images

At Turf Moor the search for a new man in the dugout was less dramatic, more of a slowburner, as Nicky Hayen belatedly took the Burnley job. He will have to cope with a squad shorn of talent after Jaidon Anthony, Maxime Estève and Florentino Luís left with the incomings creating little excitement.

Southampton may think they should not be in this league but they have only themselves to blame and will face hostility wherever they go after spygate. Tonda Eckert has kept his job but will need to justify that faith by pushing for a top-two spot. The German’s unwitting victims, Middlesbrough, will be hurting from losing to Hull at Wembley but recuperation has been aided by investment in Jeremy Sarmiento, Radek Vitek and Will Lankshear.

After surprising many with a push for automatic promotion, Millwall knew this was the time to build on success, making clever signings of young players to aid the long-term strategy, with the £5m capture of the Belgian midfielder Mathis Servais the most intriguing. Wrexham’s ownership and financial backing means they will always be talked about and having missed out on the playoffs in their first season back at this level, they will want more.

Things were very quiet in north Wales until signing Anthony Patterson for a club record fee from Sunderland.

View image in fullscreen Despite the looming threat of an FA ban for his role in the spying scandal, Tonda Eckert starts the season still in charge at Southampton. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

Hopefuls

Building on finishing 10th is a difficult task for Birmingham, who have looked far and wide for reinforcements. Their potential to threaten the top six will depend on fixing poor away form and whether August Priske can become as prolific as many believe he can, while a poor start could put Chris Davies under pressure. Roy Hodgson ended the season with Bristol City but it is Michael Skubala’s job to take them forward, hoping to continue his personal momentum after success at Lincoln. Money has not been a problem with a combined £8m spent on Lorent Tolaj and Dom Ballard, but the free arrival of Jed Wallace may be the best bit of business.

There will, undoubtedly, be a team from this category that ruffle some feathers on the way to finishing in the expanded playoffs system, bringing an additional layer of hope to the peloton. After the shambles of last summer and the start of the campaign, maybe Sheffield United have learned from their mistakes. No dreadful signings or appointments have been made, and with Tom Cannon and Patrick Bamford they possess firepower.

Stoke have thrown the cash around, most notably £10m on Ethan Galbraith from Swansea, in hope the team does not tail off after promising beginnings again but finding a consistent scorer could be a problem. Preston never give the impression of going up but turning Alfie Devine’s loan permanent implies a degree of ambition even if another mid-table finish seems more likely than a trip to the Promised Land. Another eclectic window makes Swansea a fun team to follow but whether Elijah Just or Joseph Opoku can turn them side from middle-of-the-road to challengers remains to be seen.

View image in fullscreen Preston were sufficiently impressed with Alfie Devine’s loan from Tottenham that they broke their club record to sign him permanently. Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty Images

John Eustace has instilled stability at Derby, and getting Bobby Clark and Sammie Szmodics back was shrewd, but they do not feel much more than mid-table. Building on the second half of last season under Philippe Clement is the plan for Norwich, who possess plenty of potential in Jacob Wright, Mohamed Touré and Jovon Makama but it may be a year too soon for them to lead the team upwards.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The constant churn of managers and players at Watford will catch up with them at some point. They were poor last season and finding reasons why things may have changed is difficult with Alessio Dionisi the latest tasked with the impossible job. It is evident that Portsmouth want to buy and develop players under the age of 23. It leaves John Mousinho a rewarding but complex job of balancing results and individual progress. Lincoln are great innovators, which partly explains why they have made it to the Championship. The loss of Skubala was a dent in the ambition, leaving Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw to team up as joint-head coaches, which will add an additional layer of interest.

Strugglers

The good news is that Tony Mowbray is back at Ewood Park with the aim of avoiding another Blackburn relegation battle. The bad news is that it is unclear whether he has the tools at his disposal. James Morrison is no longer a caretaker but has to oversee a young and thin West Brom squad, which does not bode well. Charlton survived somewhat comfortably in the end and they have attracted Karlan Grant back and signed the skilful Millenic Alli but they still feel like a side destined for a long 10 months. The second half of the season was forgettable for QPR, so if there is a team looking over their shoulder, they play at Loftus Road.

The promoted Bolton need Sam Dalby to prove he can take the step up, otherwise goals may be difficult to find. Cardiff, meanwhile, will be reliant on those who brought them up after a quiet summer.

Ones to watch

Mateus Mané, Wolves, 18 The Portuguese forward has already shown himself to be capable of playing in the Premier League, so may find life in the Championship child’s play. A dynamic midfield eager to attack and score goals, Wolves have done well to keep hold of him.

Micah Mbick, Charlton, 19 A fine loan spell at League Two Colchester has given the striker grounding but he will be looking to kick on and shine higher up the pyramid. He has all the physical attributes – strong, fast, good in the air – but will want to hone his technical skills.

Luke Brooke-Smith, Portsmouth, 18 Brought in from Wellington Phoenix, the winger only turned 18 in June but already has an international cap for New Zealand. A lack of options gave him an opportunity in the Carabao Cup where he soon proved his capabilities to show he already has the quality to be an asset for Pompey.

Sports.title: Coach in DR Congo banned by Fifa for 20 years for sexual abuse still training young players
Sports.content:
A coach in the Democratic Republic of the Congo who was banned from football for 20 years by Fifa in March 2023 for sexual abuse of a minor is continuing to take charge of young players, the Guardian can reveal.

Jonathan Bukabakwa, who is known as Messi and previously coached youth teams in the Limpopo and Malabo regions, was also fined 100,000 Swiss francs after a Fifa investigation found him of guilty of sexual abuse. He had also been convicted of similar offences by authorities in the DRC but was released from prison last year.

The Guardian has seen several videos of Bukabakwa coaching a group of young players at Esperanto, a club in the Limete district of the Congolese capital, Kinshasa. Several local sources have confirmed that he has been regularly spotted taking charge of groups at a school field. “Messi? He’s still coaching, you can easily meet him with his team. He doesn’t hide,” said one, who did not want to be named.

Esperanto did not respond for a request to comment but Bukabakwa, when contacted by the Guardian, did not deny that he is continuing to coach young players and even claimed he was not aware that he had been banned by Fifa. “They never told me anything,” he said. “They never questioned me or sent me anything.” He has denied the allegations.

Fifa did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. It said in the statement that announced Bukabakwa’s ban in 2023 that its decision had been taken “in line with Fifa’s zero tolerance approach to all forms of abuse in football”. The statement added: “World football’s governing body has regularly updated its regulatory framework in recent years to provide greater protection to victims of discrimination and sexual abuse or harassment.”

The case has again highlighted serious flaws with Fifa’s safeguarding processes. It is understood that the Congolese Association Football Federation (Fecofa) president, Véron Mosengo-Omba, has summoned Bukabakwa and the president of Esperanto to a meeting on Monday after being contacted by the Guardian.

“We have zero tolerance for this kind of behaviour,” he said in a statement. “We will punish anyone involved in this kind of conduct.”

Bukabakwa was provisionally suspended after allegations of widespread sexual abuse in the DRC were made in the media in November 2022. He and five other coaches were provisionally suspended by Fecofa, including Donga Epapa Cédric who was sacked by his club, JMK, after allegedly asking a player to send him photos of his penis. No action was taken against him or any of the other coaches by Fecofa or Fifa following an investigation that cleared them all due to a lack of proven evidence. Cédric has previously denied the allegations.

Mosengo-Omba, who was elected as Fecofa’s president in May having stepped down as the Confederation of African Football’s general secretary two months earlier, promised to look into the previous cases once he has re-established a disciplinary committee. Fecofa had been under a Fifa-appointed normalisation committee from 2023 until his election.

“We will make sure that no one who is behaving like this will be involved in football in this country,” he said. “It’s an absolute priority for us. You cannot accept your country’s name being linked with this kind of behaviour.”

Sports.title: We have been staring at Phil Foden for close to a decade – how well do we actually know him? | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
Phil Foden says he is excited about working under Enzo Maresca, his new manager at Manchester City. We should call this exactly what it is: a very obvious barefaced lie. No doubt Foden is excited about playing football again, about challenging for trophies with his boyhood club, the new Premier League season, his new contract, a fresh start, etc, etc.

But let’s be real. Holidays are something you get excited about. Birthdays. Weddings. Amazon deliveries. The new Charli xcx album. Christmas. Playing for Enzo Maresca inspires plenty of emotions, but excitement would probably feature pretty low down a list. At best, you brace for Maresca. You steel yourself. You look in the mirror every morning and ask yourself whether you’re man enough for him. But if you’re excited, then he simply isn’t doing his job.

Hours of classroom work and painstaking video analysis. Relentless discipline on the training pitch as he drills his blueprint into your nervous system. Blunt feedback. Homework assignments to complete on international duty. My favourite bit of Maresca fastidiousness is that when his teams score a goal, the captain is banned from participating in the celebration and must instead come to the touchline to receive further tactical instruction.

For all the churn and upheaval in east Manchester this summer, perhaps the most intriguing plotline of the nascent Maresca dynasty is something that hasn’t really changed at all. Under Pep Guardiola, Foden won everything there is to win in club football. He’s been earmarked as a generational talent since he was a child, played for England in three international tournaments, embedded himself in one of the greatest club teams ever seen. He’s now 26 years old. On some level, we have been staring at Phil Foden for close to a decade. How well do we know him?

To take one example: it’s the year 2026, and nobody really knows what his best position is. Is he a forward or an attacking midfielder? Is he at his best central, or wide, or wide coming central? Deep, on the last line, between the lines? Come to think of it, what is it he does again? Good passer, but not really a pure creator. Good feet, but not really a pure dribbler. Scores goals, but not an elite goalscorer (with the exception of 2023-24, when he inexplicably started walloping in 25-yard screamers). Arguably not top 10 in the world in any single facet of the game. Yet still incontrovertibly very good, for reasons that have long been internalised but which still feel hard to articulate. How, after 49 international caps and 225 games in the most scrutinised league in the world, is this even possible?

View image in fullscreen Pep Guardiola changed where and how much he used Phil Foden repeatedly over his time at Manchester City. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

In nine seasons as his manager, Guardiola provided all the answers, albeit not always in an intelligible order. “Winger suits him better,” he said in 2022, predicting he would eventually move to the centre. By 2023, he was warning Foden that he was too much of a “free instinct” to be trusted with a central role.

Two years later, he said Foden’s best position was as a No 10, “a little bit free and close to the box”. Occasionally, he was used as a false 9. Last season, he was deployed in a deeper midfield role. (“Not a player to control the game,” Guardiola would say just before he left.)

So over the years Foden would become a kind of footballing Calpol: a plug-in solution versatile enough to be deployed for pretty much any purpose. Does this explain the sharp decline? In 2024, he was the Premier League player of the year. By the 2025-26 run-in he was essentially a passenger: unused against Real Madrid, a 90th-minute pity substitute in the Carabao Cup final against Arsenal. Two days before England’s epochal game at the Azteca Stadium, Foden was at Wimbledon watching Iga Swiatek in the third round. What happened? How does he recapture the best version of himself? And – more pointedly – what if we’ve already seen it?

View image in fullscreen Phil Foden spent the early summer watching other sports after being left out of England’s World Cup squad. Photograph: Andy Hone/LAT Images/Getty Images

These are questions with implications that go well beyond City and Maresca. For English football, which has spent decades trying to unlock the secret of industrial talent development, to work out how players grow and why they flourish, Foden is Patient Zero. Take a preternatural teenage talent, hand-picked from a cast of millions. Furnish him with the best facilities, the best footballing education, that money can buy. Surround him with champion players and one of the best coaches in history, at a club where there is stability and a process and he can mature at his own gradual rate: neither thrown in too early, nor held back too long, nor pounded into the ground. If you were trying to engineer an elite football career from the ground up, Foden is how you would do it.

If it turns out he peaked at 24, what does that say about the system that created him? If your generational talent ultimately can’t beat Noni Madueke and Ivan Toney to a place in the World Cup squad, whose fault is that? Foden? The media hype machine? The coach who developed him, nurtured him, showed him the road to greatness, but also played him in about eight different positions and never quite allowed him to forge his own identity as a footballer?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Obviously it’s not really Pep’s fault. But Foden is perhaps unique among Guardiola’s prodigies in that he was there right from the very start of the journey. This actually happens a lot less than you think. Lionel Messi was already 21 when Guardiola took over at Barcelona and basically destined to be brilliant. Pretty much all his greatest players were refined and improved rather than nurtured wholesale from childhood. And so Foden is a kind of player English football has never really produced in its history: a street talent adapted over years, by painstaking degrees, into an incredibly complex but essentially bespoke player, a single solution for a single team.

Foden is 26 and still largely devoid of context. We don’t know how he’d play in a struggling team. We don’t know what would happen if he had the keys to dictate a game. We don’t know what happens when you give him responsibility. We don’t even know much about his tactical intelligence, because he’s played his entire career under a guy telling him exactly where and when to run. Perhaps this explains the wild discrepancy between City Foden (17 major trophies) and England Foden (a goal on average every 18 months).

View image in fullscreen Foden’s best season for City was in 2023-24 when he scored 27 goals in all competitions. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty Images

Now, under a new manager, with a new midfield, Foden faces – remarkably – a make-or-break season. Bernardo Silva has gone. Rodri may well follow. Rayan Cherki is probably ahead of him in the pecking order. In a Premier League increasingly built around lightning pace and brute physicality, where does Foden fit into the new vision? What happens if he endures a third disappointing season in succession?

But there are opportunities here too. City’s World Cup players are only just returning and there should be time for him to stake a claim. A more vertical, high-energy style may just suit him. For all his kooky control-freakery, a new manager like Maresca will never be able to exert the same stranglehold as the man he replaced. For better or worse, this may just be the season when we finally find out who Phil Foden is.

Sports.title: Fog and on time? Lech Poznan race to reach Faroe Islands for Europa League tie
Sports.content:
The Europa League second leg between Poland’s champions Lech Poznan and the Faroese champions KÍ Klaksvík on Thursday evening is at risk, with the Polish team struggling to reach the Faroe Islands on time due to heavy fog.

Lech won 1-0 in the first leg in Poznan after a late goal from Ivorian striker Yannick Agnero, but are locked in a race against time to reach the islands for Thursday’s return leg, scheduled for 6.30pm local time.

The Polish team have been trying to reach Vágar – the Faroe Islands’ only airport – for two days in a row, but heavy fog is making a safe landing difficult.

On Wednesday, the Polish team were kept waiting for hours, with an increasingly frustrated head coach, Niels Frederiksen, captured telling players that they could not “just postpone, postpone, and postpone” their departure and would need to make a call on this at some point.

“If we fly tomorrow morning and play tomorrow then we will have to leave quite early, so we still have the possibility to rest,” he told players on Wednesday.

Lech’s players boarded the plane again early on Thursday morning – with the club’s social media prematurely celebrating that they were “cleared for takeoff” – only to then be kept in a holding pattern off the west coast of Norway for 40 minutes before diverting to Bergen.

Their flight was for some time the most watched globally on Flightradar tracking service as thousands of Lech fans rushed to follow their adventures.

Lech are locked in talks with Uefa on whether the fixture should go ahead or be rescheduled to give them more time to reach the Faroe Islands.

View image in fullscreen Tórsvøllur Stadium is due to host the game on Thursday evening. Photograph: Raymond Davies/ProSports/Shutterstock

KÍ Klaksvík usually advise visiting teams to arrive two days before the game to factor in potential weather disruptions.

They also encourage clubs to fly with the Faroese national carrier, Atlantic Airways, given their experience in landing in tricky conditions. Three of the airline’s planes landed on the island on Thursday morning before the weather conditions worsened again.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Lech, however, chose a private charter service, Comlux.

The Faroe Islands are notorious for difficult weather affecting visiting teams. Two opponents of another Faroese side playing in the Conference League, NSÍ Runavík, were also hit by delays this summer, forcing late matchday arrivals.

NSÍ Runavík are set to play FC Lugano this afternoon, after the Swiss team wisely arrived on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Lech’s domestic rivals, Legia Warsaw, mocked their struggles, taking to social media to advise their next league opponents, Radomiak Radom, to plan their travel well ahead and use public transport, with a mock-up of a bus tracking service.

Sports.title: 'He'll be a big player for us this season': What's next for Brian Madjo, Aston Villa's great young hope - TOM COLLOMOSSE reveals 17-year-old in line to start season opener, why Unai Emery is perfect for him and what PSG goal means for England future
Sports.content:
Brian Madjo needed only 17 minutes to change Aston Villa’s outlook for the forthcoming season.

In that time he bullied Willian Pacho, one of the best markers in the world, and gave Marquinhos a fright, too. He had six attempts on goal and scored perhaps the most difficult, a far-post volley after outmuscling Pacho. Against Paris Saint-Germain, that would be a fair night’s work for any centre forward. For a 17-year-old making his competitive debut, it made the world sit up and take notice.

Even though they won the Super Cup, PSG were some way short of peak condition. Yet PSG are still PSG. For Madjo to make an impression like that was highly impressive and Daily Mail Sport understands he is leading the race to start the Premier League opener at Brighton on August 23, with Ollie Watkins not due back with the squad until this weekend.

Yet Madjo and fellow youngster George Hemmings, who was perhaps even more impressive, have lifted the mood around Villa Park.

Though supporters trust Unai Emery completely, they are frustrated at UEFA financial rules that have effectively forced them to sell Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne.

With Ezri Konsa also a target for Arsenal and Emi Martinez and Ollie Watkins returning to training only this weekend, there was creeping apprehension among some sections of the fanbase. For one night in Salzburg, Madjo’s performance blew that away.

Brian Madjo needed only 17 minutes to change Aston Villa’s outlook for the forthcoming season

He shrugged off the Paris Saint-Germain backline to fire in a euphoric equaliser for Aston Villa in the Super Cup on Wednesday night

What do his team-mates think?

Madjo joined Villa for £10million in January but his registration was initially blocked. The teenager is a Luxembourg international and FIFA’s regulations forbid overseas transfers of players under 18.

Yet Villa got the ruling overturned on appeal and Madjo, born in Enfield, north London, was cleared to play for them earlier this summer. Skipper John McGinn posted ‘English player allowed to play in England #freemadjo’ on his Instagram account – a sign of how well respected Madjo has become among the first-team squad.

‘He has obviously had to be very patient until he could play,’ said Tyrone Mings. ‘So, I think that says a lot about his character. He is very young and very strong. Clearly, mentally he is able to deal with setbacks.

‘He's a tough person to defend against. I think he is about 100kg (15st 11lb). He is a big old boy! He has got a very high ceiling. He is very difficult to play against.

‘He has trained with us for a long time. So when he eventually got his chance to play, he was ready. He knew our system, he knew how to press. I presume he watched a lot of Ollie Watkins and understood how we play. I’ve had a few chats with him in terms of what he’s about to go into.

‘The manager is big on what we do off the ball, probably more than what we do on the ball. Ollie’s a great person to watch, because of his work-rate and what he brings to the team.’

McGinn added: ‘He (Madjo) has been through a lot. He's not been able to play for six months to a year and he's handled that amazingly. He's kept himself in good shape. It would have been very easy for him to put his head down after those missed chances, but good strikers get themselves in those positions, and he's going to be a big player for us this season.’

He bullied Willian Pacho, one of the best markers in the world, and gave Marquinhos a fright, too, in the course of having six attempts on goal

Madjo scored twice in the first game of pre-season, a 5-0 win at Walsall last month, and also found the net against Real Sociedad and the Indonesia All Stars

Along with George Hemmings (pictured), who was perhaps even more impressive against PSG, Madjo has significantly raised the mood for Villa fans heading into the new season

What happens next?

Spotting the potential in Madjo and Hemmings, Emery deliberately loaded Villa’s pre-season schedule with fixtures. PSG were their seventh opponents of the summer programme, which Villa will complete against Borussia Monchengladbach on Saturday.

Emery wanted his younger players to grow accustomed to his style and tactical demands and on the evidence of the Super Cup, he was spot on.

Madjo has now scored five times in pre-season, with a brace against Walsall in the first friendly before also finding the net against Real Sociedad and the Indonesia All Stars.

Madjo’s rise makes it even likelier that Villa will listen to offers for Tammy Abraham between now and September 1, even though they paid £18million for the former England striker only seven months ago.

Daily Mail Sport understands Villa continue to track Nicolas Jackson and could still move in the closing hours of the window, though perhaps Madjo’s displays will make Emery wonder whether he needs two more forwards to compete with the 17-year-old.

Daily Mail Sport understands Madjo is leading the race to start the Premier League opener at Brighton on August 23

Even though he has represented Luxembourg three times, they were only friendlies, meaning Madjo is clear to play for England, for whom he has nine caps at Under-17 level

Even though he has represented Luxembourg three times, they were only friendlies, meaning Madjo is clear to play for England, for whom he has nine caps at Under-17 level. Expect him to be chosen for the forthcoming age-group squads.

He is remarkably strong for his age and loves a physical duel. Yet – quite understandably – there is work to do, particularly on his touch. The good news is that Emery has an outstanding track record of improving strikers and Madjo could not be in better hands.

As he prepares his team to meet Villa, you suspect Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler will hurriedly be making plans to contain this hugely exciting teenager.
