World.title: New indictment alleges Nick Reiner was lying in wait before killing his parents
World.content:
New indictment alleges Nick Reiner was lying in wait before killing his parents

toggle caption Evan Agostini/Invision via AP

LOS ANGELES — A Los Angeles County grand jury has indicted Nick Reiner on murder charges in the killings of his parents, Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, and adds the allegation that he was lying in wait before attacking them.

The grand jury, which had been meeting in secret, returned the indictment on July 20, and it was unsealed Wednesday, when 32-year-old Nick Reiner entered a not guilty plea.

Rob Reiner, a director, actor and Hollywood luminary, and his wife, a photographer and producer, were stabbed to death in their home in the upscale Brentwood section of Los Angeles on Dec. 14. Nick Reiner was arrested within hours and charged two days later.

The grand jury indictment is a major step toward trial and allows prosecutors to skip California's preliminary hearing process, where evidence is publicly aired.

Lying in wait means a suspect waited for or hid from victims in order to ambush them, and as an allegation it's meant to show premeditation. A finding that he was lying in wait along with a murder conviction would make Reiner eligible for the death penalty, but prosecutors said they haven't decided whether to seek it.

Sponsor Message

"This was a profound betrayal by someone who was loved and trusted by the very people he is accused of killing," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement. "We hope that by having a grand jury return an indictment in this case it will bring us one step closer to a trial and achieving justice."

Unsealed indictment gives few new details in secrecy-shrouded case

Prosecutors have said nothing about possible motives, and leaks in the case have been virtually nonexistent on both sides.

The Los Angeles County chief medical examiner told The Associated Press he would like to make their autopsy reports public, but a court order has prevented him from doing so.

The unsealed indictment reveals few new details in a case that has been shrouded in secrecy. It does not explain how or why Reiner was lying in wait. Without elaborating, prosecutors have said since December that the parents were stabbed. The indictment includes a special allegation of use of a deadly weapon — a knife — that could also contribute to a stiffer sentence.

Indictment released as Nick Reiner seeks trust funds

The indictment comes as Reiner is seeking unpaid money from a trust his parents established for him, saying he needs it to help in his defense.

Sponsor Message

Reiner said in a court petition that the trustees who oversee the funds have denied them to him without legal justification. The money was to have gone to Nick Reiner even if his parents were alive, legal filings say. The petition says the trust has at least $1.5 million in assets, but trustees would not share the exact amount.

"Nick loved his parents, and he is devastated by their deaths. But the facts about what did and did not happen to them are not at issue," the petition says.

He is seeking to hire back high-profile criminal defense attorney Alan Jackson, who initially represented him before Reiner's siblings would no longer agree to fund his defense and a public defender took over.

A hearing on the petition is set for next week.

The LA County Public Defender's Office, which is representing Reiner, declined to comment on the indictment.

Grand jury process happens in secret

California prosecutors can charge a defendant and take the case through a preliminary hearing — a sort of trial in miniature where evidence is publicly aired and a judge decides whether it should be sent to trial — as recently happened with singer D4vd.

Or they can use a grand jury to go through the process in secret. They can also publicly file charges and later seek a secret grand jury indictment, essentially creating a new version of the case, as happened here and in the Los Angeles prosecution of Harvey Weinstein.

Rob Reiner had prolific career as actor and director

Rob Reiner began as an actor, starring in the TV sitcom, "All in the Family," as Michael "Meathead" Stivic, the liberal son-in-law to a much more conservative and bigoted Archie Bunker, played by Carroll O'Connor. Reiner won two Emmy Awards for the role, and last month got a posthumous Emmy nomination for his work as a guest star on "The Bear."

Sponsor Message

He became a prolific director whose work included some of the most memorable and endlessly watchable movies of the 1980s and '90s. His credits included "This is Spinal Tap," "Stand By Me," "A Few Good Men," and "When Harry Met Sally…" during the production of which he met photographer Michele Singer. They wed soon after and were married for 36 years.

Nick Reiner was the second of the three children they had together. He and his father co-wrote the script for the 2015 film "Being Charlie," which was partly based on the son's teenage struggles with addiction and homelessness.

His older brother Jake Reiner wrote in April that the experience of losing his parents and having his brother at the center of it was "a living nightmare" that is "too devastating to comprehend."

World.title: Millions crowd cities to see Spain's first total solar eclipse in over a century
World.content:
Millions crowd cities to see Spain's first total solar eclipse in over a century

toggle caption Antonio Calanni/AP

MEDINACELI, Spain — Millions of people crowded cloudless cities and towns in Spain on Wednesday in search of the best views of a total solar eclipse, when the alignment of the sun, moon and Earth briefly plunged parts of the planet into darkness.

The crowds brought lawn chairs and umbrellas as they eagerly awaited the celestial spectacle, which began early in the evening. As the sky darkened, gradually at first and then quickly, people broke into applause and cheered. It was the country's first total solar eclipse in more than a century.

"It's simply impossible to imagine," Rosa Celiberti, a language teacher who watched from Medinaceli, a Roman-era hilltop town in northeast Spain, said with tears in her eyes. "No matter how many photos or videos you've seen, nothing comes even close to what it actually feels like."

Sponsor Message

Across a wide band of northern and central Spain and Portugal, millions of people enjoyed some of mainland Europe's best views of the eclipse. It also passed over slivers of Greenland and Iceland.

toggle caption Alberto Saiz/AP

Totality — when the moon completely covers the sun's light — was expected to last less than 2½ minutes, reaching its maximum duration off Iceland's west coast. By the time it got to a small patch of Portugal and then to Spain, just before sunset, totality dwindled to a minute or so. The total eclipse then ended over the Mediterranean.

The eclipse was expected to draw at least a half-million additional visitors, Spanish authorities said. Demand for hotel rooms along the path of totality, including in the northern cities of A Coruña, Bilbao and Santiago de Compostela, soared.

Rural areas prepared for an influx of visitors

The event unfolded against the backdrop of scorching summer temperatures and wildfires, and Spanish officials rolled out a large public safety campaign.

Temperatures across much of Spain climbed above 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) in many areas where the eclipse was observed. Some 350 official viewing sites were set up across the sparsely populated interior, and more than 33,500 law enforcement officers were deployed to observation areas and access points, the Interior Ministry said.

Sponsor Message

Only weeks ago, the most destructive wildfire in Spanish history devoured 500 square kilometers (193 square miles) and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in Ávila, in central Spain. Several smaller wildfires remain active elsewhere in southern and central parts of the country.

Despite clouds, sky watchers in Iceland witnessed darkness

In Reykjavik, clouds did not prevent hundreds of people from gathering in bright raincoats in front of the landmark Hallgrímskirkja church as the skies darkened.

toggle caption Bernat Armangue/AP

With rain falling, the disk of the sun was barely perceptible and then, suddenly, the lights went out. Only the glow of phones held aloft could be seen.

The crowd cheered the darkness as it rained harder and roared even louder when the first light returned. They did not wait to watch the remainder of the partial eclipse and quickly cleared out of the square.

Eclipse glasses sold fast

Special eclipse glasses were essential for safe viewing, even if only a sliver of the sun remained visible. The glasses are made with special filters that block solar radiation that can damage the eyes.

For months, supermarkets, department stores, museums and planetariums across Spain had sold or distributed the glasses, with many pharmacies running out of stock ahead of Wednesday.

On Tuesday evening in downtown Madrid, a long line formed outside a photo shop where a sign read, "We carry eclipse glasses."

One woman emerged triumphantly and reassured those waiting: "He has boxes and boxes of them!"

A ship circles waters near Greenland hoping to catch a glimpse

Sverre Rud, captain of the MS Spitsbergen, was circling the waters of Rypefjord in eastern Greenland trying to make sure he was perfectly positioned for his 126 passengers to view the spectacle. All day, people came up to Rud to ask if he had nailed the right spot, with no clouds.

Sponsor Message

"I will do my best," Rud said. "I will pull out my superman powers."

The eclipse may have been startling for the passengers, who had been experiencing 24 hours of daylight on a 17-day cruise in locations mostly north of the Arctic Circle.

Suddenly, for two minutes it was dark.

Even so, the mood on the polar ship had been pure anticipation.

"Everyone is very enthusiastic," Rud said. "When we were down for breakfast earlier, it was almost like a little bit of a Christmas Eve feeling here."

Hotel costs skyrocketed in Spain and Iceland

Rooms in Reykjavík, Iceland's capital, averaged more than $1,000 for Wednesday night as Icelanders prepared for their first total solar eclipse since 1954 and the first visible from the capital since 1433.

Prices were roughly double 2025 rates, according to data group Lighthouse Intelligence. Many tourists made bookings years in advance. But cloudy skies prevailed across much of the island.

Authorities expected up to 20,000 additional overseas visitors during an already busy peak tourist period. Iceland is home to fewer than 400,000 people.

The 70-room Hotel Keflavík in the Reykjanesbaer municipality was fully booked, with guests hoping to see around one minute and 45 seconds of totality.

"Eclipse time, of course, has been very demanding, and many people came to us early, like last year," said Steinþór Jónsson, the hotel's owner and manager.

Jónsson said he had seen nothing like it since 1986, the year the hotel opened, when U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held a summit in Reykjavík.

"When I opened the hotel, we had Reagan and Gorbachev meeting. It was very hectic here," he said with a smile. "Besides Reagan and Gorbachev, the eclipse is the biggest."

Sun mostly obscured in Britain

Across Britain, where the sun was more than 90% obscured, people flocked to hilltop parks and anywhere with an open view of the sky to see the best eclipse since 1999.

Sponsor Message

In Greenwich Park, with views of the River Thames and central London, the sky turned an eerie gray as a sliver of light sat atop the moon like a hat.

toggle caption Kin Cheung/AP

Veronica Orozco popped open a bottle of champagne to share with neighbors as she witnessed the second eclipse of her life.

"I was in Venezuela and I was young and I thought that the sun would not come back. My dad said, 'It is science, of course it will come back,'" she recalled. "Now sitting here at the age of 41, it is still magical."

Aja Lilit, who turned 24 on Tuesday, said the eclipse was like a "birthday present from the universe."

She said the rare event made her think of how small she was at a "cosmic level."

World.title: Canadian pediatricians document 'exponential rise' in severe e-scooter injuries, deaths in children, teens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As e-scooters become increasingly common across Canada, pediatricians, emergency physicians and other experts warn that injuries — often severe and involving younger people — are rising, while regulations struggle to keep pace.

Dr. Daniel Rosenfield, a pediatric emergency physician at SickKids hospital in Toronto and chair of the injury prevention committee for the Canadian Pediatric Society (CPS), says he has seen "a complete exponential rise" in every type of injury that can result from an e-scooter crash — from minor scrapes to major brain injuries and death.

Bad injuries used to be "once in a blue moon," he told CBC News. Now, "anytime we get a call from EMS that says, 'E-scooter trauma inbound,' we're prepared for severe injuries," he said.

E-scooter injury cases at SickKids rose from 26 in 2023 to 46 in 2024 and 107 in 2025, Rosenfield said.

"And this year we're likely on target for more than that."

The experience is mirrored across Canada and around the world. A CPS survey of Canadian pediatric specialists, conducted from late 2025 to early 2026 and published Thursday, documented 10 deaths, 12 ICU admissions and 26 hospitalizations lasting more than two days over the previous 12 months as a result of e-scooter crashes. Head injuries were present in about half the cases.

"The vast majority, if not all, are unhelmeted," Rosenfield said.

The most severe injuries tended to involve boys between 10 and 15 years old, he said.

The CPS survey records the experience of pediatric specialists rather than providing a rigorous quantitative analysis. But a separate study published Tuesday in the Emergency Medicine Journal provides multi-year hospital administrative data from three U.K. hospitals that closely aligns with what Canadian pediatricians are seeing.

That study found e-scooter cases at hospitals in Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield rose from fewer than 10 in 2019 to almost 150 in 2024. Head injuries were among the most severe, and fewer than two per cent of those injured were wearing helmets.

From 69 km/h to a critical care unit

That U.K. data mirrors what Canadian families are experiencing firsthand.

Just over a year ago in London, Ont., Crystal Dunkley's son Shaun was not wearing a helmet when he took a family friend's e-scooter out for a ride one evening, as he had done many times before.

That evening, Shaun, then 12, hit a raccoon as it ran across his path.

"He believes he was going 69 kilometres an hour when this happened," Crystal Dunkley recalled in a video interview Wednesday.

An ambulance rushed Shaun to the Children's Hospital in London, where he was intubated and admitted to the Pediatric Critical Care Unit with a fractured skull. He was in a coma for over a week.

"The doctors told us that with the brain bleed they determined he had, there was a possibility he would not make it, and if he did, then he would likely be very disabled," Crystal said.

Following his e-scooter crash, Shaun Dunkley was in a coma for over a week and spent more than a month in the London, Ont., children's hospital. (Crystal Dunkley)

Shaun ultimately recovered completely after 34 days in Children's Hospital and more time at a rehabilitation facility in Toronto. Crystal said he now approaches people riding e-scooters on the street and tells them to wear a helmet.

"Not a day goes by that I don't see multiple young children riding them without helmets, sometimes two or three to a scooter," Crystal said. "Some of these scooters can go … like I said, the one he was on was going 69 kilometres an hour."

'Anything but toys': Why regulation is lagging behind

Most parents are surprised by the extent of their child's injuries, Rosenfield said.

"And to be fair to the families, these devices are often marketed as toys," he said. "And as a device that can go zero to 40 kilometres an hour in a number of seconds, I will tell you they're anything but toys."

The CPS survey also notes that younger people may be less familiar with road rules, less risk-averse and at greater risk of injury because of their developmental stage.

But it also argues there are problems with rules and laws, describing them as "unclear and made up of a patchwork of regulations, varying depending on the province/territory."

The minimum age for riding an e-scooter varies by province, while some cities have banned the devices altogether — though those bans are often ignored. Several provinces, including B.C., Ontario and Quebec, cap e-scooter speeds at 24 or 25 kilometres per hour.

"I can tell you for sure people go faster than that," Rosenfield said.

Rosenfield is not advocating for an e-scooter ban, pointing to their utility to complement public transit and reduce automobile traffic.

"I do think they have a use in an urban environment," he said. "I just think we need to figure out what that looks like and how to make those devices safe."

World.title: Unsealed documents reveal details of RCMP's response, investigation into Tumbler Ridge shooting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Documents unsealed by CBC News and a consortium of media outlets reveal new details of the RCMP's response and investigation into the February 2026 mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C.

The documents, which include search warrants, production orders and sealing orders, provide a snapshot of a complex investigation, laying out for the first time law enforcement's account of the day shots rang out at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The newly unredacted files from the RCMP paint a picture of how front-line officers experienced the events of that day.

Significant portions of the documents remain redacted, including timestamps crucial to the chronology, such as how long it took officers to enter the school after receiving reports of shots fired.

The documents say that on Feb. 10, 2026, RCMP responded to an active shooter at the high school in Tumbler Ridge and found six deceased victims in a school littered with spent shell casings. They identify the shooter as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, who was found dead in the school with self-inflicted gunshot wounds.

Search warrants filed by the RCMP describe the evidence, physical and electronic, that police identified as they attempted to piece together what happened that day.

One sealing order filed in early March describes concern that releasing records connected to the investigation could compromise future public inquests and pose a risk to the public.

911 calls reported erratic driver, shots fired

The mass shooting, one of the worst in Canadian history, shook the small northern B.C. community, and is now the subject of a coroner's inquest investigating the role that mental health, access to weapons, and artificial intelligence played in the tragedy.

Throughout the documents, Van Rootselaar is referred to by her last name, full name, "Jesse," and "the shooter."

A production and sealing order sworn by Const. Jonathan Paquin of the RCMP North District Major Crime Unit on March 6 describes a flurry of 911 calls received the morning that chaos unfolded in Tumbler Ridge.

A memorial to the victims of the Tumbler Ridge Secondary School shooting is pictured in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., on Feb. 12, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

On Feb. 10, RCMP received a call about "an SUV that had been driving erratically from [redacted], which is the residence of Jesse."

The vehicle driven to the school was later identified as a green 2023 Hyundai Palisade.

A caller reported that "there were two dead bodies and shotgun shells on the floor" and they "thought that the eldest son was armed and had left, and that the mother and son were dead."

RCMP advised the caller to leave the scene untouched, close the door and return to their residence.

RCMP then received multiple calls of shots fired at the secondary school.

The documents include a minute-by-minute accounting of various officers arriving on the scene, hearing shots fired, entering the school, and locating deceased victims and the deceased shooter.

"Police were shot at by the suspect which caused them to hold while being shot at," it reads in part.

Because timestamps are redacted from the documents, it's unknown how much time elapsed between the events described over several pages.

For example, the documents do not relay how much time passed between the initial 911 call describing the erratic vehicle, and police entering the school. This week, CBC News and a consortium of other media have been in court to argue that some of the redacted information be made public.

The production order also reveals confusion over whether there was a second shooter in the school, possibly because the shooter went by the aliases Jesse Jacobs and Jesse Strain, in addition to Jesse Van Rootselaar.

One inspector identified the shooter as the "eldest child in the STRAIN/JACOBS family, and that they were obsessed with guns," the document reads.

"[The] inspector reported that a possible second shooter was Jesse VAN ROOTSELAAR," reads the document, though it's later detailed that police identified these were the same person.

Details of firearms remain sealed

A search warrant filed the day after the shooting describes evidence sought by police, including "human biological substances including but not limited to: blood, hair, fingerprints and human tissue," "firearms, ammunition, spent cartridge casings," and "computers, cell phones or tablets, that may belong to Jesse Van Rootselaar."

A production order lists physical evidence located inside Van Rootselaar's home, including a Sony Handycam, a black iPhone with a cracked screen inside a black case, a purple Aocwei laptop, a MacBook Air, an SD card and a purple digital camera.

An RCMP officer is pictured at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School on Feb. 11, 2026, the day after a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

A search warrant filed on Feb. 11 describes the scene at Van Rootselaar's home. It says two RCMP corporals observed "a shotgun [redacted] that was unloaded as well as a pellet gun" and "insecure firearms inside the residence."

Between Feb. 13 and 20, a firearms tracing investigation with the Canadian Firearms Program attempted to trace four firearms of those seized from the secondary school and a second, redacted address. The details of the firearms are redacted, though two shotguns and a rifle are listed.

Electronic records sought

A section of the order describes a Police Records Information Management Environment — or PRIME — review of the teen.

Any individual who interacts with law enforcement in B.C., from witnesses to suspects, is entered into PRIME's centralized database, regardless of the nature of the interaction.

The order says Van Rootselaar was carded to 12 PRIME files, dating back to April 2018 when she would have been around 10 years old. The details of those incidents are redacted.

A section about Van Rootselaar's social media accounts is redacted in its entirety, with nearly seven pages of text fully blacked out.

But the file says on Feb. 15, 2026, RCMP were notified by the FBI that OpenAI had located two ChatGPT accounts believed to be used by Van Rootselaar. Details of those accounts are also redacted.

"Jesse's ChatGPT account was subject to an internal review in June 2025 after Jesse's chat conversation discussed matters that could be related to the school shooting," it said.

"OpenAI banned Jesse's ChatGPT account and did not notify police at that time."

A request to seal

One document, an application for an order to seal filed March 6 by Paquin, shows that police were concerned that unsealing the production order filed concurrently could compromise ongoing investigations, and potentially put the public at risk.

Paquin argues that disclosure would harm a newly-announced coroner's inquest, because "while this is not a criminal trial, it is a court proceeding involving a jury." He argues that while the province had not yet called a public inquiry, any potential future inquiry could be influenced by information that had been made public.

RCMP and victim services are pictured at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School on Feb. 11, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"This is a large and complex investigation that has garnered significant national and international attention with significant media coverage of the incident and the police investigation," it reads in part.

"For this reason, I believe that evidence outlined in this Information to Obtain if prematurely disclosed would certainly be disseminated through various news outlets that would affect and influence the current ongoing criminal investigation, the coroner's inquest, and a potential Public Inquiry."

Paquin also argues that making the contents of the document public could inspire further acts of mass violence, invoking high profile incidents in the U.S.

"I am aware that mass casualty incidents can inspire copycat attacks. For example, the Columbine High School massacre is well known to have had this effect where it inspired other shootings in the following years," he writes.

"I believe premature disclosure of this Information to Obtain without a complete criminal investigation, and the following Coroner's Inquest or Public Inquiry where all the facts are known could put the public at risk."

World.title: Violence directed at West Bank family a 'horrific act of violence,' U.S. ambassador to Israel says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. ambassador to Israel condemned the actions of Jewish settlers who are besieging the home of an American Palestinian family in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

Mike Huckabee called the siege a "horrific act of terror."

Since Sunday, according to local officials and family members, settlers have gathered near the home in the village of Qusra and harassed those inside, defying efforts by the Israeli military to defuse the situation.

A group that has included up to dozens of men has thrown stones, attempted to bring down a stone wall nearby and prevented the occupants from leaving despite dwindling supplies.

Speaking to The Associated Press by phone from his home in Ohio, the home's owner, Loui Ridi, said his 48-year-old brother and nephew, who have been holed up in the home to defend it, had been unable to leave the house and did not have access to food or water for several days.

Mike Huckabee, U.S. ambassador to Israel, is shown in Jerusalem on Aug. 20, 2025. (Ohad Zwigenberg/The Associated Press)

On Thursday morning, the owner's brother, Qusai Abu Rida, said that he and his teenage son had been evacuated by Israel's military. It was unclear what would happen to the property and at least one other that has been targeted.

Israeli troops intervened in recent days to try to restore order. The military said that overnight Thursday its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" on the outskirts of Qusra and a nearby village, and detained one Israeli. It added that additional soldiers had surged to the area, which is about 16 kilometres from the city of Nablus, to "carry out defensive missions and patrols."

'Prisoners in our own house'

Journalists on the outskirts of Qusra said roads into the village were closed.

Palestinians and the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians as clashes have surged in the last few years.

Huckabee's post on X was an unusually sharp rebuke from a U.S. official, even as he defended the Israeli military's response. Huckabee is a longtime ally of Israel's settler movement and in the past has expressed support for Israeli control over the occupied West Bank while condemning settler violence.

Home security footage from Thursday morning appeared to show a few settlers still hiding by a damaged stone wall near the house.

Ridi said that settlers have been harassing his home for months before the situation escalated in recent days, saying they had cut off the water and electricity to his house and thrown stones, causing damage to the property as well as at least one more house in the area.

"We are prisoners in our own house, hostages in our own house," he said.

WATCH | Last month's deadly incident: IDF launches West Bank operation after 4 Palestinians, 2 Israeli soldiers killed | Duration 3:07 Four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers were killed in Tal, a village near Nablus in the occupied West Bank. The Israel Defense Forces have sealed off the village and say they are preparing for major military action.

Last month, a mosque in Qusra was set on fire in another apparent settler attack. That followed the killing of an Israeli settler, which triggered violence that left two Israeli soldiers and four Palestinian villagers dead.

Settlers have been building more outposts in an effort condemned by many in the international community as aimed at dismantling any remaining hopes of establishing a Palestinian state in the occupied West Bank.

The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 war, as part of a future state. Many settlers and their supporters say the entire area should belong to Israel for historical, religious and security reasons.

World.title: With U.S. midterm elections looming, Democrats are clashing over how to win
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the U.S. heads toward the midterm elections, a gruelling primary season has further entrenched a rift between the insurgent progressive and centrist wings of the Democratic Party.

At stake is control of Congress this November and, beyond that, the presidency in 2028.

The centrists argue candidates touting moderate and pragmatic policies is the path to flipping seats from Republican control. While progressives say more uninspiring, establishment candidates will not galvanize a coalition of young people, the working class and diverse voters that could propel the party to victory.

"I don't even know how I could go about being sure which group has the most appeal," said Hans Noel, an associate professor of Government at Georgetown University and co-director of the Georgetown Democracy Initiative.

He says that while progressive candidates may alienate some voters who otherwise might have voted Democrat, they will also bring new voters to the party, including those who may not have voted at all.

There are also intangible characteristics, like personal likeability, said Noel: "How do you add that all up and make a strong prediction? It's hard."

LISTEN | What direction should the Democratic Party take?: Two Blocks from the White House 29:47 As progressives win U.S. primaries, what’s the direction of the Democratic Party?

Primary wins and losses

The primary season — where Democratic voters choose their candidates for upcoming general elections against Republicans — has given both sides wins, losses and lessons.

On Tuesday, in the key battleground state of Wisconsin progressives were dealt a blow when democratic voters narrowly chose moderate David Crowley in the primary for governor over self-described Democratic Socialist Francesca Hong, who was projected to win in the polls.

Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley speaks to the media on Wednesday in Middleton, Wis., after winning the primary. Crowley will take on Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in November's midterm election. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)

Hong's campaign was plagued in its final days by past comments she made advocating for defunding the police and abolishing ICE and also saying it was time to "cancel Thanksgiving," calling it a celebration of colonialism. During the campaign, she backed away from all these comments, saying her views had evolved.

Hong ultimately wasn't endorsed by progressive flagbearers, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Other races where moderates were able to hold progressive challengers at bay included those in Washington and Missouri .

In the swing state of Michigan earlier this month, however, progressive Addul El-Sayed, who campaigned with Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders, eked out a victory against centrist candidate Haley Stevens despite over $60 million being spent on her behalf, largely from super PACs.

WATCH | What Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan victory means for Democrats: Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan victory called a win for progressive Democrats | Duration 2:04 U.S. Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed's narrow victory in a Michigan primary has been described as a win for progressive Democrats, but has some in the party worried that being seen as too progressive will hurt their chances to defeat Republicans in the upcoming midterms.

El-Sayed, like other progressive candidates, campaigned on issues like medicare for all, getting money out of politics, taxing billionaire wealth and calling for an end to military aid for Israel. He has also been praised for his communication skills.

In response to the U.S. President Donald Trump calling him "full of shit," El-Sayed shot back : "At least I don't let mine go all over the Oval Office."

El-Sayed's victory followed wins from progressive candidates who took on more moderate democrats in strongholds of New York and Colorado.

Notably, in Maine, another battleground state, progressive Graham Platner delivered a win before he dropped out due to sexual assault allegations.

Discontent among young voters

Bhaskar Sunkara, president of left-leaning magazine The Nation and former vice chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, says El-Sayed's win and others like it are a "huge check" on the Democratic Party.

"Voters, particularly young voters, are really discontent with the leadership of the party … and just generally feel that the Democratic Party doesn't stand for anything. It's not combative enough."

Progressive politicians U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, left, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, right, campaigned alongside Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed at July's the People V. The Powerful rally in Detroit. El-Sayed went on to win the Michigan senate primary nomination on Aug. 5, in a tight race. (Jose Juarez/The Associated Press)

Sunkara went on to say that El-Sayed is a better candidate than Hong with working-class voters.

"I think there is a way in which some candidates have been tarred with stances they had in 2019, 2020. This sort of abolish the police, the discussion of whiteness or whatever else. Abdul never had that problem."

Hong wasn't the only candidate backing off from past comments.

New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made headlines earlier this week when asked about her past support for defunding the police. "I have a local city councilman that has this saying: 'Woke 1 was crazy,' " she said before laughing.

Can progressives win key battleground states?

While some in the progressive wing re-evaluate past positions that could alienate voters this election cycle, many moderate democrats continue to warn of liabilities in swing states.

Fareed Zakaria, host of CNN's Sunday public affairs program GPS , cited Washington Post data to point out that while El-Sayed had the support of Michigan's most educated counties and college towns, his opponent did better in rural and lower-income areas.

"The left has the passion, but the middle still has the votes needed to win in general elections," Zakaria said.

Kate de Gruyter is the vice-president of communications at Third Way, a leading centrist democratic group that is spending $15 million between now and 2028 to discredit Democratic Socialism.

LISTEN | What's behind the wave of Democratic Socialist wins in the U.S.: Front Burner 36:53 Understanding the rise of ‘democratic socialism’

"Their theory of the case is that they're somehow going to be able to persuade all these voters in the middle that they absolutely need to win in November to back their candidate. We've never seen that happen over the entirety of the Trump era," she said in an interview.

De Gruyter added that El-Sayed's decision to campaign with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker as one example of "a whole universe of things that Republican ad makers are salivating at."

De Gruyter went on to suggest that the reason Democrat Kamala Harris lost the presidential election in 2024 was that she was seen as too lax on issues like immigration and plagued by stances she'd taken in the past on " transgender policy ."

In the final weeks of the campaign. Trump's team ran an ad using a five-year old clip of Harris saying that "every transgender inmate in the prison system would have access" to taxpayer-funded gender transitions.

"The idea that we should move further left makes no sense at all," she said.

The interesting thing is that while that can all be true, there are also plenty of arguments that suggest the opposite, according to Noel, the Georgetown associate professor.

U.S. Vice-President and then presidential candidate Kamala Harris takes part in a phone bank at the Democratic National Convention Headquarters on Nov. 5, 2024. Her unsuccessful campaign has been criticized by both progressives and moderate democrats. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images)

"And it can also be true that Harris actually lost because she was too tied to the establishment and Biden. And too close to Israel … progressives called her a cop. Either of those differences could have been enough because it was a fairly close race."

Either way, Democrats are riding favourable waves into the midterms.

Trump's polling is low . He has entered into an unpopular war in Iran . And all of this should help the Democrats, whether they're progressives or moderates in the mid-terms, said Noel, adding that if the Democrats don't do as well as expected there will be a lot of "what happened?"

"If all the progressive candidates lose and the centrist candidates win, well, that's going to be an easier story."

World.title: Quebec man receives North America’s 1st transplant using regenerated liver technology
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 64-year-old Quebec man has become the first patient in North America to receive a regenerated liver thanks to a breakthrough technology that could make dozens of additional livers available for transplant in its first year alone.

Gérard Landry, a resident of Nouvelle on the south shore of Quebec's Gaspé Peninsula, spent about 15 years dealing with liver problems that eventually progressed to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

Just before he was wheeled into surgery for a liver transplant, his doctor gave him some unexpected news about the organ: it was regenerated by a new machine, used for the first time at Montreal’s Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal, or CHUM.

“ [My doctor] told me about the new machine that he worked on for a few years,” Landry said. “It was like a Christmas gift."

The technology, called Liver Assist, allows doctors to treat and assess a donated liver outside the human body before transplanting it. For Landry, it meant receiving an organ that might otherwise have been considered too risky to use.

WATCH | A new liver thanks to new technology: This Quebec patient is the 1st in North America to receive a regenerated liver | Duration 1:51 Gérard Landry had been suffering from liver disease and cancer for 15 years. But now, he’s cancer-free thanks to a liver regenerated by a new machine – technology that could lead to more life-saving transplants.

Giving a donated liver a chance to recover

Dr. David Hénault, hepatopancreatobiliary surgeon and liver transplant specialist at the CHUM, led the project and performed Landry's operation.

He said the team had been preparing to use the technology for about three years.

The Liver Assist system works by connecting a donated liver to a machine that circulates an oxygen-rich fluid through the organ, which can help reverse some of the damage caused by a lack of oxygen while the organ is outside the body.

Dr. David Hénault, hepatopancreatobiliary surgeon and liver transplant specialist at the CHUM, led the project and performed the first operation in North America using the new technology. (Aatefeh Padidar/CBC News)

The technology then allows doctors to switch to a blood-based solution and assess how the liver functions in conditions designed to mimic the human body.

“If it works on the machine, then it’s going to work in the human,” Hénault said.

The liver Landry received was particularly well suited to the technology because it was susceptible to damage caused by a lack of oxygen during the organ transfer process, Hénault said.

Boost to number of available livers

The CHUM performs about 70 liver transplants each year. Hénault said a study done with Transplant Québec looked at livers that had previously been declined for transplantation and assessed which ones might have been recoverable using the new technology .

The team estimates the machine could make an additional 20 to 24 livers available for transplantation during its first year of use. That number could grow as the technology becomes more widely used.

“We will be able to help so many more patients in need of a liver that are waiting on the transplant list,” Hénault said.

Liver Assist is the new technology being used at Montreal’s CHUM and could make more donated livers available for transplant. (Aatefeh Padidar/CBC News)

He also says studies have shown the technology can help reduce complications, reoperations and hospital stay times for appropriate patients.

For Landry, doctors saw signs of a successful transplant almost immediately.

Hénault said Landry’s blood work the day after the operation was already better than expected for the type of transplant he received.

“I do believe that the machine really helped in this case,” Hénault said.

Landry’s recovery also appeared to be going unusually well.

“He was feeling way better than the average patient that gets a liver transplant,” Hénault said. “He did amazingly well.”

Looking forward to home

Landry is still recovering in Montreal and returns to the hospital for blood tests once or twice a week so doctors can adjust his medication.

Eventually, he hopes to return back east to Gaspésie and continue his recovery there. But after 15 years of illness, he's already thinking about what comes next.

“I’m in a hurry to see my family, my grandson, my friends and my horses,” he said.

Landry says he can't wait to go back home to his family and horses. (Submitted by Gérard Landry)

Landry also hopes his experience will encourage people to talk to their families about organ donation.

Even the most advanced technology cannot help, he said, if there are no donated organs available.

Because, as Landry put it, “if you have a horse without a rider, you don’t have a ride.”

World.title: She found an unidentified painting in storage. It turned out to be a female still-life master's work
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Hiding in plain sight, Clara Peeters painting discovered in a museum's storage: As It Happens 6:42 Hiding in plain sight: A lost masterpiece by an overlooked female artist discovered in a museum's storage

When art historian and curator Cynthia Osiecki stumbled upon an unattributed still-life painting in an Oslo museum storeroom in 2022, she couldn't shake the feeling that she knew exactly who created it.

"We were trying to buy a work by Clara Peeters, like many museums are trying to purchase women artists at the moment,” said Osiecki, who had been studying the work of the pioneering 17th-century Flemish Baroque artist.

When she spotted the painting, Osiecki wondered if it could be a long-lost work by Peeters.

“I mean, it’s almost too good to be true to have a Clara Peeters hanging right in your storage while the museum was actively looking for women artists on the art market,” Osiecki said. “Instead of having to purchase one, we might have had one all this time and right under our nose and didn’t even know it.”

Despite her groundbreaking work, the enigmatic artist remains relatively unknown to the wider public, a fate shared by many female artists of her time, Osiecki says.

That's part of the reason why the National Museum of Norway is putting a spotlight on historic female artists, with Woman Painter opening in Oslo on Oct. 8. The show will feature works by 19 female artists who worked across northern Europe and Italy between 1550 and 1650, including Judith Leyster, Lavinia Fontana, Artemisia Gentileschi, and, of course, Peeters.

Painstaking work to attribute painting

The piece Osiecki discovered, titled Still Life with Small Game and Grapes on a Gilded Tazza, had once been believed to be the work of Ambrosius Brueghel, a member of a famous family of artists in Antwerp, Belgium. It was later reclassified as "anonymous" and sent to storage.

Earlier this year, however, it was officially reattributed to Peeters, a painstaking journey spanning several years, Osiecki says.

A journey that wouldn't have begun if not for her keen eye.

When she first discovered painting, Osiecki found some telltale clues.

Another piece by Clara Peeters, created in 1621, called Still Life with fish, a candle, artichokes, crab and prawns that hangs in the Prado. (Museo del Prado)

Along with being one of the earliest specialists of still-life painting of her era, Peeters was known for embedding her own likeness into everyday objects in her works. She did this by painting tiny self-portraits in the shiny surfaces of pewter jugs, fruits or vegetables — subtly claiming ownership and asserting her own professional identity in a male-dominated world, Osiecki says.

The Oslo painting features nine dead birds — considered a delicacy in the 17th-century, Osiecki says — freshly-picked hazelnuts and apricots.

The grapes, in particular, stood out to Osiecki.

“In our grapes, there is a reflection of a person, but it’s not in any way as detailed as those silhouettes are on other paintings by [Peeters'] hand,” said Osiecki.

Then there were other details that caught her eye — the tazza, a saucer-like drinking vessel from the period that Peeters frequently featured in her paintings — as well as the distinctive positioning of the birds within the composition, Osiecki says.

WATCH | Why he’s scouring the art world for his great-great-grandfather’s lost paintings: Why he’s scouring the art world for his great-great-grandfather’s lost paintings | Duration 5:06 Jonathan Wener has spent half a century searching for his great-great-grandfather William Raphael’s lost artworks. The 19th-century Montreal artist made paintings depicting life in Quebec during that time, but Wener says his ancestor didn’t get the recognition he deserved.

“I also knew that many of her contemporaries were using the same objects in Antwerp [Belgium] at the time,” she said. “So I had to tread very, very carefully to make sure it really was Clara Peeters and not me wanting it to be Clara Peeters.”

There was also another hitch: woodworms had eaten away at the bottom edge of the painting where Peeters would have typically signed her name.

Despite this, Osiecki remained determined to ferret out the true artist behind the piece. She and her colleagues spent several years studying and comparing other works by Peeters and her contemporaries, she says. The museum's conservator cleaned the Oslo piece and took better pictures, she adds. Slowly, but steadily, the process confirmed the attribution: Peeters was the painter.

Now the painting is set to take centre stage at the Oct. 8 show.

Nora Ceciliedatter, director of collections and exhibitions and the National Museum of Norway, says the Woman Painter exhibition is part of a "broader effort to bring visibility to artistic careers and perspectives that have been historically underrepresented at the museum."

For Osiecki, the painting's long journey back to Peeters' name demonstrates how much work remains to be done to uncover female artists whose contributions have been overlooked, misattributed or simply forgotten.

“We have to continue doing this because there are so many paintings out there that are either anonymous or attributed to male artists,” she said. “The more research we do to women artists, the more works we find by them, and this is really time and effort well-spent.”

World.title: Toronto police officer in hospital after being shot during e-bike robbery investigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto police officer is injured after being shot during a robbery investigation early Thursday morning.

Officers responded to a robbery call for a stolen e-bike on Thursday morning, said Toronto police spokesperson Stephanie Miceli. She said police located a suspect near Bloor Street E. and Sherbourne Street around 3:21 a.m.

During the interaction, the suspect shot one of the officers, Miceli said.

The officer was taken to hospital with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries, she said. Toronto paramedics did not share any details and referred all responses to police instead.

The suspect has been arrested and a firearm was recovered at the scene, said Miceli. She said the investigation is ongoing.

World.content:
Article content

Was the nuclear chain of command back in the U.S. fully aware of the switch, and of the use of the old Air Force One as a decoy? Graff reminds us of a fresh outrage that got lost amid the unending chaos and the endless stream of nonsensical Trumpian verbiage last month: the president posted a message on his Truth Social site suggesting that he had given “orders” for Iran to be destroyed by “1000 missiles” in the event of his assassination. Whether or not such a “dead man’s switch” is a good idea strategically — and let’s face it: the person of the president is protected internationally by the implied threat of overwhelming retaliation — it is plainly illegal. Nuclear and other military command responsibilities would devolve upon the vice-president, along with the presidency itself, the moment the president was dead. Assuming, of course, anybody knew he was dead.
