Brazil is not fighting a war, but it faces the same trend. Criminal groups already use drones to smuggle and to scout, and the Army wants tested methods ready before it needs them.

The Two Ways to Stop a Drone

The exercise leaned on two broad approaches, often called kinetic and non-kinetic. Kinetic means physically hitting the drone, and non-kinetic means disabling it without a shot.

Kinetic answers included cannon fire and machine guns aimed straight at the aircraft. Non-kinetic answers meant jamming the radio signals that keep a drone under a pilot’s control.

The point of the drill was to make those two families work together. A jammer might cut a drone’s link, while a gun crew handles anything that keeps flying.

Jammers That Cut the Signal

Much of the non-kinetic work came down to breaking the invisible link between a drone and its operator. Cut that link, and many drones simply drift, land or fall.

Two jamming systems were named in the reporting: the SCE 0100, from the Brazilian firm IACIT, and the SCJ 2000M, from AICOX. Both are designed to scramble a drone’s control frequencies.

Soldiers also used frequency-interception rifles and signal-analysis towers. Together these let crews find a drone by its radio emissions before deciding how to bring it down.

Guns Still Have a Role

Jamming does not work on every drone, so the Army also fired live rounds. The kinetic side of the drill put older air-defense weapons to a new use.

Crews fired Gepard cannons and .50-caliber machine guns at aerial targets.

These are proven anti-aircraft tools now being pointed at a much smaller and nimbler kind of threat. The exercise also explored interception drones, meaning small aircraft flown to physically knock down a hostile one.

It is a fast-growing idea in counter-drone work worldwide.

Who Took Part

Sagitta Primus 2026 was a large undertaking rather than a small trial. More than 500 soldiers drawn from 23 Army organizations joined the exercise in Goiás.

The jammers were operated by the 1st Electronic Warfare Battalion, the 1º Batalhão de Guerra Eletrônica. Electronic warfare units specialize in the radio side of the fight.

The Brazilian Air Force also took part, contributing people and equipment. Air defense often crosses service lines, since the sky above a base belongs to no single branch.

Turning a Test Into Doctrine

The counter-drone portion was billed as the first doctrinal experiment of its kind in this exercise series. That framing matters more than it might sound.

The work was coordinated by the Army’s doctrine center, the Centro de Doutrina do Exército, through a dedicated anti-drone section. Doctrine is the written playbook that turns a good idea into standard practice.

By testing tactics under doctrine, the Army can learn what works and then teach it force-wide. A single successful drill becomes a method other units can follow.

Brazilian Industry on the Field

The exercise doubled as a shop window for Brazil’s defense industry. Companies brought equipment to demonstrate under realistic conditions rather than in a showroom.

Alongside the IACIT and AICOX jammers, firms showed off signal-identification and analysis towers and other counter-drone tools. A live drill lets buyers see how the gear performs.

For local makers, a slot at a flagship Army exercise is valuable. It signals that Brazilian-built systems can sit at the heart of the country’s air defense.

What Comes Next

Sagitta Primus 2026 was an experiment, not a finished system, and the Army framed it that way. The results will feed into how Brazil builds its counter-drone playbook.

The clearest takeaway is direction rather than a single headline weapon. The Army is treating cheap drones as a serious threat and layering jammers, guns and sensors to meet it.

For a force that spends most of its time far from open conflict, the drill is a bet on readiness. The aim is to have answers on the shelf before the problem arrives.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Sagitta Primus 2026?

It was a Brazilian Army air-defense exercise held at the Formosa training ground in Goiás in early August 2026. Coverage described it as the largest such drill in Latin America.

Where in Goiás did the test take place?

It was held at the Campo de Instrução de Formosa, a large Army training ground in Formosa, Goiás. The site is used for major live-fire air-defense exercises.

What anti-drone systems did the Army test?

Crews used radio jammers from IACIT and AICOX, frequency-interception rifles and signal-analysis towers. They also fired Gepard cannons and machine guns and explored interception drones.

Why is the Army focusing on drones now?

Cheap small drones have become a real threat to troops and equipment worldwide. Brazil wants tested ways to detect, jam and shoot them down before it needs them.

Sources: Agência Gov (Exército Brasileiro), Folha1, Aeroin, TecnoDefesa.

World.title: Lionel Messi Says He May Not Play Much Longer After Father’s Death
World.content:
Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi said Wednesday that he has “a lot of doubts” about whether he will continue playing football “for much longer,” in an emotional farewell letter to his father and agent, Jorge Messi, who died Friday at the age of 68. In his first public reaction since his father’s death, the 39-year-old star reflected on the final months of his father’s life, which were marked by the worsening cancer that ultimately killed him, according to media reports.



Jorge Messi’s declining health, after playing a central role throughout his son’s brilliant career, coincided with the 2026 World Cup in North America. Argentina lost the final 1-0 to Spain on July 19 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. “I don’t know what I’m going to do without you, I don’t know how to go on. All I ever did was play football, and now I have a lot of doubts about whether I’ll keep doing it for much longer,” Messi wrote in a letter posted on Instagram alongside photographs of himself with his father.

“You kept asking me to play in one last World Cup, and just days before it started was when you got much worse. It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament,” the Argentina captain added. “I kept telling you we were going to reach the final so you could travel.”

I Never Managed to Feel Right

The former FC Barcelona forward, whose contract with Inter Miami runs through 2028, said he wanted to win the World Cup so he could take the trophy to his father. But he acknowledged that he was unable to do so because his body failed him in the title match against a Spain side that overwhelmed Argentina.

“A huge hug to you and your family during these difficult moments, Leo. Stay strong,” Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi’s longtime rival in the debate over the world’s best player, replied to Wednesday’s post. Jorge Messi’s poor health, which became public during the World Cup, ended with his burial Sunday near Rosario.

In Argentina’s opening match against Algeria, Messi cried after scoring one of his three goals in a 3-0 victory. Afterward, he acknowledged that the unusual display of emotion was connected to his father’s condition. “Every time a match ended, I waited for and missed your message. That was when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn’t stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and so you could see one of the matches,” Messi wrote.

“We reached the final and you couldn’t be there. I wanted to win it so I could take it to you and show you another one. I couldn’t. My legs had nothing left. This time I tried to fight against my body, but I couldn’t. I never managed to feel right,” he added. After losing the final in his sixth and final World Cup, Messi returned to Argentina to visit his father. He realized that Jorge had been unable to follow much of the tournament. “When I arrived, you thought we had lost the final on penalties.

We couldn’t talk about anything that had happened. You weren’t able to enjoy any of it,” Messi wrote. “We weren’t champions, but you have no idea how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play in it,” he added.

Father, Friend and Agent

Messi, who has yet to define his international future, produced an exceptional World Cup at the end of a career that many believe has established him as the greatest footballer in history. With eight goals and performances reminiscent of his peak years, he was the driving force behind Argentina reaching a second consecutive World Cup final.



Jorge Messi is widely regarded as a fundamental figure in the career of the most decorated footballer in history. Demanding and critical of his son, but also his most constant source of support, he accompanied Lionel from the modest football fields of Rosario to the highest levels of the sport.

“You were always like that from the time I was little. You took me to every training session as soon as you got home from work,” Messi recalled. “You never missed a match. How much you suffered watching me and how much you enjoyed it, even though you never gave me many compliments.”

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner emphasized his father’s importance both on and off the field. “You were a father, a friend and an agent. You were always the person you needed to be at every moment, and you never got anything wrong,” he wrote. “Rest in peace and look after us from above the way you did here. Thank you for everything.”

Messi left Argentina for the United States on Tuesday night, according to local media. Neither he nor Inter Miami has said when he will return to competition.

World.title: Is Panama the New Costa Rica? A 2026 Expat & Real Estate Investor Comparison
World.content:
For decades, Costa Rica was the undisputed poster child of Central American expat life. However, a quiet reshuffling of priorities is underway, and a growing number of (Real Estate) investors, immigrations and retirees are now asking: Is Panama the new Costa Rica?

Fresh residency data, shifting visa requirements, and a surge in real estate acquisitions suggest the question is not just rhetorical. Panama’s streamlined immigration framework, its use of the US dollar, and a territorial tax system are redrawing the map for those seeking a second home in the tropics.

To understand the ground reality, we spoke with the team at Expat-Tations, a relocation advisory firm operating in both Panama and Costa Rica, along with their in-house law division who process residency applications daily in both countries. As well as their Real Estate division in Panama that handles property acquisitions, often to align legal residency. Their insights reveal a clear trend: more expats are crossing the border, and the numbers don’t lie.

Quick Takeaway

For investors and retirees seeking speed and a straightforward path to permanent residency, Panama is pulling ahead in 2026. Costa Rica retains its biodiversity and established expat communities, but its slower immigration processing and temporary-to-permanent residency ladder are pushing many toward Panama.

According to senior attorney, Ricardo Batres, at the law firm Expat-Tations in Panama:

“We’re seeing a 40% increase in inquiries from people who were originally targeting Costa Rica. They’ve done their research and realized Panama offers them a permanent solution in a fraction of the time.”

At a Glance: The 2026 Comparison

Feature Panama Costa Rica Permanent Residency Timeline 30–90 Days (Golden Investor Visa), 3–5 Years (Temporary to Permanent) on most programs with several complicated renewals Minimum Real Estate Investment $300k Gold Investor, $200k if Friendly Nations Residency $150,000 (Temporary residency only at first) Path to Citizenship 5 years 7 years (for most nationalities) Forced Social Security Payments Not required A requirement for residency with a monthly fee reaching often hundreds of dollars Residency Type Granted Direct Permanent in most cases (Golden Investor, Retiree) Temporary first, then Permanent Property Ownership Via corporation allowed Personal name only Currency US Dollar Costa Rican Colón Infrastructure Modern metro, fiber-optic, global airport Poor roads, power outages Cost of Living ~15% cheaper than San José Highest consumer prices in Central America Processing time of residency 3 to 6 months on all, except Golden Investor 45 days 1 to 3 years until you have a status

Residency Timelines: Speed vs. Patience

The sharpest contrast between the two neighbors lies in how quickly a foreigner can secure permanent status. According to the legal experts at Expat-Tations, this is the number one factor driving the shift toward Panama. In both countries the law sets a maximum timeline of 6 months, but Costa Rica hasn’t been able to keep that timeline ever, resulting in many cases the process taking up to 3 years.

Panama’s Qualified Investor Residency

In Panama, the Qualified Investor Visa, also called the Golden Visa, delivers permanent residency in as little as 30 to 90 days. A buyer who puts $300,000 into approved real estate walks away with permanent residency almost immediately, without any obligation to live in the country first.

The team at Expat-Tations notes that their Panama-based law firm have streamlined the process to near perfection. Applicants are often surprised at how efficient the system is compared to other countries in the region. Especially cause they also offer the required legal documents, like FBI background check with their digital fingerprint system.

Documents from Panama’s Ministry of Commerce and Industries confirm that real estate is the engine of this speed advantage. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the Qualified Investor program funneled $113.6 million into the economy. Nearly 87 percent of successful applicants chose property as their qualifying asset.

A government spokesperson familiar with immigration processing described the draw in blunt terms:

“Our Qualified Investor program is designed to provide certainty and speed. People don’t want to wait half a decade for a piece of paper when they’re ready to build a life.” [Translated from Spanish]

Costa Rica’s Inversionista Residency

Costa Rica’s main investor category, the Inversionista Residency, tells a different story. A $150,000 investment in real estate, stocks, or a productive project opens the door, but only to temporary residency at first. Holders must renew that status for three years before they can even apply for permanent residence. Many expats end up waiting five years or longer.

This is where Expat-Tations sees the most frustration among their clients. Relocation advisor and Real Estate Broker, Ismael Arcia shared: “People come to us thinking Costa Rica is the easy option. They don’t realize they’re signing up for years of renewals, paperwork, and uncertainty. In Panama, they can get the final stamp in a matter of months with the right property.”

Costa Rica’s migration authorities have been grappling with backlogs. Routine residency renewals can stretch for months, and the path from temporary to permanent status remains a bureaucratic marathon. That sluggishness, combined with a 2024 tax overhaul that began treating worldwide income often as taxable for residents, has pushed many long-time expats to explore alternatives just across the border.

Real Estate Investment: What Your Money Actually Buys

Cost-conscious buyers who compare the two markets often fixate on entry prices, yet the raw numbers rarely tell the whole story. The Expat-Tations real estate team emphasizes that buyers need to look beyond the dollar figure and understand what each investment actually secures.

Panama’s Real Estate Residency Pathway

Current minimum: $300,000 ( For Friendly Nations Residency only $200,000 )

**After October 2026 possible:** $500,000

The impending hike has lit a fire under the market. Agents and the Expat-Tations team report a frenzy of pre-qualification requests from buyers who want to lock in the lower threshold before it vanishes.

What $300,000 buys you in Panama: Direct permanent residency, no waiting period, and the freedom to live in the country immediately.

Costa Rica’s Real Estate Residency Pathway

Minimum: $150,000

Costa Rica’s $150,000 Inversionista line looks cheaper on paper, but it does not buy permanence. It buys a renewable temporary permit. The property must be registered in the applicant’s personal name, a restriction that can complicate estate planning and asset protection.

What $150,000 buys you in Costa Rica: Temporary residency with renewals for 3+ years, no guarantee of permanent status, and personal-name registration only. After 3 years of renewals another application for permanent residency follows.

Property Ownership and Corporate Structures

Property rights also differ in ways that surprise newcomers. In both countries, foreigners enjoy the same ownership rights as locals, with one major exception:

Panama: The constitution prohibits non-citizens from owning land within ten kilometers of any international border.

The constitution prohibits non-citizens from owning land within ten kilometers of any international border. Costa Rica: The Maritime Zone Law creates a similar coastal restriction, though the mechanics are different.

However, the Expat-Tations legal team highlights a critical advantage in Panama: the ability to hold real estate through a Panamanian corporation and trusts, as long as the visa applicant is listed as the Ultimate Beneficial Owner. That corporate wrapper provides layers of privacy and asset protection that Costa Rica’s more rigid personal-name requirement does not easily match.

“This is often a game-changer for serious investors,” explains a Panama-based real estate attorney Luis Mon, from the Expat-Tations Real Estate devision. “You can structure your assets efficiently, protect your privacy, and still qualify for residency. Costa Rica doesn’t offer that flexibility.”

The Currency Advantage for Real Estate Buyers

Another structural difference is currency. Panama uses the US dollar. Buyers who wire funds from North America or Europe sidestep the exchange-rate anxiety that can come with Costa Rica’s colón. In 2024 and 2025, the colón’s volatility against the dollar whipsawed household budgets and made long-term financial planning a headache for retirees and investors alike.

Dollarized pricing in Panama eliminates that variable entirely; a factor that Expat-Tations brokers cite as a decisive tiebreaker for their clients.

The ‘Is Panama the New Costa Rica?’ Debate Gains Momentum

Shift the lens from investment math to daily life, and the conversation only intensifies. Costa Rica still holds a powerful brand built on eco-tourism, biodiversity, and a “pura vida” identity that no competitor can replicate. But expats who have lived in both countries, and the advisors at Expat-Tations who guide them, point to infrastructure and processing gaps that can erode the idyllic image.

Infrastructure: Urban Edge vs. Rural Challenges

Panama City offers a modern metro system, high-speed fiber-optic network, and Tocumen International Airport as a global flight hub connecting to over 80 destinations.

offers a modern metro system, high-speed fiber-optic network, and Tocumen International Airport as a global flight hub connecting to over 80 destinations. Costa Rica’s road network, especially outside the Central Valley, remains notoriously unreliable, and power brownouts are a recurring feature of the rainy season in some regions.

Cost of Living: Panama is More Affordable

United Nations and regional bank data consistently rank Costa Rica as having the highest consumer prices in Central America. Utilities, gasoline, and imported goods carry steeper price tags there than in Panama, where the Panama Canal and the Colón Free Zone keep supply chains humming.

A 2025 cost-of-living survey by a global relocation firm placed Panama City roughly 15 percent cheaper than San José for a comparable expat lifestyle, a gap that widens considerably when housing is factored in.

Tourist Stays and Immigration Enforcement

Tourist stay limits and their observations, have tightened in both countries. Panama recently standardized to 90-180 days per visit for visa-exempt nationalities (including Americans, Canadians, and Brits) with a mandatory 30-day gap before re-entry now often enforced more strictly. Costa Rica similarly enforces a up to 180-day stay, though its exit-and-return practice has long been treated with a wink.

The difference is Panama’s clearly signaled intent to digitize and tighten enforcement while simultaneously speeding up residency approvals for those who commit to investment. The message is clear: short-term tourists are welcome, but people who want to stay should do so through formal channels, and those channels have been polished to work fast.

Junior Attorney and Legal Aid Edgar Landazuri at Expat-Tations sums it up: “Panama is saying, ‘If you’re serious about moving here, we have a fast lane for you.’ Costa Rica is still treating everyone the same, whether you’re a backpacker or a million-dollar investor. That’s starting to frustrate the high-net-worth crowd.”

Pensionado Perks: Residency Without Real Estate

Not everyone wants to buy property, and both countries recognize that.

Panama’s Pensionado Visa

Panama’s Pensionado Visa has carved out a reputation among retirees. Anyone with a lifetime pension of at least $1,000 per month can obtain permanent residency, no real estate purchase required.

The program’s signature draw is a booklet of legally mandated discounts:

25% off domestic and international airline tickets

domestic and international airline tickets 50% off movie tickets and hotel stays during the week

movie tickets and hotel stays during the week 25% off restaurant meals

restaurant meals 15–20% off medical services and hospital bills

According to the Expat-Tations legal team, this visa is processed in approximately 3 to 6 months, significantly faster than Costa Rica’s equivalent.

Costa Rica’s Pensionado Regime

Costa Rica’s pensionado regime also requires a $1,000 monthly pension and offers similar discounts on health care, transportation, and entertainment. However, the scope and depth of Panama’s menu of perks is widely seen as more generous and better enforced.

Critically, Costa Rica’s pensionado process still involves a temporary-to-permanent ladder that can take years. Applicants receive temporary residency first, with no guarantee of permanent status down the line and the need of several renewals.

Processing Speed for Retirees

A digital overhaul at Panama’s immigration authority has shortened approval windows and reduced the number of in-person appointments required. Applicants routinely report that the entire procedure, from initial application to the issuance of a cedula (national ID), can be completed in three to six months.

Costa Rica’s understaffed migration offices have struggled to match that pace. Expat-Tations advisors regularly field complaints about delayed appointments, lost paperwork, and unclear timelines.

What the Data Shows

The cumulative effect of faster residency processing, real estate flexibility, dollarized stability, no social security payments and modern infrastructure is no longer a well-kept secret. Property transactions in Panama’s beach communities and mountain towns have climbed steadily through 2025 and into 2026, fueled partly by Costa Rican expats who are shedding their residency and buying anew.

The legal team at Expat-Tations has witnessed this firsthand. One partner commented: “Three years ago, 70% of our inquiries were about Costa Rica. Today, that number has flipped. People are doing the math on time and realizing Panama gives them more certainty, while Costa Rica gives them a waiting game.”

Not everyone will be convinced to leave behind Costa Rica’s cloud forests and conservation ethos, but the question itself is telling. When even loyalists begin asking “Is Panama the new Costa Rica?” , does that mean “The axis of Central American expat life has already begun to tilt?”

World.title: Costa Rica Free-Zone Growth Slows to Weakest Pace Since 2020
World.content:
Growth in Costa Rica’s free-zone economy slowed sharply in June, falling to its weakest pace since 2020 and extending a year-long deceleration in one of the country’s most important economic sectors. Economic activity among companies operating under Costa Rica’s special regimes, which include most free-zone companies, grew 2.9% in June compared with the same month a year earlier, according to the latest Monthly Economic Activity Index, or IMAE, from the Central Bank of Costa Rica.

That was down from 17.2% annual growth in June 2025 and marked the 12th consecutive month in which the sector’s growth rate slowed. The Central Bank attributed much of the slowdown to weaker growth among manufacturers, particularly medical-device producers, as well as lower output of metal products such as electronic components and circuit boards. Professional and administrative services, including advertising, also lost momentum.

Free-zone manufacturing grew just 1.2% year over year in June. Manufacturing outside the special regime performed even worse, contracting 0.9%. The numbers matter because Costa Rica has built much of its recent export and foreign-investment success around free-zone companies, particularly medical-device manufacturers, technology firms and business-service operations.

The latest data do not show that Costa Rica’s free-zone model is collapsing or that companies are leaving the country in large numbers. Much of the slowdown follows an unusually strong period of expansion in 2025. Earlier this year, the Central Bank warned that the pace of growth in the special regime could continue moderating because it was being compared with exceptionally strong results from the previous year.

Still, the speed of the slowdown is notable. Overall economic activity in Costa Rica grew 3% in June, 2.2 percentage points less than in June 2025. Businesses operating outside the special regimes grew 3.1%, meaning the domestic economy slightly outperformed the free-zone sector during the month.

That represents a significant reversal from much of the past several years, when free-zone companies were among the main engines pulling national growth higher. The softer free-zone performance has already affected the broader economic outlook. In April, the Central Bank projected that Costa Rica’s economy would grow 3.5% in 2026, down from an earlier forecast of 3.8%.

At the time, it projected 5.5% growth for the special-regime economy, compared with preliminary growth of 12.7% in 2025. Researchers at the University of Costa Rica were somewhat more cautious in June, forecasting overall economic growth of 3.4% this year and growth of about 4% in the special regime.

They identified slower free-zone activity as one of the main reasons for the weaker national outlook.Not every part of Costa Rica’s economy slowed in June. Construction expanded 9.5%, helped by private projects and a 12.2% increase in public works. The Central Bank pointed to road and bridge projects, emergency reconstruction work and improvements at Juan Santamaría International Airport as contributors to the increase.

Services grew 3.9%, while commerce expanded 2.7%. Hotels and restaurants were among the service activities that grew faster than a year earlier. Agriculture barely grew, at 0.1%, as stronger banana, root-crop, beef and egg production was offset by declines in pineapple and coffee.



For Costa Rica, the question over the coming months will be whether the slowdown in free zones settles at a more normal growth rate after the exceptional gains of 2025 or develops into a broader competitiveness problem. The June numbers alone do not answer that question. They do, however, show that the part of Costa Rica’s economy that has delivered some of its strongest growth in recent years is no longer expanding at anything close to the pace seen a year ago.

World.title: Costa Rica Looks to Ukraine for Drone Technology in Security Fight
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Costa Rican President Laura Fernández exchanged invitations for official visits during a phone call yesterday, as the two leaders also discussed possible security cooperation involving Ukraine’s experience with drone technology. Zelensky invited Fernández to visit Ukraine, while the Costa Rican president invited Zelensky to Costa Rica, according to Ukraine’s presidential office and reports on the conversation.



Zelensky used the call to thank Costa Rica for its support for Ukraine in international forums, including votes on United Nations General Assembly resolutions concerning the war with Russia. He also highlighted Costa Rica’s backing for efforts to return Ukrainian children taken to Russia and initiatives aimed at holding Russia accountable for the war.

Ukraine said it had recovered 2,368 children as of early July. For Costa Rica, however, one of the most significant parts of the conversation centered on security. In a video of the call released by the Costa Rican government, Fernández said Costa Rica has a strong interest in learning from Ukraine’s experience with drone-based defense technology.

She linked that interest to her government’s efforts to modernize Costa Rica’s security capabilities as the country confronts drug trafficking and transnational organized crime. Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading developers and users of drone technology during its war with Russia, using unmanned aircraft for surveillance, reconnaissance, communications and battlefield operations.

Zelensky said Costa Rica had expressed specific interest in Ukraine’s security experience. The two presidents agreed that their teams would continue discussions and explore a possible format for a future meeting. No date or location for such a meeting was announced.

The exchange of invitations does not necessarily mean either presidential visit is being actively planned. Invitations between heads of state are common diplomatic gestures, and neither government has announced a timetable, itinerary or formal preparations for a visit. A trip by Fernández to Ukraine would also involve substantial security and logistical considerations because of the ongoing war.

Costa Rica has not indicated that preparations for such a visit are underway. A Zelensky visit to Costa Rica would avoid those complications, but there is similarly no indication that a trip to San José is imminent. For now, the more concrete outcome of yesterday’s conversation appears to be the possibility of technical cooperation on security.

That could move forward through government ministries, security officials and technical teams without requiring either president to travel. For Costa Rica, Ukraine’s rapidly developed expertise with drones could be particularly relevant for surveillance of borders, coastlines and areas used by organized crime and drug trafficking networks.

The conversation also adds a new dimension to relations between Costa Rica and Ukraine. San José has consistently supported Ukraine diplomatically since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, while the Fernández government is now exploring whether that relationship can produce practical security cooperation at home.

World.title: Latin American Qualifiers Face Double-Duty Day at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin America’s Cincinnati Open contingent faces a high-pressure Wednesday after severe weather disrupted the opening day of qualifying, leaving several players from the region with unfinished business and the possibility of playing twice in one day. Four Latin American players entered Wednesday still in contention for spots in the main draw: Argentina’s Marco Trungelliti and Nadia Podoroska, along with Colombians Nicolás Mejía and Emiliana Arango.

The most intriguing possibility comes on the women’s side. Arango and Podoroska were placed in neighboring sections of the qualifying draw, and both had first-round matches carried into Wednesday. If both advance, they are scheduled to face each other later in the day for a place in the Cincinnati main draw.

Arango, the No. 10 qualifying seed, faces Aliaksandra Sasnovich, while former French Open semifinalist Podoroska takes on No. 16 seed Ella Seidel of Germany. The winners are scheduled to meet no earlier than 4 p.m. Wednesday. That creates a straightforward scenario for Latin American tennis: victories by both would guarantee either Colombia or Argentina another representative when main-draw play begins Thursday.

The men’s qualifying picture offers its own storyline. Trungelliti survived one of Tuesday’s tightest completed matches, rallying past Austria’s Sebastian Ofner 4-6, 6-4, 7-6(4). The 36-year-old Argentine now gets one of the biggest names in qualifying, former world No. 4 Kei Nishikori, with a main-draw place at stake.

Nishikori had his own difficult opening round, defeating Argentina’s Francisco Comesaña 6-4, 1-6, 7-5. Their meeting with Trungelliti gives Argentina another chance to prevent the Japanese veteran from reaching the main draw. Colombia’s Mejía has an even longer potential Wednesday ahead of him.

His first-round match against Britain’s Jacob Fearnley was pushed onto the Wednesday schedule. The winner is then scheduled to return after suitable rest to face either American Marcos Giron or Portugal’s Henrique Rocha for a place in the main draw. The compressed schedule is a direct consequence of Tuesday’s weather.

Severe storms delayed qualifying at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, where 48 men’s and 48 women’s qualifying matches had originally been scheduled across the two-day preliminary event. Twelve qualifiers from each draw will advance into the 96-player main draws. Several Latin American players have already been eliminated. Brazil’s Gustavo Heide fell 6-3, 6-4 to top qualifying seed Luca Van Assche, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien lost 6-3, 6-1 to Sho Shimabukuro. Comesaña’s narrow loss to Nishikori also ended his attempt to qualify.

On the women’s side, Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa and Argentina’s Solana Sierra were eliminated in the first qualifying round. Zarazúa, the No. 2 seed, lost to China’s Yue Yuan, while Japan’s Aoi Ito defeated sixth-seeded Sierra. Regardless of Wednesday’s qualifying results, Latin America already has several players waiting in the main draw. Brazil’s João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo are among the men entered directly, while Colombia’s Camila Osorio opens against American Taylor Townsend.

The Osorio-Townsend winner would move on to face No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina. Main-draw play begins Thursday at the Cincinnati Open, one of the final major hard-court events before the U.S. Open.

World.title: Fonseca and Cerúndolo Drawn Into the Same Cincinnati Quarter
World.content:
The 2026 Cincinnati Open draws were released Tuesday, and Latin America’s two most prominent men landed in the same crowded section of the bracket. Brazil’s João Fonseca, seeded 23rd, and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, seeded 20th, were both placed in the third quarter headed by American Taylor Fritz, a section that also contains 2019 champion Daniil Medvedev, 2021 runner-up Andrey Rublev, Norway’s Casper Ruud, American Brandon Nakashima, Belgian Zizou Bergs and wildcard Marin Čilić, who won the tournament in 2016.

The two cannot meet before the quarterfinals. Both will have to survive a section stacked with former Masters 1000 winners to get there. The draw arrives under unusual circumstances. World Nos. 1 and 2 Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, who won the last two men’s titles at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, are both absent, Sinner with a knee injury and Alcaraz with a wrist injury.

Their withdrawals leave the men’s field without the two players who have decided nearly every major hard-court event of the past two seasons. Alexander Zverev, the 2021 champion, acknowledged the shift in an assessment of the field, noting Sinner’s record streak of 34 consecutive Masters 1000 match victories and six titles this year.

“I think it does change things a little bit, especially with Jannik not being here,” Zverev said. “But for me, it doesn’t change much. I still want to compete against the best.” Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo, seeded 22nd, drew a different assignment. He was placed in Zverev’s quarter alongside Flavio Cobolli, the rising Spaniard Rafael Jodar, American Tommy Paul, Valentin Vacherot of Monaco, Belgian Alexander Blockx, Hubert Hurkacz and Denis Shapovalov.

Peru’s Ignacio Buse, seeded 29th at 21 years old, sits in the bottom quarter. That section is headed by second seed Félix Auger-Aliassime and includes Ben Shelton, Lorenzo Musetti, Americans Learner Tien and Frances Tiafoe, France’s Ugo Humbert and Arthur Rinderknech, Stefanos Tsitsipas and 2017 champion Grigor Dimitrov.

Argentina’s Tomás Martín Etcheverry is seeded 26th. All 32 seeds receive a bye into the second round. Argentina again brought the region’s largest delegation, with eight men across the seeded and unseeded ranks. One of them has already made an impression on this swing.

Thiago Agustín Tirante beat Fritz in the Round of 64 in Montreal, an upset that cost the American the tournament he entered as a favorite and that now shadows the quarter Fritz heads in Ohio. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio is the region’s only player in the main draw. She opens against American Taylor Townsend, with the winner advancing to face world No. 2 Elena Rybakina.

It is an unforgiving path for a player who has spent the season rebuilding her ranking, though Townsend is beatable and the reward for an upset would be the highest-profile match of Osorio’s summer. Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia, listed on early entry publications, will not appear.

The former world No. 10 announced last week that she will not play again on tour this year and intends to return in 2027 using a protected ranking, after a season that produced a 4-19 record and eight consecutive losses. Four Latin American women entered qualifying instead. Argentina’s Solana Sierra went out Tuesday evening to Japan’s Aoi Ito, 6-1, 6-1, leaving Colombia’s Emiliana Arango, Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska and Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa to chase the twelve main-draw places on offer.



In the men’s qualifying, 36-year-old Argentine Marco Trungelliti came through his opener against Sebastian Ofner in three sets, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien and Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía were still in action late Tuesday. Main-draw play begins Thursday and runs through Aug. 23, the last significant test before the US Open. For a region sending fourteen players to Ohio, the answers about form and readiness will come quickly.

World.title: Help delivered, but…
World.content:
Tents, provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management, erected in the area of Coopers Pen, Trelawny, where 20 houses were demolished on Tuesday. (Photo: Horace Hines)

COOPER’S PEN, Trelawny — Even as the Government mobilised multi-agency help for about 40 families whose houses were demolished a day earlier, a group of irate residents of Cooper’s Pen in Trelawny staged a peaceful protest Wednesday, demanding more. The residents said they want to be relocated, after their houses were allegedly demolished by the owner of land some of them have occupied for decades.

The protesters insisted that the Government, or the landowner, must provide them with alternative accommodation. They said the temporary tents provided by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), in which some of them spent Tuesday night, are not enough.

“We get tent last night, so we can lay a head for the night. What about today? What is going to happen? We want to know where we are going to relocate to. What is going to happen to the people them that their house push down?” asked demonstrator Jessica Haye.

In a Wednesday afternoon release, while emphasising that the demolition arose from a long-standing private matter, and that the Government of Jamaica was not a party to the underlying private dispute, the Office of the Prime Minister (OPM) said a number of State agencies had been deployed “to address the immediate humanitarian and social welfare needs of affected families”. The Ministry of Labour and Social Security, ODPEM, Child Protection and Family Services Agency, Poor Relief Department within the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, and the Social Development Commission are among agencies involved. OPM said teams worked well past midnight, Tuesday, to help those who lost their homes.

“Assistance provided included food supplies, bottled water, toiletries, temporary shelter supplies, tents and lighting equipment. As part of the emergency response, ODPEM mobilised and transported relief supplies directly to affected families, including 40 family-size tents, cots, foam pads, solar lights, care packages, cases of bottled water and sanitary products. The Ministry of Labour will return on Friday, August 14, to provide additional support,” said OPM.

But while grateful for the help, residents said they expect more, and they laid out their demands during Wednesday’s protest.

“There is no way you can demolish a house like this, and no notification. No notification. We need justice,” said Haye, who stressed that many of them had not yet recovered from the devastation caused by last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“We are not going to stop this [protest] until the prime minister [Dr Andrew Holness] hear. We naw stop. We go come out here day by day because we want justice. It must be a relocation!” she insisted.

Another demonstrator, Sylvia Fisher, said while they understood that the residents could not remain on privately owned property indefinitely, they should have been given notice and assistance to relocate.

“You can’t run in pon people so. And run pon people goods… and then now put you under tent! You have pickney to go back to school. It cannot work,” she said.

She said she has lived in the community for 32 years, while her father lived there for more than 50.

Fisher is adamant that the government has a responsibility to assist affected residents whom, she said, voted them into office.

“The government need to come see this cause a we the people make the government, and is we the people put politicians in power, and a we the people have power. So they must consider poor people. A no rich man, a poor people put them in a power,” she argued.

“We know we have to go, but please relocate we, relocate we. We live pon the land 20, 30, 40 years you just come pitch we off so. No! Find somewhere and put we. The private man who them say claims to own the land, him fi find somewhere and put we. A him come mash we up,” Fisher alleged.

Even as those who have lost their homes agitate, there are fears that the wrecking crew will return. Among the worried is 69-year-old Stanley Hill, who said he has lived on the property for 51 years.

He said a marker has been placed at the doorway of the small concrete house he has occupied for decades, indicating that it is earmarked for demolition.

“Now to the age a me now, me soon 70, me a 69-year-old. And me live there from me a little boy. Where me going go now as an old man? Me can’t make house again,” said Hill.

“I need somebody to talk to me so me know where me stand. Because me can’t come sleep under tree. And me don’t have no money. Me don’t have no bank account,” he added.

The OPM has given a commitment to keep an eye on what is happening in the community and “coordinate additional interventions”. It said it is aware that those affected include senior citizens such as Hill, children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable individuals.

Said the media release issued Wednesday: “The Poor Relief Department of the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, along with the Social Development Commission, will undertake further assessments of affected residents and households. Assistance will be provided through the applicable government programmes and support frameworks. Furthermore, the Ministry of Local Government has indicated that drop-in shelters will be available to meet the needs of residents.

“The Government of Jamaica’s response is being coordinated across the relevant social protection, disaster management, child protection, local government and community development agencies, with the immediate priority being to ensure that vulnerable residents have access to essential assistance while individual and household circumstances are properly assessed.”

World.title: ‘My soul is hurting’
World.content:
A screen grab of Opposition spokesperson on Youth and Human Rights Isat Buchanan making a plea for children found with firearms to have greater access to diversion. He was speaking during a sitting of the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act on Wednesday at Gordon House.

APPEALING not just as a legislator, but also from his own experience with past convictions, Opposition Spokesperson on Youth and Human Rights Isat Buchanan has urged the Joint Select Committee reviewing the Child Diversion Act to make simple possession of a firearm or ammunition an offence that can be referred to child diversion, rather than leaving it solely to a judge’s discretion under Section 37 of the Act.

He argued that children caught in possession should be given a chance to avoid a lifelong criminal record.

But the proposal drew resistance from committee chairman Delroy Chuck and other members, who warned that making simple firearm possession a scheduled diversion offence could remove judicial discretion and allow criminals to exploit children as gun carriers, knowing they could be sent to diversion if caught.

The emotional exchange unfolded on Wednesday as the committee continued reviewing the matrices and submissions on the Child Diversion Act, 2018.

During the sitting, Buchanan repeatedly pressed his colleagues to consider what may have happened before a firearm ended up in a child’s hands.

“We are well aware that there are adults who are using children, even children below the age of criminal responsibility, to lock firearms, let’s call it that, and to carry. So if we are going to be in the business of being able to pull these children and divert them from this deviant behaviour, possession simpliciter has to be a space that we can divert them and put them in programmes. If we leave it to the discretion under section 37 in that contemplation, I’m afraid that there will be children who won’t be able to benefit,” he said.

Possession simpliciter, in this debate, means the simple fact of being found in possession of a firearm or ammunition, without necessarily alleging that the child used the weapon in another offence.

Buchanan wants that form of possession added to the First Schedule of the Child Diversion Act, which sets out offences that qualify as diversion offences. His argument is not that children should automatically be diverted in every firearm case. Rather, he wants firearm or ammunition possession placed among the offences that can be dealt with through the diversion framework, instead of relying solely on the separate discretion currently available to judges.

That distinction became the heart of the disagreement.

Section 37(2)of the Act already gives a court a route to diversion even when an offence is not listed in the First Schedule, providing that a court may make a child diversion referral order for any other offence where it is in the interest of justice.

This formed the basis of Chuck’s opposition to Buchanan’s plea.

He argued that this existing discretion is important because it allows the court to examine why the child had the gun, how the child came into possession of it, and whether the child was being used by someone else before deciding whether diversion is appropriate.

“The child may well, deliberately want to control a gun. A 16-year-old may well, deliberately want to control a gun, and having been found with the gun, he says, ‘put me on child diversion’, or automatically it has to go to child diversion, and my answer is that may not be an appropriate case for child diversion,” he argued.

He also warned that criminals could exploit diversion by using children as gun carriers, knowing they might avoid conviction.

However, Buchanan maintained that the possibility of coercion is precisely why simple possession should be included. His argument became increasingly personal as the discussion continued.

“At 47, chairman, I am still dealing with the past of convictions that have nothing to do with firearms. If you want this version of a Jamaican child to be better than me, if at all, if there’s any good in me, and you see, chairman, I’ve interfaced with you many times…all I’m asking is to empower the Jamaica Constabulary Force to drape up a boy, take the gun from him and let the don realise that you can’t buy enough guns that we can’t confiscate,” he said.

Buchanan was himself convicted in Jamaica in 1997, when he was 17, of possession of cocaine, dealing in cocaine and taking steps to export cocaine. He served 21 days in prison and paid a fine. In 2000, he was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to import cocaine and was sentenced to 10 years in prison, serving about eight and a half years. The Jamaican conviction was later expunged from his police record in 2014. The General Legal Council subsequently approved his application to practise law after considering his convictions, rehabilitation and character references.

Using his circumstance as an example, Buchanan reiterated that the purpose of child diversion was to give children another chance, not simply to punish them for behaviour that may have been shaped by their environment.

He eventually yielded the floor, visibly frustrated by the resistance to his proposal.

“If the Parliament doesn’t want to, or this committee doesn’t want to agree with me and we don’t want to put it to a vote and we don’t want to be brave enough to protect our children.. I will yield, chairman, but I’m hurt by this. I must tell you my soul is hurting,” he said.

Buchanan’s proposal did not face opposition only from Government members.

Opposition Senator Donna Scott Mottley said she had long had concerns about aspects of the Firearms Act but was uncomfortable supporting the change without evidence showing how children charged with firearm possession are currently being treated in the courts.

“I do agree that there should be some guidance to the judiciary. Whether or not it should be a part of the schedule is what concerns me. Because our discussion does disclose that the judges have discretion. And I wonder if it is not more that the judges should be aware of the policy of the administration as it pertains to children rather than for us to have it in the schedule,” she said.

She also warned that the proposal required more analysis, particularly because of the possibility that it could be abused by people with influence.

State minister in the ministry of National Security and Peace Juliet Cuthbert Flynn was more firmly opposed to including firearm possession in the Child Diversion Act’s First Schedule.

“We do have a gun problem in Jamaica, and so with this proliferation of guns, and, you know, just our culture, I think a standard has to be set. And these children, they might be young, but I think they all know right from wrong,” she said.

By the end of the exchange, the committee had not reached a consensus on Buchanan’s proposal.

Chuck suggested that the committee could record itself as divided rather than take a formal vote, while maintaining that the existing Section 37 mechanism could still protect children in appropriate firearm cases.

World.title: Masicka declares career longevity with new album Forever Reign
World.content:
Masicka.

For Masicka, staying power has never been something to take for granted.

The dancehall star has spent years carving out his own space in a genre in which competition is fierce and staying relevant can be just as difficult as breaking through.

From the hunger of his early years to international stages, major collaborations, and a record deal with Def Jam Recordings, the journey has taken him further than he once could have imagined.

Now, as he prepares to release his third studio album, Forever Reign, on August 14, Masicka appears increasingly interested not just in how far he can go, but in how long he can stay.

The 17-track project finds the artiste reflecting on many of the experiences that have shaped him — faith, survival, ambition, loyalty, success, and the sacrifices that often remain hidden behind the glamour of an artiste’s rise.

Even the title is deliberate.

“Forever Reign means I’m here to stay. Yes, there’s room for everyone, but my lane is carved out, and we’re going to soak up the space,” Masicka said. “The most important thing is to stay humble and focused.”

That balance between ambition and humility runs throughout the album.

Masicka has never been shy about his desire to reach the highest levels of dancehall, but Forever Reign suggests that the journey has also given him a greater appreciation for the things that cannot be measured by streams, charts, or sold-out venues.

That is evident from the album’s opening track, 1 Psalm, featuring Damian “Jr Gong” Marley.

Rather than opening with a declaration of dominance, Masicka begins with prayer.

The collaboration sets a reflective tone as the two Jamaican voices come together on a record centred on faith, protection, forgiveness, and perseverance.

For Masicka, the message is simple.

“One prayer a day, if we can pray and ask God to forgive us for our sins and protect us, then we’re good,” he said.

From there, Forever Reign moves through the different sides of the artiste’s personality and experiences.

Tracks including Oak Tree, Pointless, Shakazulu, Spend, Good, Slip and Slide, Boasty, Cross the Waters, Wicked Spell, It’s Not Too Late, AK Fire, Time and Palace, Breaking Chains, and Parables exploring the album’s varying moods, with collaborations with Nigerian rapper Blaqbonez, KraffGad, and reggae singer Lila Iké.

One of the more personal collaborations comes on Honor Roll, where Masicka links with KraffGad. The younger artiste’s hunger reminds Masicka of an earlier version of himself — the young lyricist trying to establish his name.

“His style is different, and he reminds me of myself when I was coming up and hungry,” Masicka said. “All of the young youths are ‘bad’, and I respect anybody brave enough to embark on this journey. I never had any doubt he was going to shell down this record.”

It is perhaps one of the clearest signs of Masicka’s own evolution, helping to push his music to an even wider international audience.

Just one day after the album drops, Masicka will headline a major performance at Barclays Center in Brooklyn, New York, on Saturday, August 15.

It is the kind of back-to-back moment that makes the title Forever Reign feel less like a boast and more like a statement of intent.

But if the journey so far has taught him anything, it is that longevity is built project after project.

World.title: Teachers yearn for end to wage negotiations before new school year
World.content:
Mark Malabver, president of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association

JAMAICA Teachers’ Association (JTA) President Mark Malabver said Wednesday that it was unfortunate that another school year is just around the corner and long-standing issues with educators’ wages have not been settled.

Malabver said teachers were looking forward to receiving official documentation from the Government Friday, indicating a favourable revision of their wage package.

“I know that a number of teachers are unhappy with respect to salaries and conditions of service. Where we are now is that we went to negotiations [Tuesday] with the Ministry of Finance. They have placed an offer on the table. We are expecting that the offer will be formalised in writing and we can take it to our members [to vote on]. What I can say is that there has been some improvement,” Malabver told the Jamaica Observer.

He said the needle shifted during Tuesday’s meeting with respect to one particular item of concern among teachers, but suggested that there are concerns about another important item.

“We have asked the ministry to have another look at that, and hopefully they can update or upgrade their offer in that department so that we can formally put it to our members next week. The teachers would like to see the end of negotiations,” he said.

“They are anxious, but we continue to maintain that our teachers must be paid a salary in keeping with their value and their work,” he pointed out.

The JTA president expressed that if the members say, “Continue to negotiate”, the association will do exactly that.

“That is exactly where we will have to go if they are dissatisfied with the offer. And if they say ‘accept’, we are duty-bound to formally accept the offer. We are going to put it clearly in the hands of the delegates, and they will ultimately be the ones to make the decision.”

In the meantime, Malabver said that based on pronouncements coming out of the Ministry of Education and from conversations with school administrators in western Jamaica, many schools will not be ready in time for the new school year which starts in September.

“The physical schools will not be ready to accommodate students for classes, and for me, that is unfortunate. I certainly believe that there was ample time to get the schools up and running in time,” he said.

“I think firm deadlines should have certainly been given, and the necessary oversight mechanisms that were absent should have been in place to ensure that repairs were effected in time for the new school year. That has created a sort of balloon effect, because whilst a lot of work is going on in that side of the island, the other side of the island needs to get some focus as well.”

At the same time, he has given some credit to the Ministry of Education for “taking steps to alleviate the funding crisis in some of our schools”.

“A number of schools will get some relief. The primary schools will get some amount of relief. Our special needs institutions will also get a bump up in terms of funding for these institutions. At the high school level, there still is a lot to be desired.

“I would like for the Government and the Ministry of Education to get to a point where we can truly fund our institutions,” he said.

And for parents anxious and struggling, Malabver advised them to use their resources wisely. “I just want to caution parents not to go and spend money buying up all of the books all at once. They should engage the respective schools, they should engage the respective teachers, to make a determination as to which school books are critical, which supplemental books they should purchase versus which ones they don’t have to purchase at this time. Because we understand [the issues with] finances,” he said.

World.title: ‘THAT EXTRA 5%’
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen star player Andre Russell acknowledges the crowd after scoring a half-century in their Caribbean Premier League T20 match against Barbados Tridents at Sabina Park on Tuesday night. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA Kingsmen captain Ravman Powell says his team must find “that extra five or 10 per cent” as they look to bounce back and secure a first win in the 2026 Caribbean Premier League (CPL) when they host the Guyana Amazon Warriors on Thursday at Sabina Park at 7:00 pm.

The Kingsmen are still searching for their first points of the season after two tight losses, including a five-run defeat to the Barbados Tridents on Tuesday.

Sent in to bat, the Barbados Tridents made 206-3 from their allotted 20 overs thanks to a dominant top-order display. The Jamaica Kingsmen fought back from the brink but came up just short, ending on 201-9 off 20 overs.

“Obviously, we are still searching for our first win. We have some time to sit down, get our plans right, guys recover, and come on Thursday and see if we can give a better account of ourselves,” Powell said in a post-match interview.

“I think as a bowling group we kind of struggle to string proper overs together. And, you know, 206 is a lot of runs on the board but having said that, I think we have fought well,” Powell added.

Powell identified the team’s biggest issue.

“But another thing that we didn’t do well is that we keep on losing wickets in clusters. The statistics say if we keep on losing wickets in clusters, majority of the times you will come up on the defeating end of the games.

“I think it’s just for us to give that extra five or 10 per cent, that it is what it comes down to. And it is for us as a group to stay together,” he said.

Brandon King led the way for the Tridents with a fluent 73 from 50 balls, hitting five fours and four sixes. He anchored two big partnerships — 72 with Quinton de Kock who made 42 from 25, and then 93 with Sherfane Rutherford.

Rutherford finished the innings in style, unbeaten on 50 from 28 balls with four fours and three sixes, ensuring the Tridents crossed the 200-mark.

The Tridents started fast at 33-0 after 2 overs, lost Zachery Carter for 27, but never really slowed down after that.

For the Jamaica Kingsmen, the bowling was shared around. Jediah Blades, Hunain Shah, and Andre Russell all picked up a wicket apiece, but they struggled to contain King and Rutherford in the back end.

The chase for the Kingsmen collapsed early at 8-3 after just nine balls being bowled jwith Daniel Sams removing Reeza Hendricks (2) and Kirk McKenzie Jr (0) and Tridents captain Chris Greem removing Shayan Jahangir (0) cheaply.

Powell and Keacy Carty rebuilt with a 50-run fourth wicket stand. Powell hit four sixes in his 38 from 24 balls before Gudakesh Motie broke the partnership in the eighth over at 58-4. It became 60-5 when Hassan Khan fell to Green without scoring from two deliveries.

The momentum shifted when Russell came in. He and Carty put on 72 for the sixth wicket to take Kingsmen to 132 in the 14th. Carty was then bowled by Sams for 45 from 27 balls — one four, four sixes.

With the game looking done, Russell and Vitel Lawes staged a stunning comeback. They added 69 runs and brought the equation down to six needed off three balls at 201-7. That’s when it unraveled. Russell fell for a blazing 68 from 38 balls to Ramon Simmonds, Lawes was run out at the non-striker’s end next ball, and Shah failed to connect from the last ball of the innings.

Despite the 0-2 start, the Kingsmen captain is keeping the mood positive in the camp.

“We have two tight games. You know two games that could have gone either way. We could have been 2-0 up. Having said that, I think it left a good taste in the fans mount and I think they will come out and support us for the rest of the games,” Powell said.

He also praised the conditions at home, giving credit to the groundsmen for producing good batting surfaces.

“I think oftentimes as cricketers, we give the groundsmen a hard time in the Caribbean, but credit have to be given to them tonight. They provided a very good surface, an entertaining surface and you know fans come out to watch sixes, fours, and sort of things and I think tonight the wicket conducive to proper cricket, hence we got a very good game,” Powell said.

World.title: Classic French Chocolate Mousse
World.content:
Classic French Chocolate Mousse (Photo: Alan Smith)

Light, silky and intensely chocolatey, the third dish, this classic French chocolate mousse from Mia Hair Artistry principal Shanice Gore is far easier to master than its elegant name might suggest.

“This is a recipe I learned from my French teacher’s father, Sam, who is from France,” Gore shares. “He taught it to us as a treasured family recipe, and it has stayed with me ever since. In fact, it might just be the only thing I remember learning in French class!”

Ingredients

• 200g butter

• 200g good-quality semi-sweet chocolate

• 8 large eggs, yolks and whites separated

• 200g sugar

For serving

• ½ cup cold heavy cream

• 2 teaspoons sugar

• Chocolate shavings

Method

1. Melt the chocolate in a heatproof bowl over a bain-marie, making sure the bottom of the bowl does not touch the simmering water.

2. Once the chocolate has melted, add the butter and sugar, stirring until smooth and fully incorporated.

3. Allow the chocolate mixture to cool slightly. Add the egg yolks two at a time, stirring well after each addition until completely incorporated.

4. In a separate, clean bowl, beat the egg whites until they form stiff peaks.

5. Gently fold the beaten egg whites into the chocolate mixture in batches. Take care not to overmix, as you want to keep the mousse light and airy.

6. Divide the mousse among six individual glasses. Cover and refrigerate until completely set, preferably for at least 24 hours.

To serve

A few hours before serving, prepare the whipped cream. Place the cold heavy cream in a bowl and whip until it begins to thicken. Add the sugar and continue whipping until medium peaks form.

Top each chocolate mousse with a dollop of whipped cream and finish with chocolate shavings.

Kitchen Note: The key to a light chocolate mousse is gently folding in the egg whites without deflating them. And if you can wait the full 24 hours, the mousse develops an even richer, more luxurious texture.

Happy indulging from my kitchen!

Photos: Alan Smith

World.title: US$25-m yacht bet
World.content:
Jamaican American businessman Denton Douglas is confident that within three years a boatbuilding plant he is establishing in Jamaica will be an international success.Photo: Karl Mclarty

JAMAICAN American businessman Denton Douglas is embarking on an ambitious plan to take his boatbuilding business to Jamaica and is prepared to spend US$25 million, initially, to make it a success.

Douglas, who operates Monarch Yachts — a Florida-headquartered company which began operations in China and now operates two plants in Turkey — is pushing to open a yacht-building and repair facility in Jamaica and is confident that within three years it will become profitable while employing scores of Jamaicans.

“I want Jamaica to be a manufacturing hub. Over the years we have been mainly on primary goods; we export bananas, we export ore, but we never make something. We import our cars. We import everything else. I want to move Jamaica from that primary [producer] to a manufacturing hub, and I think we have the know-how. For sure we have the skills, and we have the logistics to do it,” Douglas told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

“We make luxury yachts, commercial boats like fishing boats. We also have ferries… for shuttling people… and our biggest business now are military boats, which is surprisingly patrol boats. We have a line of patrol boats and we have a contract for a country in Africa to do 20 to 40 small ferries… and about 10 patrol boats… We want to do that here because those are easy to build,” added Douglas, who wants to start operating locally before the end of this year.

The Munro College graduate, who received a track scholarship to study at Howard University in the United States in 1988, worked on Wall Street for years before moving into the boating business some 20 years ago.

“When I was in China we were price-competitive, [but] my idea was this: Anyone can come cheaper than you are; they can cut more corners and be cheaper. So I changed my business to quality, meaning… no one in the world can make a better yacht,” declared Denton, who now designs and builds yachts for some of the world’s super-rich.

He said Monarch’s services, which include yacht design, construction, brokerage, charters, and refits/repairs, can all be done in Jamaica, which would be convenient for many of the company’s clients.

“I want to come here and build yachts. Why? First, to be selfish. I fly 12 hours every time to Turkey and Italy to the shipyard, or 21 hours to China. An hour and a half [from Miami to Jamaica] is a lot better than flying so long,” said Douglas.

He pointed out that a customer in the US can jump on a plane in the morning, view his yacht in production in Jamaica and be back in the US the same day, something that cannot happen where he now operates in Turkey.

In addition, it will be much cheaper to build a yacht in Jamaica and ship it to the US.

“For example, my 45-footer, to take it from Turkey to the United States, it’s US$50,000. If I build that same boat here, I’m saving that much money. To take that boat from China is another US$25,000, so that’s US$75,000,” said Douglas as he pointed to the practicality of operating on the island.

According to Douglas, he is now in talks with local authorities to identify a site to set up shop, and while he would love it to be based in St Elizabeth, where he is from, for practical reasons the main shipyard will be in the eastern end of the island — either the Corporate Area, St Catherine, or Portland.

“We need access to skilled labour and access to a port. The key thing is an airport, so if an American businessman comes to Jamaica, comes to see his boat, [he can] fly in [to Jamaica in] the morning, see his yacht, and fly back. So we need somewhere that’s close to an airport where you have access to skilled labour,” said Douglas.

He added that, while his shop will be in one location, the operation could be islandwide as Monarch will operate differently from the American yacht companies which manufacture everything in a single plant.

“I want to adopt the European model, where the shipyard may be in Kingston, but the woodwork could be in St Elizabeth. The piping could be somewhere else, so the wealth and the labour skills are spread throughout Jamaica. So everyone benefits, not just one area,” declared Douglas.

He told the Observer that the plan is not just to build boats, but to establish an ecosystem that will include carpenters, welders, seamstresses, and others who will contribute to all aspects of the production of the yachts.

Douglas said he has already made contact with the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) which are helping with his application for a special economic zone (SEZ) designation, while Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) has already indicated its readiness to help with the training of workers.

“What I would do first is take a bunch of Jamaicans to China and Turkey and teach them on-the-job how it works. Then, once they get a basic understanding of whether it’s aluminium welding, steel welding for marine, or fibreglass, or epoxy work, then they will come back and start working.

“And so it will be maybe 15 to 20 foreign nationals and the rest Jamaicans. If it’s 100 Jamaicans, it will be 10 foreign nationals. It’s more of a teaching model, not a working model,” said Douglas.

“It’s just once we get the right people who can learn and are extremely meticulous, then we’ll be successful. The goal is never to have a lot of foreigners working at the shipyard. It’s always to have them teach us at the shipyard. That is the only way I’m going to do it. If I was going to have a lot of foreigners, I might as well stay where I am in Turkey,” Douglas explained.

He said Monarch will be prepared to pay the tuition for Jamaicans to study at CMU and work for the company for a period under a bonded arrangement.

“But I expect many of them to move on to companies in Germany and Italy because they will be able to pay them more. One of the highest-paid engineers on a yacht now is Jamaica[n],” said Douglas.

World.title: Rewarding resilience
World.content:
From left: Executive director at Sandals Foundation Heidi Clarke; consultant paediatrician at Falmouth Public General Hospital Dr Kerry-Ann McKenzie; Minister of Tourism Edmund Bartlett; and director of operations at Sandals Foundation Karen Zacca engage in conversation during Tuesday’s launch of Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica 2026 at AC Hotel Kingston. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

CONSULTANT paediatrician at Falmouth Public General Hospital Dr Kerry-Ann McKenzie was visibly moved, Tuesday, as she welcomed the Sandals Foundation’s annual Island Challenge, which will raise £100,000 to replace paediatric and neonatal equipment destroyed by Hurricane Melissa.

Operating out of Trelawny, a parish still recovering from last October’s devastation, McKenzie shared that even after the hospital replaced its roof, the paediatric unit’s Accident and Emergency Department looked forlorn, with only one bed to spare.

“We were pretty much very badly affected by Hurricane Melissa, and our paediatric unit was destroyed. We lost everything; every incubator, every monitor, every bed except one, our departments, where we fight every single day for the lives of our smallest, and our future leaders of our country were devastated,” said McKenzie, her voice trembling slightly.

She was extending her thanks to the Sandals Foundation during the launch of the annual Island Challenge at the AC Hotel Kingston.

Beginning October 2, the four-day expedition will take 30 athletes from the United Kingdom and 15 Jamaican participants across Trelawny, St Ann, St Mary, and St Andrew, where they will trek, hike, and paddle around the island to raise funds for paediatric equipment at Falmouth Public General Hospital.

McKenzie told the launch that doctors and nurses have been resilient in the face of disaster, showing up daily despite not having the equipment to provide comprehensive care. She noted that she was happily anticipating the addition of the medical instruments.

“Jamaicans are resilient. We are a resilient people, and we’re a resilient health facility. With the help of Sandals Foundation, we are going to show forth brighter than what we were previously.

“But resilience can’t buy an incubator. It can’t replace a cardiac monitor. It cannot give us back the beds that we lost. That’s why we’ve joined the Sandals Foundation now in this Island Challenge in getting us the essential equipment that we need for our paediatric and neonatal units at the Falmouth Public General Hospital,” she said.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer, McKenzie explained that the paediatric unit was badly in need of beds, incubators, resuscitators, and monitoring equipment such as pulse oximeters, vital signs monitors, as well as phototherapy lights, warming blankets, and cooling blankets.

“We’ve struggled, but we have been able to keep the department afloat despite the lack of resources. We’re really looking forward to getting the extra help that we need to do what we need to do. We’ve had to do a lot of transfers out because we just don’t have the capacity to keep as many children as we want. But there are scenarios where we can’t get babies out and we’ve really had to take our hand and make fashion. It’s been an exhausting journey, but this is the beginning of a new one, so I’m so excited,” she said.

The head paediatrician also extended her gratitude to athletes participating in the event, telling the launch that their contribution to the hospital’s recovery was invaluable.

“To every runner, every hiker, every donor, every partner standing with us today, on behalf of every child that will pass through the doors of Falmouth Public General Hospital, and every family who will sit beside them holding their hands, we say thank you. You’re not just raising funds. You’re giving our children a lifeline, a fighting chance. You’re rewarding our resilience. And it will go a long way in making sure that we’re able to offer the care that they need,” she said.

Delivering her remarks, executive director at Sandals Foundation Heidi Clarke spoke of the event’s importance. She said the past three challenges raised £300,000 across Antigua & Barbuda in 2023, Saint Vincent & the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025 collectively, benefiting about 1,800 babies.

“I’m very excited to see this finally come home to Jamaica, and as our road to recovery continues here in Jamaica, we know it all too well and [so do] the dedicated teams at the hospitals. It has been a difficult and long road, but with many partners, we’ve been able to work together to make things come to life. We have to recognise, more than ever, the strength of our health care systems are what matter and make communities stronger. Everybody in this room today helps to make events like this possible. And we could not be more grateful,” she said.

Meanwhile, Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett told the launch that the testimonial from McKenzie very nearly moved him to tears, hailing the event as a well-needed lifesaving mechanism.

“The passion that drives the Island Challenge, for example, is a powerful one. Because it’s not just one of physical fitness, discipline, dexterity, agility, and ability to use GPS (global positioning system) to navigate through and find your places. It’s not just about that only. It’s about why you do it…

“In the end, you will say, ‘I’m not here for me. I’m here because of others.’ And so what the foundation is doing is demonstrating practically that we are here for others. And tourism connects others,” said Bartlett.

World.title: Scorching summer will cost France €10B to €15B, environment minister estimates
World.content:
The initial figures are based on an extrapolation of costs compiled by France’s official statistics agency.

PARIS — France’s historically hot summer will end up costing the country €10 billion to €15 billion — the equivalent of as much as 0.5 percent of French gross domestic product — according to an estimate shared by Minister for Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

Barbut said the preliminary estimate, which she advised treating “with great caution,” was based on an extrapolation of heat-related costs compiled by France’s official statistics agency, Insee, in past years. She added that the figure could rise as temperatures remain well above seasonal averages in many French regions. Eighty-five percent of the country was also under drought warnings as of mid-July.

Barbut said recent wildfires and drops in agricultural output were the biggest estimated costs and warned they would continue to grow in the future if governments fail to implement policies to limit the impacts of climate change.

World.title: Privacy watchdog warns of ‘serious risks’ over EU police agency surveillance
World.content:
The exterior of the Europol headquarters in The Hague is pictured on March 28, 2026. | Jasper Jacobs/BELGA/AFP via Getty Images

Changes would allow Europol to hold data on vast numbers of people with no links to criminality, data watchdog says.

A plan to ramp up the data processing powers of the EU’s policing agency Europol poses “serious risks” to people’s privacy, Europe’s data protection supervisor warned Thursday.

The European Commission in June unveiled a plan to make Europol the central system for police forces to trade and analyse data using the latest technologies — part of a wider strategy to give EU justice agencies more firepower to tackle cross-border crime and terrorism.

The reforms include a fundamental shift in how Europol sifts through the data it collects, relaxing current rules that require data to be sorted into different categories before determining if Europol can legally use it. That’s been a “key operational bottleneck,” the Commission has said, since Europol deals with high volumes of unstructured data.

World.title: ‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Putin enrages Japan with trip to disputed island
World.content:
