Tech.title: Here’s Why Creative’s New XF1 PC Speakers Hit the Sweet Spot for Me
Tech.content:
The Creative XF1 in white. / Creative Creative XF1 Desktop Speakers 8.4 $180 at Creative Pros & Cons Compact, elegant design

Impressive sound for the size and price, with ample bass and good clarity

Detachable cork stands

Good wired and wireless connectivity

Can add subwoofer for more bass

Volume control on front They look nice but don't feel that premium

No HDMI eArc or optical input

Creative is known for its value PC speakers, including its popular orb-shaped Pebble speakers, which start at $20. In recent years, the company has dabbled in more premium models, such as the $280 Pebble Nova, which sits at the top of our best PC speakers list. Its new XF1 desktop powered speaker set is a slightly different animal in that it has a subdued, straightforward boxy design and a more midrange price of $180. But it still follows the same value formula, delivering very good sound for the price along with pretty robust connectivity options.

Creative XF1 design and connectivity

Measuring 7.5 inches tall, 6.1 inches deep and 3.9 inches wide, the speakers are fairly compact and won’t take up too much room on a desk. Available in matte black or white finishes, the XF1s have an appealing, understated, elegant design that gives off a mini-studio-speaker vibe and lends them a bit of seriousness. Each speaker has a 3-inch woofer and a 3/4-inch tweeter, and the drivers are fully exposed, as the speakers have no grilles. They sit on detachable cork stands that tilt the speakers upward at a 15-degree angle.

The speakers are pretty compact and don’t take up too much room on a desk. Creative

With a rated continuous power output of 72 watts and a frequency range of 55 hertz to 40 kilohertz, the XF1s require an external power adapter. They are wired together with a detachable speaker interconnect cable. There’s a volume knob on the front-right speaker (you hold it down to enter Bluetooth pairing mode), and around back, you’ll find a 3.5-millimeter line-in, a USB-C port and a dedicated subwoofer output, so a subwoofer can be added to produce bigger sound with more bass. Bluetooth 6.0 is on board for wireless streaming, whether that’s from your phone, tablet or PC. I connected an iPhone 16 Pro and Google Pixel 9 to the speakers, but for most of my testing, I used a HyperX Omen gaming desktop.

While the speakers have some decent heft to them (the left speaker weighs 2.8 pounds, the right is 3 pounds), they just don’t look or feel as premium as some more expensive models, including the Audioengine A2 that cost about $100 more (the newer Audioengine HD3 cost around $360) and even pricer KEF speakers like the LSX II LT that retail for well over $500. I’d put these somewhere between Edifier’s similarly styled M60 ($170) and M90 speakers ($300), with Edifier’s recently introduced MR4.5 near-field studio monitors ($250) also being a close competitor. The M90 is a larger speaker that’s also equipped with an optical input and a TV-friendly HDMI eArc port (you don’t get either with the XF1s) to go along with Bluetooth 6.0, and it comes with a remote. But it costs significantly more than the XF1.

The connectivity options on the back. David Carnoy/CNET

Creative XF1 sound quality

My initial impression out of the box (without jumping into the EQ settings) was that the speakers were slightly bass-forward, but were quite pleasant overall, with good detail and a nice warmth and natural quality to the sound. The speakers are intended for near-field listening — and they sound best when you sit about 3 to 5 feet away, with them angled slightly toward your ears — although they can fill a small room with sound if you crank the volume up to around 80%. They would be pretty ideal for a dorm room or home office.

You’re not going to get the deep, harder-hitting bass you’d get from larger speakers or from adding a separate subwoofer, and they lack a bit of refinement and clarity compared to more expensive powered speakers. However, the speakers do produce a fairly rich, full sound with decent depth, and they maintain a good tonal balance with minimal distortion, even at higher volumes. Their sound quality exceeded my expectations for the price.

The default music EQ setting is a bit V-shaped. Screenshot by DavidCarnoy/CNET

Creative says the XF1 carries “dual hi-res audio certification,” supporting playback up to 40kHz over USB audio and analog line-in, as well as wireless hi-res audio over LDAC with Bluetooth 6.0 (many Android devices support LDAC streaming, while Apple devices use the AAC audio codec). The sound quality improves slightly with a wired connection, but these aren’t high-end speakers, so it won’t make a huge difference.

Previous Creative speakers I’ve tested linked up with Creative’s Acoustic Engine software to customize the sound, but the XF1 supports Creative’s new Nexus app, which offers a 10-band parametric EQ along with more than 120 EQ presets. It’s a bit plain-looking, but it’s well-designed and offers robust fine-tuning options that are easy to understand and dial in. The default music profile has a bit of a V-shaped curve, which is not surprising given my initial listening experience. But Creative says the EQ presets cover over 20 types of music and close to 100 games, so there are plenty of sound customization options to choose from. The app is available for Windows, MacOS, Android and iOS.

Creative XF1 final thoughts

I’ve reviewed more affordable speakers from Creative, like the $90 Pebble X, which also comes in a version with a subwoofer that gets high marks for its $120 price, and I’ve been pretty happy with the sound quality. The XF1 gets you a nice boost in sound quality from the Pebble X, and while the step-up Pebble Nova delivers bigger bass, the XF1’s tonal balance and treble performance measure up well to the Nova’s and may even be slightly better, particularly after tweaking the EQ settings to your liking with the Nexus app.

Due to their compact size, the speakers have some sonic limitations, and yes, adding a subwoofer would help. However, their small size, combined with the sound they can produce, is what I found quite appealing about them. They deliver good bang for the buck and are a fine option for someone looking for an entry-level audiophile desktop speaker with some power.

Tech.title: Best Apple Siri Voice Commands for Your Home: A Complete Guide
Tech.content:
These Siri commands will save you time and much more. Chris Monroe/CNET

As more advanced Siri AI features start rolling out and Apple preps to release new smart home devices, it’s never been a better time to try Siri out in your home, but where should you begin? Whether you’ve got a HomePod, the Apple Home app on your phone or a similar option, I’ve got the “Hey Siri” voice commands everyone needs.

From my years of testing Apple devices at home, here are my favorite Siri orders and why they work so well. Think about adding a few to your list, too. And as Siri AI continues to expand into new areas, I’ll keep this list updated with the latest, most useful options so you’ll always know where to go.

Smart home Siri commands

Siri is quick at controlling common smart home devices. Tyler Lizenby/CNET

I use the Apple Home for everything from Ikea security sensors and smart locks to kitchen lights and bedroom lamps. Connecting a device to Apple’s home platform also means you can use your phone or a speaker like the HomePod mini to take control of it with Siri, no matter where you are. Try out useful commands like these:

“Hey Siri, turn on the heater” lets you control common smart appliances from afar.

“Hey Siri, turn off the kitchen lights” allows you to target a room for specific controls, as long as you’ve correctly labeled your smart lights in Apple Home (something I encourage). You can create as many rooms as you need, including offices, bedrooms, upstairs areas and whatever other label you need.

“Hey Siri, set the playroom smart lights to blue” gives you the option to adjust shades, and you can use similar commands for brightness, etc. Just make sure the lights have those capabilities in Apple Home.

“Hey Siri, turn the thermostat down by two degrees” gives you control over a smart thermostat, no matter where you are.

Pro tip: If you ever find one of these commands stops working, check for firmware updates and reboot both the brand’s own app, Apple Home and your phone or other device. You may need to reboot your Wi-Fi router, too.

Home security Siri commands

Aqara’s mini system is great for watching over small spaces and is Apple-compatible. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

If you have a compatible security device, you can also give Siri orders to control it or learn more about how it’s functioning. This is a field that’s currently seeing quick growth as Apple is expanding Siri AI’s capabilities to more security cameras and similar devices, letting you use commands like these:

“Hey Siri, unlock the front door” is useful if you have a connected smart lock. Some of my favorite smart locks have excellent Apple compatibility, so this is a great place to begin using Siri around the home. If you don’t have autolocking, you can use Siri to lock the door on demand, too.

“Hey Siri, arm the security system.” Commands like these are handy if you’re heading out the door and want to arm quickly to save time.

“Hey Siri, show me the backyard camera” can display a live view in Apple Home, as long as your camera is supported.

“Hey Siri, show me the front door camera on Apple TV.” With the right Apple TV and Home compatibility, Siri can also show a camera feed on your TV screen if something goes bump in the night.

“Hey Siri, did the driveway camera see any deliveries today?” is an option rolling out with Siri AI, which is adding the ability to analyze home security videos via Apple Home. I’m still not sure how it’s going to work yet, but in a couple of months I’ll be able to try out this new tech, so it’s certainly worth noting for future use. If you’d like to see how those features work on other platforms, check out my reviews of the Blink and Google Nest cams, which have similar features.

Scheduling with Siri commands

Siri also makes scheduling a snap. Chris Wedel/CNET

Not every order you give Siri has to be immediate. Just like setting reminders for the future, you can also tell Siri to schedule upcoming home changes to help you prepare for your day. Here’s what works:

“Hey Siri, lock the front door at 7 p.m.” lets you make sure the door will be locked before bedtime, keeping it open for now.

“Hey Siri, turn on the outdoor porch light at sunset” works because Siri is smart enough to know when sunset and sunrise are, opening up a variety of scheduling options.

“Hey Siri, turn off the home fan in 3 hours” works if any connected device you only want turned on for a certain period.

Siri home status commands

Thermostats like Ecobee’s work with Siri and Apple. Ecobee

Not sure what’s going on with your smart home? Just ask Siri. These commands shine when you have smart versions of traditional home devices that you can update as you decide what you want to do.

“Hey Siri, are the lights in the living room off?” and similar commands can give you updates about the status of smart devices without needing to check.

“Hey Siri, did I close the garage door?” With the right garage cam or smart controller, Siri can also answer questions about doors, even if you’re far away from home.

“Hey Siri, what temperature is the kid’s room?” can work if you have a standalone temperature sensor or a smart thermostat in a specific room. Nest, Ecobee and other smart thermostat brands offer satellite sensors for this purpose.

Location commands for Siri

You can ask Siri about locations if you use Family Share. Jeff Carlson/CNET

It’s not technically part of the smart home, but location requests are closely related, and a highly useful addition for keeping your family safe. These commands utilize data in the Find My app, so you’ll see the iPhones, AirPods, AirTags and other devices your family uses correctly labeled and identified with the right people in Find My before you begin. You must also turn on Family Sharing settings for everyone using this feature, and for some devices like AirTags, the user must share them with you in Find My.

“Hey Siri, where is [family member name]” will show you the location of whoever you name, as long as Family Sharing is on and they are labeled correctly in Find My.

“Hey Siri, where is [name’s] backpack?” works well if you put an AirTag in a bag, handy for students or busy workers. You could use this for pet collars too, but we recommend choosing a different tracker than the swallowable AirTags for pets.

Siri scenes and routines

Scenes work with smart locks and more. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

If you’re ready to take Siri commands to the next level, Apple Home also allows you to create scenes, or routines that combine multiple devices and commands into one. They can be a real timesaver if you set them up properly, allowing you to use commands like these.

“Hey Siri, I’m home” can start a routine that turns on lights, fans, music and even adjusts lamps to a certain shade while disarming the security system.

“Hey Siri, good morning” can begin a scene that turns on lights, stops nighttime fans, plays a wake-up song, bumps up the temperature and even turns on devices like a coffee maker connected to a smart plug.

“Hey Siri, I’m off to work” can arm security systems and sensors, lock the door, lower the thermostat to save money and close smart blinds to help keep the house cool while everyone is away, among other tricks.

If you’re interested in adding more Apple functionality to your home, head over to my guide on the best home security cameras that work with Apple, too.

Tech.title: Could a Shirt Fool Facial Recognition? The Answer Is Complicated
Tech.content:
A camera and its software labeled Bill Swearingen as a person. Then it suddenly wasn’t sure — all because of some weird pattern that he held up to disguise himself.

I watched it happen from my seat at annual hacker convention Defcon. Swearingen, a longtime cybersecurity professional and founder of the Kansas City security community SecKC, stood onstage in front of a live camera feed as a person-detection system analyzed him. On the giant screen behind him, the software’s confidence score cleared 0.75, the threshold it needed to declare that, yes, there was a human being in the frame.

Then Swearingen raised a flat panel covered in a bizarre black-and-white pattern. The score started falling. It slipped below the threshold, eventually landing at 0.21.

“No person detected,” the screen announced in bright green letters.

It felt like a low-budget magic trick. Swearingen was still standing there, plainly visible to everyone in the room. The software was still receiving the camera image, but it no longer detected a person above the configured confidence threshold.

Swearingen has spent the past year searching for patterns that can confuse the computer-vision systems used to identify people. His project is called noRecognition, and its end goal is to create clothing that makes the wearer harder for AI surveillance systems to detect. It’s a fascinating project, but it’s still a work in progress.

The camera wasn’t trying to identify him

We tend to call this kind of technology “facial recognition,” but surveillance systems can involve several separate layers of AI-based detection.

A person detector asks whether a human body is in the frame. A face detector finds and isolates a face. Facial recognition then compares that face with a database and asks whether it knows who the person is.

Person detection, face detection and facial recognition perform different jobs, though each step can depend on the one before it.

The demonstration I saw targeted the first step. The system didn’t mistake Swearingen for somebody else or decide the room was empty. It simply stopped reporting a person detection above the threshold set for the demonstration.

If you break the first link, the rest of the surveillance chain may never get started. If a camera fails to detect a person, it may never crop out that person’s face, send it to an identity database, then track them across a series of images.

An AI detector doesn’t “see” a person in the way we do. It generates thousands of guesses about what might be in an image, assigns a score to them and discards anything that fails to clear a chosen confidence threshold.

Swearingen was still there. The detector’s math just wasn’t sure he was a person.

How the patterns are made

Swearingen didn’t sit down and draw the patterns himself. He built a program to create them.

Security researchers normally use programs called fuzzers to bombard software with strange inputs in an attempt to break it. Swearingen’s fuzzer does something similar with computer vision. It creates a pattern, digitally places it on an image of a computer-generated person and then shows the altered image to several AI models.

If a pattern causes a major change, like making the person’s detection box disappear or sharply lowering the model’s confidence score, then the fuzzer flags it for more testing.

The most successful designs are altered and combined to produce new patterns, much like selectively breeding specific traits in animals. Swearingen’s software repeats that process automatically, allowing it to work through far more possibilities than a person could design and test by hand.

He currently tests each pattern against 11 models: five that detect people, four that find faces and two that try to recognize whose face it is. In many cases, he tested a public model that works similarly to proprietary systems, not the actual software being used by companies in the wild. Most are publicly available models that researchers can run themselves.

Swearingen said the project had run 31.7 million tests as of June. About 534,600 triggered one of his system’s anomaly rules. That could mean a detector found fewer people or faces than it did in the original image, invented extra ones, produced a much lower confidence score or returned the wrong identity. It doesn’t mean he found 534,600 patterns that could hide someone from a camera.

Swearingen’s custom fuzzer automatically generates patterns, tests them against computer-vision models and flags designs that produce unusual results.

Of those results, 85 met the project’s definition of “extreme,” which means the pattern defeated at least one person detector and at least one face detector in the same test.

The tests also showed that covering more of the body isn’t always more effective. Torso patterns had the greatest effect on person detectors, while patterns closer to the head mattered more to systems looking for faces. In one comparison, Swearingen said a small collar pattern worked better than a much larger print across the torso.

Even the winning patterns can lose

Some of Swearingen’s results looked promising until he tested the designs on different people.

One pattern lowered the detector’s confidence for all four people whose images were used while it was being developed. But when Swearingen applied that same design to images of eight new people, it didn’t work once.

Swearingen used computer-generated people wearing different garments and accessories to test where adversarial patterns might work best.

Counted together, the pattern had worked on four of 12 people. Swearingen withdrew the resulting 33% performance claim because every success involved people whose images had been used to develop the pattern. It hadn’t worked on anyone new.

Another pattern, designed to fool a different detector, worked on all eight new people. That contrast shows how much the results can change between detectors — what works with one person or detection model may fail with another.

Even a successful pattern may have a short shelf life. A camera company could retrain its software to recognize it. Swearingen compared the patterns to software “zero-days” vulnerabilities — they take advantage of a weakness that may disappear once the system is updated.

The shirt doesn’t exist yet, and the tech isn’t field-tested

On one of Swearingen’s slides, in large type, were the words “Still unproven: The worn garment.”

During the demo, Swearingen held the pattern in front of his body on a rigid panel. It wasn’t printed on clothing, which would be a much harder test. Ink on a flat board stays exactly where the software expects it to be. Fabric drapes, folds and stretches. Sunlight, shadows, wrinkles, viewing angles and distance all change what reaches the camera.

Swearingen said most of his 31.7 million tests were digital, with patterns pasted onto images and scored by computer-vision models. The panel demonstration was a limited physical test using a model he said came from a fielded Flock Safety unit. Until a pattern works while printed on fabric, worn by a moving person and viewed through deployed hardware, he isn’t claiming that the clothing itself works.

In a noRecognition digital test, the detector reported the plain-shirt image as a person with 86% confidence but produced no person detection after the pattern was added.

The noRecognition website is promoting a Kickstarter-backed run of T-shirts, hoodies and neckwear, with each pattern scored against 11 models before it ships. Swearingen said the money would help pay for test fabrics, a dye-sublimation printer and additional cameras so he can see whether the patterns still work once they’re printed and worn.

So could a pattern on your clothing fool facial recognition?

Maybe. But the real test begins when he prints it on clothing and steps back in front of the camera.

Tech.title: Apple Faces Lawsuit Over iCloud Private Relay Vulnerability
Tech.content:
The revelation that Apple’s iCloud Private Relay feature hasn’t been as secure as Apple says has spawned a lawsuit against the iPhone maker.

Last week, a blog post by Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk exposed a vulnerability in how iCloud Private Relay, in some circumstances, doesn’t shield a customer’s IP address, which is the entire purpose of the feature. Even when it’s enabled, their information can be exposed when using a passkey to sign in or when a website uses two methods (DNS prefetching and WebTransport) to load data faster.

In a complaint filed by Clarkson Law Firm on Aug. 6, plaintiff Edward Rickman says he subscribed to iCloud Plus believing that iCloud Private Relay would hide his IP address and Safari browsing activity.

“Instead, Apple delivered a system that recreates through its own credential service the precise harm Apple told the world it had made impossible,” reads the complaint, which seeks class action status.

The lawsuit also seeks an injunction against Apple requiring it to change its business practices to mitigate the risk of consumer deception, as well as monetary relief and attorneys’ fees.

An Apple representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Craig Federighi, Apple’s senior vice president of software engineering, describes new privacy features at an Apple event. James Martin/CNET

A core component of the lawsuit is that iCloud Private Relay is a paid service of iCloud Plus, which costs between 99 cents and $60 per month. The feature is available only if you’re subscribed to iCloud Plus, not the basic iCloud service.

Also key is the fact that Apple has advertised for years that iCloud Private Relay is a safe way to browse the web and avoid the types of tracking that services such as Facebook use to connect people’s browsing habits and assemble profiles on them that can be monetized.

“Apple built its entire brand on the promise that it would protect its users’ privacy when no other company would,” Tim Giordano, a partner at Clarkson Law Firm, said in a statement. “For Apple’s iCloud users to now learn that for years they were paying Apple a premium for a protection that simply didn’t work, exposing them to the very tracking, profiling and targeting Apple warned them about, is an outrageous violation and betrayal of consumer trust and law.”

Clarkson recently won a $250 million settlement from Apple over the company’s marketing of AI features for the iPhone 16 Pro that were never delivered.

The researchers who discovered the flaw set up a website that lets anyone check whether iCloud Private Relay is protecting their IP address. They say they released the information publicly rather than first alerting Apple because of the company’s lengthy review process.

The information in the red box was the IP number of my home router. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

In an email to CNET, Mysk wrote, “If we had a better experience with the Apple Security Bounty program that would make us feel confident the issue would be addressed promptly for the benefit of iCloud Private Relay users as well as Psylo users, we would have reported this iCloud Private Relay issue to Apple without having to release a Psylo update addressing the issue, and as a result having to disclose it to our users.” Psylo is the developers’ privacy-focused web browsing app.
